width.typical: Apply multiple estimation strategies to rational number problems: benchmark fractions, 10%-building for percentages, compatible numbers for decimals; select the most efficient strategy for a given problem; estimate financial calculations (e.g. approximate total after percentage discount).
wider: Compare front-end, rounding, and benchmark strategies on the same set of problems and evaluate which produces closer estimates
Investigate contexts where estimation is the expected output (e.g. reading graphs, navigating, budgeting) and distinguish from contexts requiring exact answers

modes.reason: Estimation fluency comes from having multiple strategies available and recognising which applies. Students need to accumulate a repertoire — not just know one estimation method — to handle the diversity of rational number problems they will encounter.

nodes.label: Approximation in financial and real-world contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and apply appropriate estimation strategies to approximate solutions to problems involving rational numbers and percentages in financial and practical contexts.
criteria: Student selects an appropriate estimation strategy for a financial context problem and explains why it suits the situation.
Student communicates an approximate solution with an appropriate level of precision for the context.

width.minimum: Solve at least two estimation problems in financial contexts (e.g. approximate total cost, approximate discount amount, approximate share of an expense) using an appropriate strategy; interpret the approximation in context.
width.typical: Apply estimation to financial contexts including percentage discounts, unit pricing, GST approximation, budget estimates; identify when an approximation is sufficient for the decision being made; communicate the estimate and its precision level.
wider: Investigate a real financial context (e.g. planning a class event on a given budget) using estimation as the primary tool for decision-making
Explore how financial approximation is used in professional contexts — journalists reporting figures, builders quoting costs, shoppers comparing prices — and discuss the expected precision in each

modes.reason: Financial estimation integrates rounding skills, benchmark strategies, and contextual judgment. Students must coordinate these while also interpreting the result in terms of the situation — the integration of these is the defining challenge of this node.

descriptors.title: Model with rational numbers
descriptors.description: Use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving natural and rational numbers and percentages, including in financial contexts; formulate the problems, choosing operations and efficient calculation strategies, and using digital tools where appropriate; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation, justifying the choices made
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use mathematical modelling to solve additive and multiplicative problems including financial contexts (AC9M5N09). They can formulate problems and interpret solutions in terms of the situation. They have not yet modelled problems involving rational numbers and percentages using the full modelling cycle (formulate → calculate → interpret → justify).
descriptors.endpoint: Students can use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving rational numbers and percentages, formulating problems, choosing strategies, interpreting solutions, and justifying choices.

nodes.label: Formulating rational number problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the mathematical structure of a practical problem involving rational numbers or percentages and formulate it as a mathematical calculation.
criteria: Student writes a mathematical expression or equation that correctly represents the structure of a practical problem.
Student explains why they chose the operations they did.

width.minimum: Read a practical problem involving fractions, decimals or percentages; identify the operation(s) required; write the calculation that represents the situation before solving.
width.typical: Formulate mathematical representations for a range of practical problems involving rational numbers and percentages; identify when multiple operations are needed; check that the formulation matches the problem structure before calculating.
wider: Investigate problems that are ambiguous in their formulation — where the same words could suggest different operations — and discuss which formulation fits the situation
Compare different students' formulations of the same problem and evaluate which is more efficient

modes.reason: Students often recognise the calculation type in familiar problem formats but fail to formulate unfamiliar ones correctly. Encountering rational number problems across diverse contexts (cooking, sport, finance, data) builds recognition of the mathematical structure across surface differences.

nodes.label: Choosing efficient strategies and digital tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select efficient calculation strategies for rational number problems, including deciding when digital tools are appropriate, and execute the calculation accurately.
criteria: Student selects a strategy appropriate to the problem and explains their choice.
Student uses estimation to check that their answer is reasonable.

width.minimum: Solve a rational number or percentage problem using a chosen strategy; state why the strategy was chosen; use a digital tool for at least one calculation.
width.typical: Select from mental, written, and digital strategies based on the complexity and context of the problem; justify the choice; apply estimation to check reasonableness of digital tool output.
wider: Compare the results from mental, written, and digital methods for the same problem and discuss any discrepancies
Investigate problems where a digital tool could give a misleading or unreasonable answer if inputs are entered incorrectly — the importance of estimation as a check

nodes.label: Interpreting and communicating solutions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret the mathematical result of a rational number calculation in terms of the original situation and communicate the solution with appropriate precision and justification.
criteria: Student answers a practical problem with a complete contextual statement (not just a number).
Student justifies whether their answer is reasonable and whether any rounding decision was appropriate.

width.minimum: State the answer to a practical problem in context (not just as a number); explain what the number represents in the situation; note any constraints on precision (e.g. you can't buy a fraction of an item).
width.typical: Interpret results including cases requiring rounding to realistic precision (cents, whole items, nearest centimetre); communicate the solution as a complete response to the original question; justify why the answer is reasonable.
wider: Investigate problems where the mathematical answer needs to be rounded up (packaging, tickets) vs rounded down (money remaining) and explain the direction of rounding in each case
Present a solution to a financial modelling problem as a recommendation with supporting calculations — as a consumer report, advice letter, or class presentation

modes.reason: Communicating and justifying solutions requires students to move fluidly between the mathematical representation and the real-world context, evaluating reasonableness and making decisions about precision. This integration of mathematical and contextual reasoning is the defining goal of mathematical modelling at this level.

descriptors.title: Probability scale 0 to 1
descriptors.description: Recognise that probabilities lie on numerical scales of 0 – 1 or 0% – 100% and use estimation to assign probabilities that events occur in a given context, using common fractions, percentages and decimals
descriptors.knowledge: Students can list outcomes of chance experiments and compare equally and unequally likely outcomes (AC9M5P01). They can estimate likelihoods from frequency (AC9M5P02). They have not yet connected likelihood to the 0–1 numerical scale or used fractions, decimals, and percentages as probability representations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can recognise that probabilities lie on numerical scales of 0–1 or 0%–100% and use estimation to assign probabilities using fractions, percentages and decimals.

nodes.label: The probability scale
nodes.checkpoint: Students can place events on a 0–1 probability scale and connect impossible (0), certain (1), and unlikely/likely/even chance positions to their numerical values.
criteria: Student places at least three events at appropriate positions on a 0–1 probability scale with justification.
Student explains what 0, 1, and 0.5 represent on the scale.
nodes.hinge_reason: The 0–1 scale is the representational foundation for Nodes 2 and 3. Students who cannot anchor impossible/certain/even chance to specific numerical values cannot place estimated probabilities meaningfully or verify that outcome probabilities sum to 1.

width.minimum: Place at least six events on a 0–1 probability number line; explain what 0, 1, and ½ represent; identify events at approximately ¼, ½, and ¾ probability.
width.typical: Position events at a range of probability values on the 0–1 scale; connect the scale to 0–100% and 0–1 decimal forms; explain why probability cannot be less than 0 or greater than 1; compare qualitative probability language (unlikely, likely) to approximate numerical values.
wider: Investigate sports or weather forecasting contexts that use probability — what does '70% chance of rain' mean on the 0–1 scale?
Compare different cultures' ways of expressing likelihood — how do different languages describe probability? Is there a universal understanding of 'likely'?

modes.reason: Students who understand likelihood qualitatively often struggle to connect to the 0–1 numerical scale. The reasoning chain — impossible = nothing out of nothing = 0, certain = everything = 1, even chance = half = 0.5 = 50% — needs explicit scaffolding before the scale becomes a useful tool.

nodes.label: Representing probability as fractions, decimals and percentages
nodes.checkpoint: Students can express the same probability value as a fraction, decimal, and percentage, and convert between these representations.
criteria: Student expresses a probability as a fraction, decimal, and percentage.
Student selects a representation appropriate to the context.

width.minimum: Express at least five probability values as both a fraction and a percentage; convert between probability fraction and decimal form.
width.typical: Represent probabilities using common fractions (½, ¼, ¾, ⅓, ⅔), their decimal equivalents, and percentage forms; connect to fraction-decimal-percentage equivalence from AC9M6N07; select the most appropriate representation for a given context.
wider: Investigate contexts where percentage probability is most intuitive (weather, sport) vs fraction (dice, cards) and discuss why representation choices matter
Explore odds as an alternative probability representation (e.g. 3:1 against) and convert between odds and probability fractions

modes.reason: Students who learn probability only in fraction form often fail to recognise probability expressed as percentages in real-world contexts. Encountering diverse contexts that naturally use different representations builds the flexibility needed for real-world probability literacy.

nodes.label: Estimating probabilities in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use estimation to assign reasonable probabilities to events in a given context, justifying their estimates using the 0–1 scale.
criteria: Student assigns reasonable estimated probabilities to events in a context and justifies the estimates.
Student checks that probabilities for complementary events sum to 1.

width.minimum: Assign estimated probabilities to at least four events in a realistic context; justify each estimate using scale reasoning; check that probabilities for all possible outcomes sum to 1.
width.typical: Estimate probabilities for a range of real-world contexts using fractions, decimals, and percentages; justify estimates with reasoning; verify mutual exclusivity and complementary probability (probabilities of event and non-event sum to 1); update estimates based on context changes.
wider: Investigate contexts where probability estimation requires background knowledge (e.g. weather, sports) vs pure reasoning (e.g. dice, cards) and discuss what each type requires
Explore First Nations Australian games of chance and investigate the probability structures within them

modes.reason: Estimating and justifying probabilities integrates scale understanding, fraction/decimal/percentage representation, and contextual reasoning. The check that all outcome probabilities sum to 1 coordinates all three into a coherent probability assignment.

descriptors.title: Simulations with increasing trials
descriptors.description: Conduct repeated chance experiments and run simulations with an increasing number of trials using digital tools; compare observations with expected results and discuss the effect on variation of increasing the number of trials
descriptors.knowledge: Students can conduct repeated chance experiments and use frequency to estimate likelihoods (AC9M5P02). They have observed that results vary. They have not yet used digital simulations, systematically compared experimental with theoretical probability, or investigated the effect of increasing trial numbers.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can conduct repeated chance experiments and run simulations with increasing numbers of trials; compare observations with expected results; discuss the effect on variation of increasing trial numbers.

nodes.label: Experimental vs theoretical probability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between theoretical probability (what should happen) and experimental probability (what did happen), and recognise that they may differ in small samples.
criteria: Student calculates experimental probability from a set of trials.
Student compares experimental to theoretical probability and explains why they may differ.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate theoretical and experimental probability cannot meaningfully engage with Node 2 or Node 3 — the entire discussion of convergence with more trials requires the distinction to be clear. Students who treat these as interchangeable will misinterpret simulation results.

width.minimum: Conduct a chance experiment (e.g. 20 coin flips); calculate experimental probability from results; compare to theoretical probability; note the difference.
width.typical: Calculate experimental probability from results of a chance experiment; compare to theoretical probability; explain why experimental results vary from theoretical; recognise that the gap between experimental and theoretical tends to decrease with more trials.
wider: Investigate contexts where theoretical probability is unknown and only experimental probability is available — e.g. what is the probability a thumbtack lands point-up?
Compare the gambler's fallacy — 'I've flipped heads 5 times so tails is 'due'' — to the correct understanding of independent events

modes.reason: The distinction between theoretical and experimental probability requires students to reason about two different things that can both be called 'the probability of an event.' Scaffolding 'theoretical is what the maths predicts, experimental is what actually happened' prevents conflation of the two.

nodes.label: Effect of increasing trials on variation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how increasing the number of trials in a probability experiment reduces variation in the experimental probability estimate.
criteria: Student describes how experimental probability changes as the number of trials increases.
Student explains why more trials generally gives a more reliable estimate.

width.minimum: Compare the experimental probability from 10 trials to that from 50 trials for the same experiment; describe how the result changes; note which gives a more reliable estimate.
width.typical: Track cumulative experimental probability across an increasing number of trials; observe convergence toward theoretical probability; describe the effect of increasing trials on variation using appropriate language; explain why a larger sample gives a more reliable estimate.
wider: Graph cumulative experimental probability against number of trials and describe the shape of the resulting curve
Investigate how many trials are 'enough' for different precision requirements — connecting to real-world sample size decisions

modes.reason: Students often accept that 'more trials = more reliable' as a rule without understanding why. Seeing the convergence pattern across different experiment types (coins, dice, spinners, digital simulations) builds a principled rather than rule-based understanding.

nodes.label: Digital simulations for large trial counts
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use digital tools to run simulations with large numbers of trials and use the results to compare experimental and expected outcomes.
criteria: Student runs a digital simulation and records experimental probabilities.
Student compares results from different trial sizes and describes the trend.

width.minimum: Use a digital tool to run a simulation of at least 100 trials; record results; compare to theoretical probability; describe the comparison.
width.typical: Use digital simulations to run 100, 500, and 1000 trial experiments; compare results across trial sizes; identify the trend; compare experimental frequency to expected frequency for the whole simulation; draw conclusions about the effect of trial size on reliability.
wider: Design a simulation for an event where theoretical probability is difficult to calculate analytically (e.g. two dice sum) and use simulation results to estimate probabilities
Investigate Monte Carlo methods at a conceptual level — the idea that random simulation can approximate mathematical quantities (e.g. estimating π from random point drops in a square and circle)

modes.reason: Running digital simulations and comparing results to expected outcomes integrates experimental/theoretical probability, the effect of trial size, and digital tool use. The interpretation of large-trial results — and connecting back to theoretical expectations — coordinates these into the descriptor's full demand.

descriptors.title: Cross-sections and prisms
descriptors.description: Compare the parallel cross-sections of objects and recognise their relationships to right prisms
descriptors.knowledge: Students can connect objects to their nets and build objects from nets using spatial and geometric reasoning (AC9M5SP01). They understand faces, edges, and vertices of 3D objects. They have not yet explored cross-sections as a tool for understanding 3D shapes, or identified the defining property of a right prism.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can compare the parallel cross-sections of objects and recognise their relationship to right prisms.

nodes.label: What a cross-section is
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe a cross-section as a 2D slice through a 3D object and identify the shape of a cross-section from a given object.
criteria: Student describes a cross-section as a 2D slice through a 3D object.
Student correctly identifies the cross-sectional shape of at least two common objects.
nodes.hinge_reason: A robust concept of cross-section as a 2D slice is the prerequisite for Node 2, where constancy of cross-section is the defining property of a prism. Students with a fragile or incomplete cross-section concept cannot evaluate whether cross-sections are constant.

width.minimum: Describe what a cross-section is; identify the cross-sectional shape of at least four 3D objects (cube, rectangular prism, cylinder, triangular prism); sketch the cross-section.
width.typical: Identify horizontal, vertical, and diagonal cross-sections of common 3D objects; draw cross-sections; describe what changes about the cross-section shape when the cutting angle changes; connect cross-sections to the faces of prisms.
wider: Investigate cross-sections of food — cutting a capsicum, carrot, or orange at different angles — and sketch the resulting shapes
Explore CT scans and MRI imaging as real-world applications of cross-sectional thinking in medicine

modes.reason: Cross-section is a genuinely unfamiliar concept for most Year 6 students. Multiple physical contexts — food, construction materials, everyday objects — help students build a robust concept of 'slice' before the geometric formalisation.

nodes.label: Constant cross-sections and prisms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify objects whose parallel cross-sections are identical (constant) and connect this to the definition of a right prism.
criteria: Student identifies objects with constant parallel cross-sections and names them as prisms.
Student explains what distinguishes a prism from a non-prism using cross-section reasoning.

width.minimum: Identify at least three objects whose cross-sections are the same shape and size when cut parallel to the base; explain what is constant; name these objects as prisms.
width.typical: Compare the cross-sections of prisms and non-prisms; identify the defining feature of a right prism (constant cross-section perpendicular to the length); classify a range of 3D objects as prisms or non-prisms with justification.
wider: Investigate why the volume of a prism can be calculated as cross-sectional area × length — connect the constant cross-section to this formula
Identify prism structures in architecture and manufactured objects — bridges, buildings, packaging — and discuss why prism geometry is used

modes.reason: The definition of a prism through constant cross-sections is a conceptual claim that students need to reason through rather than memorise. Scaffolding 'what makes a prism different from a pyramid?' through the cross-section lens builds a principled understanding.

nodes.label: Comparing and classifying 3D objects by cross-section
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare parallel cross-sections of different objects and use this comparison to classify and describe relationships between 3D shapes.
criteria: Student correctly classifies a set of 3D objects as prisms or non-prisms with cross-section justification.
Student describes how cross-sections differ between prisms and non-prisms.

width.minimum: Compare the cross-sections of at least four 3D objects; identify which are constant (prisms) and which change (cones, pyramids, spheres); explain the difference in terms of the cross-section property.
width.typical: Classify a range of 3D objects as prisms or non-prisms based on cross-section analysis; describe how the cross-section changes in non-prisms (tapers, grows, changes shape); connect cross-section understanding to everyday 3D object recognition.
wider: Investigate oblique prisms — do they have constant cross-sections? How does this compare to right prisms?
Explore architectural cross-sections — how architects and engineers use cross-section diagrams to represent buildings and structures

modes.reason: Classification by cross-section integrates the cross-section concept, the prism definition, and spatial reasoning about 3D objects. Using cross-section as the classification tool — rather than familiar face-counting approaches — represents a new spatial lens.

descriptors.title: Cartesian plane — 4 quadrants
descriptors.description: Locate points in the 4 quadrants of a Cartesian plane; describe changes to the coordinates when a point is moved to a different position in the plane
descriptors.knowledge: Students can construct and use grid coordinate systems to describe position and movement in the first quadrant (AC9M5SP02). Students can locate integers on a number line (AC9M6N01). They have not yet extended the coordinate system to all four quadrants using negative integers.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can locate points in all 4 quadrants of a Cartesian plane and describe how coordinates change when a point is moved.

nodes.label: Extending coordinates to all four quadrants
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and name the four quadrants of the Cartesian plane and locate points with integer coordinates in all four quadrants.
criteria: Student correctly plots points in all four quadrants.
Student reads coordinates of points in all quadrants and correctly identifies the quadrant from coordinate signs.
nodes.hinge_reason: Reliable four-quadrant plotting and coordinate reading is the prerequisite for Node 2. Students who confuse coordinate signs or quadrant membership cannot describe coordinate changes for movements that cross axes.

width.minimum: Label the four quadrants of a Cartesian plane; plot at least eight points, two per quadrant; read the coordinates of plotted points in all quadrants.
width.typical: Plot and read coordinates in all four quadrants including on the axes; identify the quadrant from the signs of the coordinates (++, −+, −−, +−); describe the position of a point relative to the origin and the axes.
wider: Use the four-quadrant plane to map a local area, game board, or treasure hunt with reference point at origin
Connect four-quadrant coordinates to integer number lines: each axis is a number line — why does this mean four quadrants?

modes.reason: Students must learn to identify quadrants from coordinate sign patterns (++, −+, −−, +−) rather than re-counting from the origin each time. This sign-convention reasoning needs explicit scaffolding before students can describe coordinate changes that cross axes in Node 2.

nodes.label: Describing coordinate changes when moving a point
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how the coordinates of a point change when it is translated horizontally, vertically, or diagonally in the Cartesian plane.
criteria: Student correctly identifies which coordinate changes when a point is moved horizontally or vertically.
Student predicts the new coordinates of a point after a described movement.

width.minimum: Move a point horizontally and describe the change to x-coordinate; move a point vertically and describe the change to y-coordinate; state which coordinate changes and by how much for each movement.
width.typical: Describe coordinate changes for horizontal, vertical, and diagonal movements including movements that cross axes (changing sign); predict the new coordinates of a point after a described movement; connect movements to positive/negative integer addition.
wider: Investigate systematic translations of shapes on the Cartesian plane — if every vertex moves +3 horizontally and −2 vertically, how do coordinates change?
Explore reflections across axes: if a point at (3, −4) is reflected across the x-axis, what are the new coordinates? Identify the sign pattern.

modes.reason: Students often confuse horizontal and vertical movements with x- and y-coordinate changes. The explicit reasoning chain — horizontal movement changes only x, vertical movement changes only y — prevents persistent confusion and provides a tool for checking transformations.

descriptors.title: Tessellations and transformations
descriptors.description: Recognise and use combinations of transformations to create tessellations and other geometric patterns, using dynamic geometric software where appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe and perform translations, reflections and rotations of shapes and identify symmetries (AC9M5SP03). They understand each transformation individually. They have not yet combined transformations or used combinations to create tessellations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can recognise and use combinations of transformations to create tessellations and other geometric patterns.

nodes.label: Combining transformations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply a sequence of two or more transformations to a shape and describe the combined effect.
criteria: Student applies two transformations in sequence to a shape and correctly sketches the result.
Student describes each transformation in the sequence.
nodes.hinge_reason: Accurate combined transformation is the prerequisite for Node 3 (creating tessellations). Students who lose track of orientation when combining transformations cannot describe or execute the repeating transformation rule needed to tile a plane.

width.minimum: Apply two transformations in sequence to a shape (e.g. reflection then translation); describe each transformation; sketch the result at each stage.
width.typical: Apply and describe combinations of translation, reflection, and rotation; recognise that the order of transformations may affect the result; use dynamic software to experiment with transformation sequences.
wider: Investigate whether two reflections across parallel axes produce the same result as a translation — verify with examples
Explore whether the order matters: does rotate then translate give the same result as translate then rotate? Test systematically.

modes.reason: Students often apply transformations correctly individually but lose track of orientation when combining them. A systematic 'track each vertex' approach scaffolds accurate combined transformation before geometric intuition develops.

nodes.label: What makes a tessellation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify what properties of a shape and transformation allow it to tessellate (tile a plane without gaps or overlaps).
criteria: Student identifies whether a polygon tessellates and explains the reason using interior angles.
Student identifies the transformation(s) generating a given tessellation.

width.minimum: Identify whether a given regular polygon tessellates by testing with the interior angle; explain why equilateral triangles, squares, and regular hexagons tessellate and pentagons do not.
width.typical: Test whether regular and irregular polygons tessellate; connect tessellation to the interior angle sum at each vertex (must be 360°); identify the transformation rule that generates a given tessellation.
wider: Investigate which regular polygons tessellate and explain the mathematical reason using angle sums
Explore semi-regular tessellations (combinations of two or more regular polygons) and identify the transformation rules generating them

modes.reason: Students who test only familiar shapes may form an incomplete rule for tessellation. Testing diverse shapes — irregular polygons, shapes with curved edges, combinations — and confronting the 360° angle-sum explanation builds a principled understanding.

nodes.label: Creating tessellations and geometric patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can create a tessellation or geometric pattern using a specified combination of transformations and describe the rule generating the pattern.
criteria: Student creates a tessellation using a specified shape and transformation combination with no gaps or overlaps.
Student describes the transformation rule generating their tessellation.

width.minimum: Create a tessellation using at least one shape and one transformation; describe the transformation rule that generates the pattern; verify that there are no gaps or overlaps.
width.typical: Create tessellations using combinations of transformations including translations, reflections, and rotations; describe the generating rule; use dynamic geometric software to create and modify patterns; identify the transformation rule in a given tessellation created by someone else.
wider: Create a modified tessellation in the style of M.C. Escher by distorting a tessellating shape while preserving the transformation properties
Investigate and re-create geometric patterns from First Nations Australian art or Islamic art traditions, identifying the transformation rules and explaining their mathematical structure

modes.reason: Creating tessellations integrates transformation knowledge, angle reasoning, and spatial planning. Generating and describing the rule requires students to move between doing (applying transformations) and explaining (articulating the pattern structure).

descriptors.title: Compare distributions
descriptors.description: Interpret and compare data sets for ordinal and nominal categorical, discrete and continuous numerical variables using comparative displays or visualisations and digital tools; compare distributions in terms of mode, range and shape
descriptors.knowledge: Students can acquire and represent nominal and ordinal data and report on distributions in terms of mode and shape (AC9M5ST01). They can interpret line graphs representing change over time (AC9M5ST02). They have not yet formally compared distributions across two data sets or used range as a comparative measure.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can interpret and compare data sets for ordinal, nominal categorical, discrete and continuous numerical variables using comparative displays; compare distributions in terms of mode, range and shape.

nodes.label: Variable types and appropriate displays
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify whether a variable is ordinal categorical, nominal categorical, discrete numerical, or continuous numerical and select an appropriate display for each.
criteria: Student correctly classifies a variable by type.
Student selects and justifies an appropriate display for a given variable type.

width.minimum: Classify at least four variables by type; match each to an appropriate display type with justification.
width.typical: Classify variables across all four types; justify display choices (e.g. why a histogram suits continuous data, why a bar chart suits categorical data); identify mismatched display/variable combinations in given examples.
wider: Investigate real datasets and identify cases where variable classification is ambiguous (e.g. age as discrete or continuous, rating scales as ordinal or discrete)
Compare how different display choices for the same data emphasise different features of the distribution

modes.reason: Students often default to one display type regardless of variable type. Encountering varied variable types and their appropriate displays across diverse contexts builds the classification judgment needed for independent data work.

nodes.label: Mode, range and shape as comparative tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate or identify the mode and range of a data set and describe its shape, and use these to make comparative statements between two data sets.
criteria: Student identifies the mode, range, and shape of a dataset.
Student makes at least two specific comparative statements between two datasets using these measures.

width.minimum: Find the mode and range of two given data sets; describe the shape of each distribution (symmetric, skewed, uniform, bimodal); make at least two comparative statements using these measures.
width.typical: Calculate mode and range for a range of dataset types; describe shape using appropriate vocabulary; compare two datasets systematically using mode, range, and shape; explain what differences in range reveal about spread; recognise the mode's limitations for comparison.
wider: Investigate how the same shape description can fit very different datasets — what additional information is needed for useful comparison?
Explore what median and mean could add to comparisons that mode and range miss — introduce informally without requiring formal calculation

modes.reason: Students who use mode and range in isolation often make superficial comparisons. Multiple dataset contexts — survey data, sports data, measurement data — help students develop judgment about when mode is informative, when range is the key comparison, and when shape matters most.

nodes.label: Comparative displays and interpretation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct or read comparative displays (side-by-side bar charts, parallel dot plots) and use them to compare distributions, stating conclusions in the context of the data.
criteria: Student reads a comparative display and states two specific distributional differences between the datasets.
Student relates the statistical comparison to the context of the data (not just the numbers).

width.minimum: Read a provided comparative display; identify differences in mode, range, and shape between the two distributions; state at least two conclusions in context.
width.typical: Construct comparative displays from provided data; identify and discuss distribution differences using mode, range, and shape; consider what the comparison reveals about the context; acknowledge limitations of the comparison.
wider: Investigate comparative displays from media sources (sports statistics, survey results, health data) and evaluate the claims made from the comparison
Compare distributions from First Nations Australian community data contexts — e.g. comparing outcomes across contexts — and discuss what fair and respectful data comparison looks like

modes.reason: Comparative interpretation requires students to read the display, apply mode/range/shape reasoning, and construct contextual statements. This coordinates statistical literacy, mathematical reasoning, and contextual judgment simultaneously.

descriptors.title: Plan and refine investigations
descriptors.description: Plan and conduct statistical investigations by posing and refining questions or identifying a problem and collecting relevant data; analyse and interpret the data and communicate findings within the context of the investigation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan and conduct statistical investigations, choose appropriate displays and communicate findings (AC9M5ST03). They have experience with the full investigation cycle. They have not yet practised refining questions based on initial findings or working with the full range of variable types from AC9M6ST01.
descriptors.endpoint: Students can plan and conduct statistical investigations by posing and refining questions, collecting relevant data, analysing and interpreting results, and communicating findings in context.

nodes.label: Posing and refining the investigation question
nodes.checkpoint: Students can pose a statistical question for investigation, identify what data is needed, and refine the question based on feasibility or initial findings.
criteria: Student poses a statistical question and explains what data is needed to answer it.
Student identifies at least one way the question could be refined for better investigation.

width.minimum: Pose a statistical question; identify what data would answer it; consider whether the data is collectible; refine the question if needed to make it answerable.
width.typical: Pose questions that lead to interesting statistical investigations; distinguish statistical questions (expecting variability) from mathematical questions (single answer); anticipate potential issues with data collection before starting; refine based on a pilot sample.
wider: Investigate question design — how does the wording of a question affect what data is collected? Compare two different phrasings of the same question.
Pose a question from a real community context and discuss how the question framing affects who would want to investigate it

modes.reason: Students who generate only one investigation question type (e.g. 'how many...') develop a narrow concept of statistical investigation. Exposure to comparison questions, association questions, and change-over-time questions broadens the concept of what statistical investigation can address.

nodes.label: Collecting and organising relevant data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can select and use data collection methods appropriate to their investigation question, collect data systematically, and organise it for analysis.
criteria: Student collects data using a method appropriate to the investigation question.
Student organises the data in a form that supports analysis.
nodes.hinge_reason: Errors or gaps in data collection and organisation propagate directly into Node 3 — analysis and interpretation can only be as reliable as the dataset permits. Students with poorly organised or incomplete data cannot draw valid conclusions regardless of analytical skill.

width.minimum: Design a simple data collection method for a given investigation question; collect data from at least 20 observations; organise in a table or frequency display.
width.typical: Design appropriate collection instruments (survey, observation tally, measurement record); consider sample selection; collect and organise data for analysis including categorical and numerical variables; check data for recording errors.
wider: Investigate secondary data sources — existing datasets from government, sport, or census sources — and discuss how they differ from primary collection
Consider ethical data collection: what questions are appropriate to ask? How should data about people be stored and shared?

modes.reason: Systematic data collection and organisation are procedural skills requiring care and precision. Errors in recording or organisation propagate through the entire investigation. This is a genuine consolidation point — accuracy here is the prerequisite for meaningful analysis.

nodes.label: Analysing, interpreting and communicating findings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse collected data using appropriate measures and displays, interpret the findings in context, and communicate conclusions that address the original investigation question.
criteria: Student produces an appropriate display and states findings using statistical measures.
Student communicates conclusions that specifically address the original investigation question.

width.minimum: Calculate mode and range from collected data; create an appropriate display; state at least two findings that address the investigation question in context.
width.typical: Analyse data using mode, range, shape, and appropriate displays; interpret findings in context; connect findings back to the original question; acknowledge limitations of the investigation (sample size, bias, data quality); communicate as a written or presented report.
wider: Refine the investigation based on findings — pose a follow-up question that the initial investigation raised and plan how it could be addressed
Communicate findings to a real or simulated audience (class, school community, partner class) and respond to questions about methods and conclusions

modes.reason: Communicating findings integrates data analysis, contextual interpretation, and critical reflection on the investigation's limitations. The coordination of these — producing a coherent response to the original question — is the defining capability goal of this descriptor.

descriptors.title: Variables and formulas
descriptors.description: recognise and use variables to represent everyday formulas algebraically and substitute values into formulas to determine an unknown
descriptors.knowledge: Students can find unknown values in equations involving brackets and combinations of operations, and recognise rules in growing patterns (from AC9M6A01, AC9M6A02). Students understand that a letter can represent an unknown.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise variables as quantities that can change, represent everyday formulas algebraically, and substitute values to determine unknowns.

nodes.label: Variables as generalised quantities
nodes.checkpoint: Students recognise that variables represent quantities that can change, and distinguish a variable from an unknown constant.
criteria: Correctly identifies what each variable represents in a given formula.
Explains the difference between a variable that can take many values and a specific unknown.
Does not treat all variables as things to 'solve for'.

width.minimum: Identify the variables in a given formula and describe what each represents in context.
width.typical: Link variables to the attributes they model; explain the difference between a variable (can take many values) and a specific unknown (one value to find).
wider: Investigate how the same letter variable is used differently in different formulas (e.g. A for area in one, for amplitude in another) — variables are context-specific labels.
Explore formulas from other subjects: distance = speed × time; explore what each variable represents.

modes.reason: Students entering Y7 typically treat all letters as 'the unknown x to solve for'. The variable-as-generalised-quantity concept requires multiple formula contexts to become stable.

nodes.label: Substituting values into formulas
nodes.checkpoint: Students substitute given numerical values into a formula and calculate the result.
criteria: Correctly substitutes values into a formula and evaluates.
Applies correct order of operations during substitution.
Does not multiply the coefficient by the variable label (e.g. does not treat 3A as 3×'the letter A' rather than 3 times the value of A).
nodes.hinge_reason: Arithmetic errors during substitution propagate directly into Node 3 — students who cannot substitute correctly cannot find unknowns, since the finding-unknown step builds on a correctly evaluated substitution.

width.minimum: Given a formula and values for all but one variable, substitute and evaluate.
width.typical: Substitute values into formulas from practical contexts (area, perimeter, wage, density); evaluate correctly including with fractions and decimals.
wider: Substitute values into formulas from science and everyday life (e.g. heart rate formula, body mass index) and interpret the result in context.
Investigate Country/Place formulas: investigate formulas used in Indigenous land management or navigation contexts.

modes.reason: Substitution is a mechanical skill that requires fluency before finding unknowns. Errors here are typically arithmetic (not algebraic) but propagate into node 3.

nodes.label: Finding an unknown by substitution and backtracking
nodes.checkpoint: Students determine the value of an unknown variable in a formula by substituting known values and solving.
criteria: Correctly finds an unknown in a formula given all other values.
Verifies the solution by substituting back into the formula.
Interprets the result in context (with units and meaning).

width.minimum: Given a formula with one unknown and all other values provided, find the unknown by substituting and solving.
width.typical: Find unknowns in formulas in practical contexts (e.g. find the base wage given total wage and overtime details); verify by substituting back.
wider: Compare finding unknowns using substitution + backtracking vs formal algebraic rearrangement — note both methods are valid.
Apply to a range of real formulas: perimeter to find a missing side, density formula to find mass or volume.

modes.reason: Finding an unknown brings together variable understanding, substitution, and arithmetic operations simultaneously. The coordinated application is the learning.

descriptors.title: Algebraic expressions
descriptors.description: formulate algebraic expressions using constants, variables, operations and brackets
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise variables in formulas and understand that letters represent quantities (from AC9M7A01). Students can write rules for patterns using words (from AC9M6A01).
descriptors.endpoint: Students formulate algebraic expressions using constants, variables, operations and brackets to represent mathematical relationships.

nodes.label: Translating words to algebraic expressions
nodes.checkpoint: Students translate verbal descriptions of mathematical relationships into algebraic expressions using constants, variables and operations.
criteria: Correctly translates a verbal description into an algebraic expression.
Correctly translates an algebraic expression into a verbal description.
Does not confuse 'n less than 5' (5 − n) with 'n minus 5' (n − 5).
nodes.hinge_reason: Translation errors (especially 'five less than x' vs 'x minus five') propagate directly into Node 2 bracket formulation and AC9M7A03 equation solving — students who mis-translate a verbal problem cannot set up correct equations.

width.minimum: Write an algebraic expression for a simple verbal description (e.g. 'three more than x', 'twice n').
width.typical: Translate multi-step verbal descriptions; identify the correct order of operations; translate in both directions (words → algebra, algebra → words).
wider: Investigate common translation errors: 'five less than x' vs 'x less five' — use substitution to check which is correct.
Create word problems that match given algebraic expressions, building translation fluency in both directions.

modes.reason: Translation between verbal and algebraic forms is error-prone and context-sensitive. Students who only translate simple phrases fail with relational descriptions ('five less than x'). Multiple verbal structures across varied contexts are required.

nodes.label: Expressions with brackets and multiple operations
nodes.checkpoint: Students formulate algebraic expressions involving brackets, including those where brackets are required to preserve intended meaning.
criteria: Correctly writes expressions requiring brackets to preserve intended meaning.
Can explain why brackets are necessary in a given expression.
Evaluates expressions with brackets correctly applying order of operations.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who omit necessary brackets formulate expressions with different meanings than intended — this error cascades into AC9M7A03 equation solving where setting up the equation incorrectly means the solution is always wrong regardless of solving skill.

width.minimum: Write an algebraic expression that requires brackets (e.g. 'the sum of x and 3, multiplied by 4').
width.typical: Formulate expressions from multi-step descriptions; explain when brackets are necessary; evaluate expressions for given values.
wider: Compare equivalent expressions with and without brackets: 2(x + 3) vs 2x + 6. Verify equivalence by substitution.
Apply distributive property to expand and factorise simple expressions — preview of Y8 algebra.

modes.reason: Deciding when brackets are required demands explicit reasoning about order of operations and meaning. Students routinely omit necessary brackets or add unnecessary ones without a clear reasoning process.

nodes.label: Generalising arithmetic to algebraic expressions
nodes.checkpoint: Students recognise that algebraic expressions generalise arithmetic relationships, and can identify what an expression represents across multiple cases.
criteria: Writes an algebraic expression that correctly generalises a given arithmetic pattern.
Verifies the expression by substituting specific values.
Does not confuse the generalised expression with a specific equation to solve.

width.minimum: Given an arithmetic pattern (e.g. 7+7+7 = 3×7), write the algebraic generalisation (x+x+x = 3x).
width.typical: Formulate algebraic expressions that represent general mathematical relationships; test with multiple values to verify the generalisation.
wider: Investigate how the same relationship can be expressed in multiple equivalent algebraic forms — which is simplest? Which shows structure best?
Apply to pattern generalisation: write an expression for the nth term of a visual growing pattern.

modes.reason: The shift from arithmetic to algebraic generalisation is a conceptual threshold. Students need multiple examples where the same arithmetic pattern is generalised before the generalising move feels natural.

descriptors.title: Solve linear equations
descriptors.description: solve one-variable linear equations with natural number solutions; verify the solution by substitution
descriptors.knowledge: Students can find unknown values in equations using backtracking and balance (from AC9M6A02). Students can formulate algebraic expressions (from AC9M7A02).
descriptors.endpoint: Students solve one-variable linear equations with natural number solutions using algebraic methods and verify solutions by substitution.

nodes.label: Equation as a balance statement
nodes.checkpoint: Students understand that an equation is a statement of equality and that the solution is the value that makes it true.
criteria: Correctly identifies whether a given value satisfies an equation by substitution.
Distinguishes between an expression and an equation.
Understands that a solution must make both sides equal.

width.minimum: Use substitution to check whether a given value is the solution to a simple equation.
width.typical: Explain what it means to 'solve' an equation; test multiple candidates for a solution; distinguish between expressions and equations.
wider: Investigate equations that have no natural number solution vs those that do — develop the habit of verifying.
Use a balance model to demonstrate what 'maintaining equality' means concretely.

modes.reason: Students often confuse solving an equation with simplifying an expression. Multiple contexts and the explicit distinction between 'expression' and 'equation' help establish this foundational understanding.

nodes.label: Solving by backtracking
nodes.checkpoint: Students solve one-step and two-step linear equations by backtracking (undoing operations in reverse order).
criteria: Correctly solves a two-step linear equation using backtracking.
Identifies the inverse operations used.
Applies backtracking to multi-operation equations in the correct order.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot execute the backtracking scaffold cannot transition to the algebraic balance method in Node 3 — both methods require identifying the order of operations, and the backtracking scaffold makes this explicit before the abstract method is introduced.

width.minimum: Solve equations of the form ax = b and x + a = b by backtracking; show the inverse operations used.
width.typical: Solve two-step equations (e.g. 3x + 7 = 19) using backtracking; explain the process at each step.
wider: Compare backtracking and the balance/algebraic method for the same equation — note they produce the same result.
Apply to contextual problems: write and solve an equation from a word problem.

modes.reason: Backtracking requires students to map the order of operations forward then reverse it. An explicit scaffold (draw the 'machine', identify steps, reverse) is needed before students apply this fluently.

nodes.label: Solving algebraically and verifying
nodes.checkpoint: Students solve one-variable linear equations algebraically, using the balance model, and verify the solution by substitution.
criteria: Solves a one-variable linear equation algebraically with correct steps shown.
Verifies the solution by substituting back into the original equation.
Does not skip verification.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who lack automatic algebraic solving and the verification habit cannot apply equations to modelling problems in AC9M7N09 and AC9M7M06 — the modelling contexts require fluent solving, and missing verification means errors go undetected.

width.minimum: Solve a two-step linear equation algebraically (performing the same operation to both sides) and verify by substitution.
width.typical: Solve a range of one-variable linear equations; choose between backtracking and algebraic methods; always verify.
wider: Create and solve equations from contextual problems (e.g. 'I think of a number, double it and add 5 to get 19').
Investigate equations where the unknown appears in a context requiring interpretation of the solution (e.g. 'x must be a whole number of people').

modes.reason: Algebraic solving and verification together form the method students need to have automatic before applying equations to modelling contexts. The verification habit specifically needs consolidation.

descriptors.title: Graphs of functions
descriptors.description: describe relationships between variables represented in graphs of functions from authentic data
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate points in all four quadrants of the Cartesian plane and describe coordinate changes (from AC9M6SP02). Students understand dependent and independent variables in patterns.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe relationships between variables in graphs from authentic data, identifying key features and interpreting what the graph communicates about the relationship.

nodes.label: Reading and interpreting graphs of real data
nodes.checkpoint: Students read values from graphs of authentic data and describe what the graph shows in context.
criteria: Reads specific values from a graph accurately.
Describes trends (increasing, decreasing, constant, periodic) in contextual terms.
Does not interpret a graph in isolation from its axes labels and units.

width.minimum: Read specific values from a graph and describe the overall trend in plain language.
width.typical: Identify increases, decreases, peaks, plateaus, and interpret what these mean in the context of the data (e.g. energy usage, stock value).
wider: Investigate travel graphs: identify periods of travel, stopping, and return; compute average speed from slope.
Compare two graphs representing the same phenomenon (e.g. gas vs electricity usage) and discuss what each reveals.

modes.reason: Interpreting a graph requires understanding the specific context of the data. Students who only practise with constructed graphs often fail to interpret authentic messy data. Varied authentic contexts build flexible reading skills.

nodes.label: Identifying and describing the relationship between variables
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify and describe the relationship between the two variables in a graph, including direction, rate of change, and any notable features.
criteria: Describes the relationship between variables including direction and approximate rate of change.
Identifies and interprets at least one notable feature (e.g. peak, plateau, sudden change) in context.
Uses the variable names from the axes in their description.

width.minimum: State the relationship between the two variables in a graph (e.g. 'as time increases, distance increases at a constant rate').
width.typical: Describe the relationship, rate of change, turning points, and intervals; explain what unusual features (sudden changes, plateaus) indicate in context.
wider: Compare linear and non-linear relationships in graphs from authentic data — informally describe what makes one 'linear looking'.
Tell the 'story' behind a graph of a function: describe what events might explain the shape (e.g. a graph representing water level in a bathtub).

modes.reason: Relating graph shape to contextual events (the 'story' behind a graph) requires experiencing many different authentic contexts. Students who only describe slope fail to interpret contextual meaning.

descriptors.title: Tables and graphs from patterns
descriptors.description: generate tables of values from visually growing patterns or the rule of a function; describe and plot these relationships on the Cartesian plane
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plot points in all four quadrants of the Cartesian plane (from AC9M6SP02). Students can write rules for growing patterns (from AC9M6A01, AC9M6A03).
descriptors.endpoint: Students generate tables of values from growing patterns or function rules, plot the relationships on the Cartesian plane, and describe the resulting graph.

nodes.label: Generating tables of values from patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify the rule in a visually growing pattern and use it to generate a table of values.
criteria: Correctly generates a table of values from a growing pattern.
Identifies the rule that generates the values.
Can find the value for a term not shown in the original pattern.

width.minimum: Given a visual growing pattern, complete a table of values for the first 5 terms.
width.typical: Identify the rule in words and algebraic notation; use the rule to generate values including for non-consecutive terms.
wider: Investigate growing patterns using physical materials (tiles, blocks) and connect the physical growth to the algebraic rule.
Compare two growing patterns — which grows faster? How can you tell from the table?

modes.reason: Students who only see numerical patterns without visual context often generate tables mechanically without understanding the rule. Visual pattern contexts anchor the algebraic structure.

nodes.label: Generating tables from function rules
nodes.checkpoint: Students generate a table of ordered pairs from a given function rule and identify the relationship between input and output values.
criteria: Correctly generates a table of ordered pairs from a given function rule.
Labels the table with input (x) and output (y) columns.
Does not substitute the same value for both x and y.
nodes.hinge_reason: Errors in the table of ordered pairs cascade directly into Node 3 — incorrectly generated pairs produce a graph that doesn't represent the function rule, meaning students cannot see or describe the relationship they were supposed to plot.

width.minimum: Given a simple function rule (e.g. y = 2x + 1), generate a table of at least 5 ordered pairs.
width.typical: Generate tables from various linear function rules; describe the pattern in the output values; identify the effect of changing the rule.
wider: Use a function machine or spreadsheet to generate tables for multiple rules and compare outputs side by side.
Investigate what happens to the table when the rule changes: how does doubling the coefficient change the values?

modes.reason: Systematic generation of ordered pairs requires procedural care that students need to practise before plotting. Errors in the table cascade into errors in the graph.

nodes.label: Plotting and describing relationships on the Cartesian plane
nodes.checkpoint: Students plot ordered pairs from a table of values on the Cartesian plane and describe the resulting relationship.
criteria: Correctly plots ordered pairs from a table on the Cartesian plane.
Draws a line through plotted points for a linear relationship.
Describes the relationship shown in the graph using appropriate language.

width.minimum: Plot a set of ordered pairs from a table and connect them; describe whether the relationship is linear.
width.typical: Plot and describe relationships for several linear rules; identify that linear functions produce straight lines; describe slope informally.
wider: Compare two functions plotted on the same axes — identify what differs (steepness, y-intercept) and connect to the rule.
Investigate the graphical representation of a non-linear function (e.g. y = x²) from a table — contrast with linear.

modes.reason: Plotting connects the table of values, the function rule, and the Cartesian plane simultaneously. Describing the resulting graph requires coordinating all three representations.

descriptors.title: Manipulate formulas
descriptors.description: manipulate formulas involving several variables using digital tools, and describe the effect of systematic variation in the values of the variables
descriptors.knowledge: Students can substitute values into formulas and generate tables of values (from AC9M7A01, AC9M7A05). Students have used digital tools for calculation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use digital tools to systematically vary values in multi-variable formulas, and describe the effect of each variable's change on the output.

nodes.label: Systematic variation of one variable
nodes.checkpoint: Students vary one variable in a formula while holding others constant, and describe the effect on the output.
criteria: Correctly varies one variable while holding others constant.
Describes the effect of the variation on the output in words.
Uses a table or digital tool to organise the systematic variation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who vary multiple variables simultaneously in Node 1 cannot describe the effect of any single variable — this blocks Node 2, where comparing the effect of different variables requires having isolated each one first.

width.minimum: Using a spreadsheet or table, vary one variable in a simple formula (e.g. V = l × w × h, vary h) and describe the effect on V.
width.typical: Systematically vary each variable in turn in a multi-variable formula; describe the relationship between each variable and the output.
wider: Investigate formulas where the output changes non-linearly with one variable (e.g. area of a square vs side length) — describe the difference.
Use spreadsheet formula functions to automate systematic variation across a range of values.

modes.reason: Systematic variation requires the explicit strategy of holding all variables constant except one. Students without this scaffold vary multiple things simultaneously and cannot isolate the effect of each variable.

nodes.label: Describing effects of variation across multiple variables
nodes.checkpoint: Students describe how changing each variable in a multi-variable formula affects the output, and identify which variables have the greatest effect.
criteria: Correctly describes the effect of changing each variable on the output.
Identifies which variable produces the largest change in output for an equal proportional variation.
Uses digital tool output systematically rather than performing isolated calculations.

width.minimum: Compare the effect of equal proportional changes in two different variables on the output of a formula.
width.typical: Analyse a real formula (e.g. distance = speed × time; volume of a prism) and describe which variable has the most/least impact on the output for a given change.
wider: Explore parameter variation in formulas used in machine learning or AI contexts (as described in elaborations) — model the concept of tuning parameters.
Investigate the formula for compound scenarios: if both speed and time double, what happens to distance? Connect to proportional reasoning.

modes.reason: Comparing the effect of variables requires varied formula contexts to develop generalised understanding. Students who only explore one formula see the pattern as context-specific rather than a feature of multi-variable relationships.

descriptors.title: Area of triangles and parallelograms
descriptors.description: solve problems involving the area of triangles and parallelograms using established formulas and appropriate units
descriptors.knowledge: Students can establish and apply the area formula for a rectangle (from AC9M6M02). Students understand area as the measure of a 2D region and can use appropriate units.
descriptors.endpoint: Students solve problems involving the area of triangles and parallelograms using established formulas with appropriate units.

nodes.label: Deriving the triangle area formula
nodes.checkpoint: Students understand why the area of a triangle is half the area of a related rectangle or parallelogram, and can state the formula A = ½bh.
criteria: States the area formula for a triangle and explains its derivation.
Correctly identifies the base and corresponding perpendicular height.
Does not confuse the slant side with the perpendicular height.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who believe the formula only applies to right-angled triangles misidentify the height in Node 2 problems — applying A = ½bh with the slant side instead of the perpendicular height produces systematically wrong answers for all non-right-angled triangles.

width.minimum: Explain using a diagram why A = ½bh for a triangle, connecting to the rectangle formula.
width.typical: Derive the formula using multiple triangle types (right-angled, acute, obtuse) and verify the connection to the enclosing rectangle in each case.
wider: Investigate using dynamic geometry software: slide the apex of a triangle at a fixed altitude and observe that the area is constant — explain why.
Explore how the formula applies when the height is outside the triangle (obtuse case).

modes.reason: Students who derive the formula only for right-angled triangles often believe the formula changes for acute or obtuse triangles. Multiple triangle types resolve this.

nodes.label: Applying area formulas to triangles and parallelograms
nodes.checkpoint: Students calculate the area of triangles and parallelograms using established formulas, selecting appropriate units.
criteria: Correctly calculates the area of a triangle using A = ½bh.
Correctly calculates the area of a parallelogram.
Uses appropriate units and converts if necessary.

width.minimum: Calculate the area of a given triangle and a given parallelogram using their formulas.
width.typical: Solve problems involving composite shapes (decompose into triangles and rectangles); select appropriate units; convert between units if needed.
wider: Solve practical problems: floor plans, sail areas, land parcels — requiring decomposition into triangles and parallelograms.
Investigate First Nations design elements that use triangular and parallelogram forms — calculate areas in context.

modes.reason: Area formula application errors are common in non-standard orientations and composite shapes. Varied practical contexts with different orientations are necessary.

descriptors.title: Volume of right prisms
descriptors.description: solve problems involving the volume of right prisms including rectangular and triangular prisms, using established formulas and appropriate units
descriptors.knowledge: Students can calculate area of triangles, rectangles and parallelograms (from AC9M7M01, AC9M6M02). Students understand volume as the measure of 3D space and have worked with rectangular prisms using unit cubes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students solve problems involving the volume of right prisms (rectangular and triangular) using V = Ah with appropriate units.

nodes.label: Volume as cross-section area times height
nodes.checkpoint: Students understand that the volume of any right prism equals the area of its cross-section multiplied by its height.
criteria: States that V = Ah for right prisms and explains what A and h represent.
Correctly identifies the cross-section and its area for a given prism.
Does not confuse the total surface area with the cross-sectional area.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't generalise beyond V = lwh cannot calculate the volume of triangular prisms in Node 2 — they lack the cross-section principle that makes V = Ah work for any right prism.

width.minimum: Explain and demonstrate why V = Ah for a rectangular prism using unit cubes; state that the same principle applies for triangular prisms.
width.typical: Connect the area of the base (cross-section) to the volume; explain why the cross-section must be consistent (uniform) throughout the height.
wider: Build rectangular prisms from unit cubes and verify V = l × w × h = Ah for various dimensions.
Explore why V = Ah only holds for prisms with uniform cross-section — investigate what changes for a pyramid.

modes.reason: Students who learn V = lwh as a formula for rectangular prisms only often fail to generalise to triangular prisms. The cross-section principle requires reinforcement across multiple prism types.

nodes.label: Calculating volume of rectangular and triangular prisms
nodes.checkpoint: Students calculate the volume of rectangular and triangular right prisms using V = Ah with appropriate units.
criteria: Correctly calculates volume for both rectangular and triangular prisms.
Uses appropriate cubic units.
Converts between units where required (e.g. cm³ to litres).

width.minimum: Calculate the volume of a rectangular prism and a triangular prism given all necessary dimensions.
width.typical: Solve practical volume problems including selecting appropriate units (cm³, m³, litres); convert between units.
wider: Solve real-world problems: volume of concrete for a triangular ramp, volume of a storage container — with unit conversion.
Investigate the volume of composite prisms: e.g. an L-shaped prism decomposed into two rectangular prisms.

modes.reason: Volume problems in varied practical contexts (construction, storage, water capacity) build the habit of appropriate unit selection and conversion, which students neglect in decontextualised practice.

descriptors.title: Pi and circle features
descriptors.description: describe the relationship between π and the features of circles including the circumference, radius and diameter
descriptors.knowledge: Students are familiar with circle vocabulary (centre, radius, diameter) from informal prior experience. Students can measure length and calculate with decimals (from AC9M6M01, AC9M7N06).
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe π as the constant ratio of circumference to diameter and use this relationship to calculate circumference and diameter.

nodes.label: Features of circles and their relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify and name the features of a circle (radius, diameter, circumference, chord) and state that diameter = 2 × radius.
criteria: Correctly identifies and labels all key features of a circle.
States that diameter = 2 × radius and applies it correctly.
Does not confuse radius with diameter.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who confuse radius and diameter use the wrong measurement when calculating C/d in Node 2, making π appear to be approximately 6.28 or 1.57 — this completely undermines the discovery of π's constancy and all subsequent circumference calculations.

width.minimum: Label all features on a circle diagram; state the relationship between radius and diameter.
width.typical: Measure radius and diameter of several circles; verify d = 2r consistently; identify chord, arc, sector informally.
wider: Investigate circles in First Nations Australian contexts: circular designs in weaving, significance of circles in cultural practices.
Explore how changing the radius changes both the diameter and circumference proportionally.

modes.reason: Circle vocabulary and the d = 2r relationship must be automatic before investigating π. Students who confuse radius and diameter make systematic errors in all circle calculations.

nodes.label: Discovering π as a constant ratio
nodes.checkpoint: Students investigate the ratio C/d for multiple circles and recognise that it is always approximately 3.14 — this constant is π.
criteria: Measures and calculates C/d for at least two circles and observes the result is approximately 3.14.
States that π ≈ 3.14 and explains what it represents.
Does not treat π as just a button on a calculator without understanding its meaning.

width.minimum: Measure the circumference and diameter of at least two circles; calculate C/d and observe the approximate constancy.
width.typical: Calculate C/d for several circles with different sizes; record results; discuss why the ratio is constant; state that this constant is named π.
wider: Investigate the history of π and how mathematicians approximated it using polygons.
Explore why π is irrational — it cannot be written as an exact fraction, only approximated.

modes.reason: The constancy of C/d is not obvious from a single measurement. Multiple circles of very different sizes make the invariance of π compelling rather than arbitrary.

nodes.label: Using π to calculate circumference and diameter
nodes.checkpoint: Students use C = πd (or C = 2πr) to calculate the circumference given the diameter or radius, and rearrange to find diameter given circumference.
criteria: Correctly calculates circumference given diameter or radius.
Correctly finds diameter given circumference.
Uses an appropriate approximation for π and specifies it.

width.minimum: Calculate the circumference of a circle given its diameter or radius; find the diameter given the circumference.
width.typical: Solve practical problems involving circumference: wheel rotations, perimeter of semicircles, circular paths.
wider: Investigate how many rotations a wheel of a given diameter makes over a set distance.
Explore applications of circumference in First Nations contexts: circular fish traps, traditional circular dwelling dimensions.

modes.reason: Students need varied practical contexts to understand when C = πd is the right tool. Purely procedural practice leads to application failures in novel problems.

descriptors.title: Angles with parallel lines
descriptors.description: identify corresponding, alternate and co-interior relationships between angles formed when parallel lines are crossed by a transversal; use them to solve problems and explain reasons
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify angle relationships on lines and at points and determine unknown angles (from AC9M6M04). Students understand that angles on a straight line sum to 180° and angles at a point sum to 360°.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify corresponding, alternate and co-interior angle relationships and use them with geometric reasoning to find unknown angles.

nodes.label: Parallel lines and transversals
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify parallel lines and transversals in diagrams and name the eight angles formed.
criteria: Correctly identifies and labels the eight angles formed.
Correctly identifies at least one example of each: corresponding, alternate, co-interior pair.
Does not confuse vertically opposite angles with the parallel line angle relationships.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who confuse angle pair types (corresponding, alternate, co-interior) apply the wrong property in Nodes 2 and 3 — they may apply the equal-angles rule to co-interior pairs (which are supplementary), producing wrong answers throughout.

width.minimum: Identify and label all eight angles formed by a transversal crossing two parallel lines.
width.typical: Draw parallel lines with a transversal; identify corresponding, alternate, and co-interior pairs by position.
wider: Investigate designs and structures where parallel lines and transversals appear (roof trusses, railway tracks, tiled floors).
Use dynamic geometry software to verify that corresponding angles remain equal as the transversal angle changes.

modes.reason: Correct identification of angle pairs is prerequisite to all reasoning in this descriptor. Students who confuse corresponding with alternate make systematic errors in every subsequent problem.

nodes.label: Properties of corresponding, alternate and co-interior angles
nodes.checkpoint: Students state and apply the angle properties: corresponding angles are equal, alternate angles are equal, co-interior angles are supplementary.
criteria: States each angle property correctly.
Calculates missing angles using the correct property.
Does not apply the equal-angle property to co-interior pairs.
nodes.hinge_reason: The co-interior/alternate confusion produces persistent errors in Node 3 multi-step reasoning — students who apply the wrong property at step 1 propagate wrong values through the entire chain, with no self-correction possible without restating geometric reasons.

width.minimum: State each property and calculate a missing angle using one of the three relationships.
width.typical: Apply multiple properties in sequence to find all unknown angles in a parallel lines diagram; give reasons for each step.
wider: Investigate why these properties hold — informally, by translating or rotating the transversal to show correspondence.
Apply properties to real-world geometric problems: angles in roof pitch design, alignment of structures.

modes.reason: Students frequently misapply the properties, especially confusing co-interior (supplementary) with alternate (equal). Multiple diagram orientations — not just the standard vertical layout — resolve this.

nodes.label: Using angle reasoning to solve problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students solve multi-step angle problems involving parallel lines, giving geometric reasons for each step.
criteria: Solves a multi-step angle problem correctly.
