States a geometric reason for each step.
Does not assume angle values without justification.

width.minimum: Solve a problem requiring two steps of angle reasoning and state the reason for each step.
width.typical: Solve problems combining parallel line angle properties with straight line and vertically opposite angle facts; write full geometric reasons.
wider: Design a problem requiring at least three angle reasoning steps — write the solution with full justification.
Investigate how angle properties are applied in geometric proofs (informal): show that a given pair of lines must be parallel.

modes.reason: Multi-step geometric reasoning requires an explicit scaffold: identify what you know, select the applicable property, state the reason. Students who calculate without reasons cannot self-check and lose marks systematically.

descriptors.title: Angle sum of triangles
descriptors.description: demonstrate that the interior angle sum of a triangle in the plane is 180° and apply this to determine the interior angle sum of other shapes and the size of unknown angles
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify angle relationships on straight lines and at points (from AC9M6M04). Students understand that angles on a straight line sum to 180°.
descriptors.endpoint: Students demonstrate that the interior angle sum of a triangle is 180° and apply this and the decomposition principle to find interior angle sums of polygons and unknown angles.

nodes.label: Demonstrating the triangle angle sum
nodes.checkpoint: Students demonstrate, using concrete or dynamic methods, that the interior angles of any triangle sum to 180°.
criteria: Demonstrates the angle sum of a triangle is 180° using at least one method.
States the property applies to all triangles.
Measures angles in a triangle and verifies the sum is approximately 180°.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who don't believe the 180° sum is universal make errors in Node 2 decomposition — if they think obtuse triangles have a different angle sum, the formula (n-2) × 180° breaks down and polygon calculations become unreliable.

width.minimum: Tear off the corners of a triangle and arrange them on a straight line to show they sum to 180°; verify with measurement for two different triangles.
width.typical: Demonstrate using paper tearing and using dynamic geometry software; explain why the property holds for any triangle.
wider: Investigate what happens to the angle sum if you draw a triangle on a sphere — explore non-Euclidean geometry informally.
Use the parallel lines result from AC9M7M04 to prove why the angle sum is 180° (formal derivation).

modes.reason: Students who only see one demonstration believe the angle sum might be different for unusual triangles. Testing acute, obtuse, right-angled, and very flat triangles builds confidence in the universality of the property.

nodes.label: Interior angle sum of polygons by decomposition
nodes.checkpoint: Students use decomposition of polygons into triangles to determine the interior angle sum formula for n-sided polygons.
criteria: Correctly decomposes a polygon into triangles and calculates the interior angle sum.
States the general formula (n−2) × 180° and applies it correctly.
Can verify their result by measuring.

width.minimum: Decompose a quadrilateral and pentagon into triangles and calculate their interior angle sums.
width.typical: Derive and apply the formula (n−2) × 180° for any polygon; verify for specific cases.
wider: Investigate the exterior angle sum of polygons (always 360° for convex polygons) — connect to interior angle sum.
Apply to regular polygons: find the interior angle of a regular hexagon, octagon — connection to tessellation.

modes.reason: Decomposition requires a systematic approach: draw diagonals from one vertex, count triangles, multiply by 180°. Students who decompose randomly get inconsistent results.

nodes.label: Finding unknown angles using angle sums
nodes.checkpoint: Students use triangle and polygon angle sum properties to find unknown angles, giving reasons.
criteria: Correctly finds unknown angles using angle sum properties.
States the property used as the reason for each step.
Applies the correct angle sum for the polygon type.

width.minimum: Find an unknown angle in a triangle or quadrilateral using the angle sum property.
width.typical: Solve multi-step problems combining angle sum, straight line, and parallel line properties; give geometric reasons.
wider: Solve problems involving isosceles triangles where the angle sum property combines with the equal base angles property.
Design angle puzzles for peers — create a figure with multiple unknown angles that can be found step by step.

modes.reason: Finding unknown angles requires students to select and apply the right angle property from their repertoire simultaneously — a genuine integration of angle sum, supplementary, and parallel line results.

descriptors.title: Mathematical modelling with ratios
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving ratios; formulate problems, interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation, justifying choices made about the representation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise, represent and solve ratio problems (from AC9M7N08). Students have used mathematical modelling in numerical contexts (from AC9M7N09).
descriptors.endpoint: Students use mathematical modelling to formulate and solve practical problems involving ratios of measurement quantities, communicating and justifying solutions in context.

nodes.label: Recognising ratio structure in measurement problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify when a practical measurement problem involves a ratio relationship and represent it using ratio notation.
criteria: Correctly identifies the ratio structure in a practical measurement problem.
Represents the ratio using appropriate notation.
Distinguishes part-part from part-whole ratio in context.

width.minimum: Identify the ratio relationship in a given practical measurement problem (e.g. mixing paint, scaling a recipe) and write it in a:b form.
width.typical: Distinguish part-part and part-whole ratio structures in measurement problems; represent both using diagrams and notation.
wider: Investigate ratio applications in scale drawings and maps — connect scale ratios to measurement.
Explore ratio in construction and design contexts: concrete mix ratios, fertiliser dilution rates.

modes.reason: Ratio problems in measurement span a wider variety of contexts than number strand ratio problems — scale, mix, division of space — and students need exposure to multiple contexts to recognise the common structure.

nodes.label: Formulating, solving and interpreting ratio models
nodes.checkpoint: Students formulate a ratio model for a practical measurement problem, solve it, and interpret and communicate the solution in terms of the original situation.
criteria: Formulates the ratio model correctly from the problem description.
Solves the problem and expresses the answer with appropriate measurement units.
Justifies the representation choice and checks the solution for reasonableness.

width.minimum: Formulate and solve a practical ratio problem (e.g. mixing liquids, dividing a length) and express the answer with appropriate units.
width.typical: Solve multi-step ratio problems in measurement contexts; justify representation choices; check reasonableness.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' applications of ratio in substances and land use — formulate and solve a contextualised ratio problem.
Model a design problem where a ratio constraint must be satisfied (e.g. designing a scale model at 1:50 ratio).

modes.reason: Formulating, solving and communicating a ratio model requires simultaneous application of ratio understanding, measurement, unit reasoning, and modelling conventions. This integration is the core learning.

descriptors.title: Perfect squares and square roots
descriptors.description: describe the relationship between perfect square numbers and square roots, and use squares of numbers and square roots of perfect square numbers to solve problems
descriptors.knowledge: Students can multiply and divide whole numbers fluently, use arrays to represent multiplication, and understand that area of a square = side × side (from Y6 measurement and number work).
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe the relationship between perfect square numbers and their square roots, and apply this relationship to solve problems including finding the perimeter of squares given area.

nodes.label: Squares as area models
nodes.checkpoint: Students can connect squaring a number to the area of a square with that side length, and list perfect square numbers from 1 to 144.
criteria: Lists perfect square numbers from 1² to 12² without error.
Represents a given perfect square as an area model and states its side length.
Does not confuse the square number with its root (e.g. does not say '9 squared is 3').
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who lack automatic recall of perfect squares to 144 cannot access the inverse relationship in Node 2 — the square root concept is not legible without the forward mapping being secure.

width.minimum: List perfect squares 1–144 and represent at least three using area diagrams.
width.typical: List perfect squares 1–400, connect each to its area diagram, and identify patterns in the sequence (e.g. differences between consecutive squares).
wider: Investigate the last-digit pattern in perfect squares (last digits cycle: 0,1,4,9,6,5,6,9,4,1,0) and use this to quickly rule out non-perfect-squares.
Explore why perfect squares always have an odd number of factors, connecting to divisibility.

modes.reason: Students need automatic recall of perfect squares to 144 before the square root relationship is legible. Fluency here is prerequisite to node 2.

nodes.label: Square root as inverse operation
nodes.checkpoint: Students understand that square root is the inverse of squaring and can find the exact square root of any perfect square up to 144.
criteria: States the square root of any perfect square from 1 to 144 when prompted.
Explains in words what √25 means ('the number that when multiplied by itself gives 25').
Does not conflate squaring with multiplying by 2.
nodes.hinge_reason: The squaring/doubling and √/halving misconceptions, if unresolved, produce systematic errors in Node 3 (bounding non-perfect squares) and Node 4 (applied problems) — students cannot reason about intervals or side lengths if the inverse relationship is confused.

width.minimum: Find the square root of any perfect square from 1 to 144 and explain what it means.
width.typical: Use √ notation fluently, explain the inverse relationship, and verify: √(n²) = n for concrete examples.
wider: Explore perfect squares beyond 144 (e.g. 169, 196, 225) using the area model and extend the pattern.
Investigate √(a × b) = √a × √b for perfect square cases (e.g. √36 = √4 × √9), building intuition without formalising the rule.

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse squaring with doubling (thinking 5² = 10) or treat √ as halving. Multiple concrete representations — area diagrams, calculator verification, number line — help resolve this.

nodes.label: Locating non-perfect square roots
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify which two consecutive integers a square root falls between for numbers that are not perfect squares.
criteria: For any given number, correctly identifies the two consecutive perfect squares it lies between.
States the corresponding square root interval (e.g. '√43 is between 6 and 7').
Explains the reasoning, not just the answer.

width.minimum: For a given non-perfect-square (e.g. 43), identify the two consecutive perfect squares it lies between and state the corresponding root interval.
width.typical: Estimate √n to one decimal place for non-perfect squares by reasoning about the interval, e.g. √43 ≈ 6.5.
wider: Use a number line marked with perfect squares to plot approximate positions of several non-perfect square roots.
Investigate: between which perfect squares does √200 fall? Extend to three-digit numbers.

modes.reason: Students need an explicit reasoning scaffold: 'find the perfect squares either side, take their roots, the answer lies between'. Without this structure students often guess randomly or over-rely on a calculator without understanding the bounds.

nodes.label: Applying square roots to problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students use the relationship between perfect square numbers and square roots to solve practical problems, including finding the side length of a square given its area.
criteria: Given the area of a square, correctly determines the side length using square root reasoning.
Solves a two-step problem involving squares and square roots in a practical context.
Checks that their answer is reasonable (e.g. side length must be positive).

width.minimum: Given the area of a square, find its side length and perimeter using square root reasoning.
width.typical: Solve a range of problems involving squares and square roots in practical contexts (tile layouts, garden beds, square frames) including problems requiring identification of perfect square areas.
wider: Design a problem involving square tiles covering a floor area that requires checking whether a given area is a perfect square.
Connect to Pythagoras preparation: identify whether a² + b² is a perfect square for simple triples (3,4,5).

modes.reason: The transition from abstract square root to applied problem-solving requires varied contexts — students who only practise decontextualised calculations often fail to recognise when square root is the required operation in a problem.
This node connects squaring, square roots, area, and perimeter simultaneously — coordinating these is the learning.

descriptors.title: Prime factorisation and exponent notation
descriptors.description: represent natural numbers as products of powers of prime numbers using exponent notation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify prime and composite numbers and know their basic properties (from AC9M6N02). Students can use factor trees to find factors of numbers.
descriptors.endpoint: Students represent any natural number as a product of powers of prime factors using exponent notation, and apply this to find lowest common multiples and greatest common divisors.

nodes.label: Exponent notation for repeated multiplication
nodes.checkpoint: Students understand exponent notation as shorthand for repeated multiplication and can convert between expanded and exponent forms.
criteria: Correctly converts between repeated multiplication and exponent notation.
States the meaning of the base and exponent in a given expression.
Does not confuse aⁿ with a×n (e.g. does not evaluate 2³ as 6).
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot fluently read and write exponent notation cannot record or interpret prime factorisation results in Node 2 — the symbolic system is the medium for all subsequent work in this standard.

width.minimum: Write 2×2×2×2 as 2⁴ and vice versa for small bases and exponents.
width.typical: Convert fluently between repeated multiplication and exponent notation for bases 2, 3, 5, 7 and small exponents; state what the base and exponent each mean.
wider: Investigate the sequence 2¹, 2², 2³, ... and connect to powers of 2 in computing contexts (bytes, storage).
Explore 10¹, 10², 10³ and connect to place value notation (links to AC9M7N03).

modes.reason: Exponent notation is a new symbolic system. Students need fluency reading and writing it before applying it to prime factorisation.

nodes.label: Prime factorisation via factor trees
nodes.checkpoint: Students can express any natural number as a product of prime factors using a factor tree, and write the result using exponent notation.
criteria: Produces a correct factor tree and writes the result in exponent notation.
Verifies the factorisation by expanding and multiplying.
Understands that the prime factorisation of a number is unique.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who believe prime factorisation is non-unique cannot apply the LCM/GCD algorithm in Node 3 correctly — the entire method depends on there being one canonical factorisation to compare.

width.minimum: Use a factor tree to find the prime factorisation of a given composite number (e.g. 36 = 2² × 3²).
width.typical: Find prime factorisations for a range of composite numbers including larger ones (e.g. 360), write results in exponent notation, and verify by expanding.
wider: Show that different factor trees for the same number always yield the same prime factorisation (Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic — informally).
Investigate which numbers have only one prime factor (powers of primes) and what their factor trees look like.

modes.reason: Students often believe different factor trees can produce different prime factorisations. Seeing multiple paths to the same result across several numbers resolves this misconception.

nodes.label: LCM and GCD from prime factorisations
nodes.checkpoint: Students use prime factorisations to find the lowest common multiple and greatest common divisor of pairs of natural numbers.
criteria: Correctly finds LCM and GCD for a given pair using prime factorisations.
Can explain why the method works (not just apply it).
Applies LCM or GCD appropriately when presented with a contextual problem.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot apply the systematic LCM/GCD algorithm from prime factorisations revert to listing methods — this blocks the connection to AC9M7N04 fraction simplification and AC9M7N06 common denominator work where the prime factorisation method is the efficient path.

width.minimum: Find the LCM and GCD of two numbers using their prime factorisations.
width.typical: Apply the LCM and GCD in context: e.g. find when two cyclic events coincide (LCM), or find the largest equal shares (GCD).
wider: Explore the relationship LCM(a,b) × GCD(a,b) = a × b and verify for several pairs.
Apply LCM to scheduling problems: if two buses leave every 12 and 18 minutes, when do they next leave together?

modes.reason: The algorithm (take highest power of each prime for LCM; lowest power for GCD) requires an explicit systematic scaffold. Students who proceed by listing multiples/factors miss the prime factorisation connection.
LCM and GCD require coordinating prime factorisation, exponent comparison, and contextual interpretation simultaneously.

descriptors.title: Expanded notation and powers of 10
descriptors.description: represent natural numbers in expanded notation using place value and powers of 10
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand place value for large whole numbers and can multiply and divide by powers of 10 (from AC9M6N06). Students can write numbers in expanded form using place value (e.g. 7000 = 7 × 1000).
descriptors.endpoint: Students represent natural numbers in expanded notation using powers of 10, and explain the connection between place value and exponent notation.

nodes.label: Powers of 10 as place value columns
nodes.checkpoint: Students connect each place value column to a power of 10 and write powers of 10 in exponent notation (10⁰=1, 10¹=10, 10²=100, etc.).
criteria: Correctly states the power of 10 corresponding to each place value column up to millions.
Writes 10⁰ = 1 and explains why.
Does not confuse the exponent with the value (e.g. does not say 10³ = 30).
nodes.hinge_reason: Students with a patchy place-value-to-power mapping produce systematic errors in Node 2 — wrong exponents mean wrong expanded forms, and the entire purpose of this descriptor is lost.

width.minimum: Match place value columns (ones, tens, hundreds, thousands) to their corresponding power of 10 and write each in exponent notation.
width.typical: Extend to at least 10⁶; explain why 10⁰ = 1; connect the exponent to the number of zeros.
wider: Investigate 10⁻¹, 10⁻², 10⁻³ as a preview of decimal place value extending the pattern.
Connect to scientific notation contexts: the diameter of Earth is approximately 1.27 × 10⁷ metres.

modes.reason: The mapping of place value to powers of 10 must be automatic before expanded notation is learnable. Students who have this mapping patchy make systematic errors in node 2.

nodes.label: Expanded notation using powers of 10
nodes.checkpoint: Students write any natural number in expanded notation using powers of 10 (e.g. 7000 = 7 × 10³) and convert back from expanded to standard form.
criteria: Correctly writes any given natural number in expanded notation using powers of 10.
Reconstructs a number correctly from its expanded notation.
Explains what each term in the expanded form represents.

width.minimum: Write a given 4–5 digit number in expanded notation using powers of 10 and reconstruct a number from expanded notation.
width.typical: Work fluently with expanded notation for numbers up to 7 digits; identify the value of each digit expressed as a power of 10.
wider: Compare expanded notation with and without exponents (e.g. 7×1000 vs 7×10³) and explain what the exponent adds.
Explore how expanded notation makes computation transparent: why is 6300 × 100 = 6300 × 10² easy to compute mentally?

modes.reason: Students who only see standard expanded form (7×1000 + 3×100) often fail to make the connection to exponent notation. Multiple representations across the same numbers are needed.

descriptors.title: Rational numbers on a number line
descriptors.description: find equivalent representations of rational numbers and represent rational numbers on a number line
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare and order fractions using equivalence, add and subtract fractions, and convert between simple fractions and decimals (from AC9M6N03, AC9M6N04, AC9M6N07). Students understand percentage as parts per hundred.
descriptors.endpoint: Students find equivalent representations of rational numbers across fraction, decimal and percentage forms, simplify fractions, and place positive and negative fractions and mixed numerals on a number line.

nodes.label: Equivalence and simplification of fractions
nodes.checkpoint: Students find equivalent fractions using common multiples and express fractions in simplest form using common divisors.
criteria: Generates multiple equivalent fractions for a given fraction.
Correctly simplifies a fraction to lowest terms.
Can explain why the fractions are equivalent (multiplying/dividing numerator and denominator by the same value).
nodes.hinge_reason: Simplification errors propagate into every subsequent conversion and operation with rational numbers — Node 2 conversions, Node 3 number line placement, and all of AC9M7N06 depend on fractions being in comparable forms.

width.minimum: Find two equivalent fractions for a given fraction and simplify a fraction to its lowest terms.
width.typical: Use the fraction wall and number line to verify equivalence; apply simplification in computation contexts.
wider: Investigate what the simplest form of a fraction tells you about the relationship between numerator and denominator (coprime numbers).
Connect simplification to GCD from AC9M7N02: simplest form means GCD(numerator, denominator) = 1.

modes.reason: Fraction equivalence and simplification underpin every subsequent operation with rational numbers. Precision here matters — small errors in simplification compound.

nodes.label: Converting between fraction, decimal and percentage
nodes.checkpoint: Students convert fluently between fraction, decimal and percentage representations of rational numbers.
criteria: Correctly converts a given rational number between fraction, decimal and percentage forms.
Identifies when representations are equivalent without performing full conversion.
Does not confuse 0.5 with 5% (confusing decimal and percentage forms).

width.minimum: Convert a given rational number between all three representations (fraction, decimal, percentage) for common values.
width.typical: Explain the conversion process for each direction; identify equivalent representations for less familiar fractions (e.g. 3/8 = 0.375 = 37.5%).
wider: Investigate repeating decimals (e.g. 1/3 = 0.333...) and understand these as rational numbers.
Explore how percentage, decimal and fraction choices affect ease of computation in different contexts.

modes.reason: Students often have strong conversion skills in one direction (fraction to decimal) but poor skills in others. Encountering the same rational number across varied contexts and conversion directions resolves partial understanding.

nodes.label: Rational numbers on the number line
nodes.checkpoint: Students place positive and negative fractions, decimals and mixed numerals accurately on a number line, including intervals other than 0–1.
criteria: Correctly places a given set of rational numbers (including negatives and mixed numerals) on a number line.
Selects and labels appropriate scale for the interval.
Correctly orders the set from least to greatest.

width.minimum: Plot a given set of positive and negative fractions and mixed numerals on a number line with appropriate scale.
width.typical: Construct a number line for a given interval, select appropriate scale, and place a mixed set of rational numbers including fractions, decimals and percentages on it.
wider: Given a number line with some rational numbers marked, identify and justify the positions of unlabelled points.
Explore density of rational numbers: between any two rational numbers, find another — repeat and discuss what this implies.

modes.reason: Placing negative fractions requires a reasoning scaffold: students must convert to a comparable form and reason about which direction is more negative. Without explicit steps, students often mirror positive fractions incorrectly.

descriptors.title: Rounding and estimation
descriptors.description: round decimals to a given accuracy appropriate to the context and use appropriate rounding and estimation to check the reasonableness of solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can round whole numbers and simple decimals. Students understand decimal place value and can multiply/divide decimals by powers of 10 (from AC9M6N04, AC9M6N06).
descriptors.endpoint: Students round decimals to a specified accuracy appropriate to the context and use estimation to judge whether solutions are reasonable.

nodes.label: Rounding decimals to specified places
nodes.checkpoint: Students round decimals to a given number of decimal places using standard rounding conventions.
criteria: Correctly rounds a decimal to a specified number of decimal places.
Applies the 'round half up' convention consistently.
Does not confuse rounding to 2 decimal places with rounding to the nearest 100.

width.minimum: Round a decimal to 1, 2 or 3 decimal places as specified.
width.typical: Round to specified decimal places across a range of contexts; explain the rounding rule and why the convention exists.
wider: Investigate contexts where rounding up or rounding down is more appropriate than standard rounding (e.g. buying enough paint — always round up).
Explore the effect of rounding at each step of a multi-step calculation vs rounding only at the end.

modes.reason: Students who only practise decontextualised rounding often fail to select appropriate accuracy in context. Varied practical contexts are needed to build judgment about what 'appropriate' means.

nodes.label: Context-appropriate accuracy
nodes.checkpoint: Students choose an appropriate level of rounding for a given context and explain why that accuracy is suitable.
criteria: Selects a contextually appropriate level of decimal accuracy and justifies it.
Recognises that different contexts require different precision.
Can explain why rounding to too many places can give a false sense of precision.

width.minimum: Given a practical problem (e.g. measuring fabric, calculating cost), state appropriate rounding and justify the choice.
width.typical: Compare the effect of different levels of rounding across several contexts and evaluate which is most appropriate for each.
wider: Investigate situations where over-precision misleads (e.g. reporting a population estimate to the nearest unit).
Discuss how measurement accuracy relates to rounding: a ruler accurate to 1mm supports reporting to 1dp in cm.

modes.reason: Judging appropriate accuracy requires a reasoning process students rarely apply spontaneously: What is the purpose of the answer? What precision is the measurement tool capable of? Does the context require over- or under-estimation?

nodes.label: Estimation to check reasonableness
nodes.checkpoint: Students use estimation strategies (front-end, rounding, compatible numbers) to check whether a calculated solution is reasonable.
criteria: Produces a reasonable estimate before or after computing.
Identifies whether a given answer is unreasonable based on estimation.
Explains the estimation strategy used.

width.minimum: Estimate the answer to a calculation and compare with the computed result to check reasonableness.
width.typical: Apply multiple estimation strategies; identify when a computed answer is unreasonable and diagnose the likely error.
wider: Use estimation as a first step in multi-step problems to set bounds on the expected answer before computing.
Investigate how a calculator error (e.g. missing a decimal point) is caught by estimation.

modes.reason: Estimation as a reasonableness check only becomes habitual across a wide variety of problem types. Students who practise estimation only in drill exercises rarely apply it spontaneously in problem-solving.

descriptors.title: Four operations with rational numbers
descriptors.description: use the 4 operations with positive rational numbers including fractions, decimals and percentages to solve problems using efficient calculation strategies
descriptors.knowledge: Students can add and subtract fractions using equivalence, and multiply and divide decimals (from AC9M6N05, AC9M6N06). Students can find percentages of quantities (from AC9M6N07).
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply all four operations to positive rational numbers including fractions, decimals and percentages, selecting efficient strategies appropriate to the numbers and context.

nodes.label: Addition and subtraction of fractions and decimals
nodes.checkpoint: Students add and subtract fractions (including mixed numerals) and decimals fluently, using common denominators and place value alignment.
criteria: Correctly adds and subtracts fractions with unlike denominators.
Correctly adds and subtracts decimals using place value alignment.
Does not add numerators and denominators directly when adding fractions.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students without fluency in addition and subtraction of fractions and decimals cannot access Node 2 multiplication and division, which require the same fraction manipulation skills — errors here propagate into every subsequent rational number operation.

width.minimum: Add and subtract two fractions with unlike denominators; add and subtract decimals to at least 2 decimal places.
width.typical: Solve multi-step addition and subtraction problems mixing fractions and decimals; choose efficient representations (e.g. convert to decimals when convenient).
wider: Investigate when it is more efficient to work with fractions vs decimals for addition and subtraction — develop personal decision rules.
Explore adding fractions with large unlike denominators using LCM from AC9M7N02.

modes.reason: Addition and subtraction of fractions requires procedural fluency (finding common denominators, converting mixed numerals) before multiplication and division can be layered on.

nodes.label: Multiplication and division of fractions and decimals
nodes.checkpoint: Students multiply and divide fractions and decimals using appropriate strategies including area models and algorithm.
criteria: Correctly multiplies two fractions and simplifies the result.
Correctly divides a fraction by a whole number or simple fraction.
Does not apply addition rules (common denominator) to multiplication.
nodes.hinge_reason: The misconception that multiplication always makes larger (and division always makes smaller) persists through to Node 3 percentage calculations and Node 4 strategy selection — students who hold this belief cannot reason about whether their percentage or fraction computation is in the right range.

width.minimum: Multiply two fractions; divide a fraction by a whole number; multiply and divide decimals by whole numbers.
width.typical: Multiply and divide fractions by fractions; multiply and divide decimals; apply distributive and associative properties to simplify.
wider: Investigate why multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes a number smaller — connect to area model.
Explore the 'invert and multiply' rule for fraction division with a concrete justification.

modes.reason: Fraction multiplication and division is the most common site for persistent misconceptions. Multiple representations (area model, number line, algorithm) across varied contexts are needed to build robust understanding.

nodes.label: Operations with percentages
nodes.checkpoint: Students calculate percentages of quantities and solve problems involving percentage increase, decrease, and finding the whole given a percentage.
criteria: Correctly finds a percentage of a quantity using an efficient method.
Solves a percentage increase or decrease problem correctly.
Selects an appropriate representation (fraction, decimal, or percentage) for efficient computation.

width.minimum: Find a given percentage of a quantity; find what percentage one quantity is of another.
width.typical: Solve problems involving percentage increase and decrease; select efficient strategy (mental, fraction, or decimal multiplication).
wider: Investigate percentage change in financial contexts: GST, discounts, interest — connecting to AC9M7N09.
Explore how the choice of representation (fraction vs decimal vs percentage) affects computational efficiency for the same problem.

modes.reason: Percentage problems span a wide range of structures (find the percentage, find the quantity, find the whole). Students who only practise one structure fail to recognise others. Multiple problem structures across varied contexts are essential.

nodes.label: Efficient strategy selection
nodes.checkpoint: Students choose the most efficient calculation strategy for a given rational number problem, drawing on number properties and representation choices.
criteria: Selects and applies an efficient strategy (not just the standard algorithm) for a given computation.
Justifies why the chosen strategy is efficient.
Applies at least one number property (commutative, associative, distributive) explicitly.

width.minimum: Given a problem, identify and apply at least one efficient strategy, justifying why it is more efficient than a standard algorithm.
width.typical: Compare strategies for the same problem and evaluate efficiency; apply commutative, associative and distributive properties consciously.
wider: Construct a personal reference of 'efficiency rules' for rational number computation — when to use mental, when to use fraction form, when to use decimal.
Investigate how spreadsheet formulas encode these strategies and compare outputs.

modes.reason: Efficient strategy selection requires students to draw on all prior nodes simultaneously — representations, operations, number properties. The integration of these is the learning at this node.

descriptors.title: Add and subtract integers
descriptors.description: compare, order and solve problems involving addition and subtraction of integers
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate integers on a number line and recognise negative integers in context (from AC9M6N01). Students understand magnitude and direction in simple contexts (above/below zero, gain/loss).
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare and order integers using inequality notation and solve problems involving addition and subtraction of integers.

nodes.label: Comparing and ordering integers
nodes.checkpoint: Students compare and order integers using less-than and greater-than notation, including negative integers.
criteria: Correctly orders a set of integers including negatives.
Uses < and > notation correctly between integers.
Does not confuse the magnitude of a negative with its value (e.g. understands −10 < −1).
nodes.hinge_reason: The magnitude-vs-direction confusion (believing −7 > −2) produces systematic errors in Node 2 addition and subtraction — students who cannot correctly order integers cannot set up or check integer calculations.

width.minimum: Order a given set of integers (including negatives) from least to greatest and use <, > notation to compare pairs.
width.typical: Place a mixed set of integers on a number line; use inequality notation in expressions; explain why −7 < −2.
wider: Investigate absolute value informally: distance from zero on a number line. Compare |−7| and |2| without formal notation.
Connect ordering to real contexts: temperature below zero, sea level, financial debt.

modes.reason: Students commonly believe −7 > −2 because 7 > 2. Multiple real-world contexts (temperature, floors below ground, financial loss) help resolve the magnitude vs direction confusion.

nodes.label: Addition and subtraction of integers
nodes.checkpoint: Students add and subtract integers using a number line and understand the effect of adding or subtracting a negative number.
criteria: Correctly adds and subtracts integers including cases with negative operands.
Interprets adding a negative number as movement in the negative direction.
Does not treat subtraction of a negative as subtraction (e.g. 5 − (−3) = 8, not 2).
nodes.hinge_reason: The operation-sign/number-sign confusion produces persistent errors in AC9M7N06 rational number operations and AC9M7N09 modelling contexts — students who cannot confidently add and subtract integers cannot handle any signed number computation downstream.

width.minimum: Calculate simple integer additions and subtractions using a number line (e.g. −3 + 5, 4 − 7, −2 − 3).
width.typical: Calculate integer sums and differences without a number line; interpret addition of a negative and subtraction of a negative; apply in context.
wider: Investigate the pattern: subtracting a negative equals adding a positive — explain using number line movement.
Explore temperature change problems requiring chaining multiple integer additions and subtractions.

modes.reason: Integer addition and subtraction is a major misconception site. Students confuse the sign of the number with the operation sign. Number line contexts, thermometer contexts, and financial contexts each address different facets of the misconception.

The rule 'subtract a negative = add a positive' requires explicit reasoning: movement on a number line combined with meaning of the operation. Without scaffolding, students apply rules inconsistently.

descriptors.title: Ratios
descriptors.description: recognise, represent and solve problems involving ratios
descriptors.knowledge: Students can find fractions and percentages of quantities (from AC9M6N07). Students have experience with part-whole relationships and multiplicative thinking (from AC9M6N08, AC9M6N09).
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise and represent ratios, distinguish part-part from part-whole relationships, share quantities in given ratios, and apply ratios to practical problems.

nodes.label: Ratio as a relationship between quantities
nodes.checkpoint: Students recognise that a ratio expresses a multiplicative relationship between two quantities and can represent ratios using diagrams and notation.
criteria: Writes a given ratio correctly in a:b notation.
Distinguishes between part-part and part-whole interpretations of a ratio.
Represents a ratio accurately using a diagram.

width.minimum: Represent a given ratio using diagrams (e.g. bar model) and write it in ratio notation a:b.
width.typical: Distinguish part-part and part-whole interpretations of the same situation; represent both and explain the difference.
wider: Investigate equivalent ratios (simplifying and scaling) and connect to equivalent fractions.
Explore ratios in design contexts: aspect ratios of screens, mixing colours, recipe scaling.

modes.reason: Students frequently confuse part-part and part-whole ratio interpretations. Multiple contexts where both interpretations are valid (e.g. 2 red, 3 blue beads: 2:3 part-part; 2:5 red-to-total) are needed to resolve this.

nodes.label: Equivalent ratios and simplification
nodes.checkpoint: Students find equivalent ratios by scaling up and down, and express a ratio in simplest form.
criteria: Correctly simplifies a ratio to lowest terms.
Generates equivalent ratios by multiplying or dividing both parts by the same value.
Does not confuse simplifying a ratio with subtracting the same value from both parts.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot generate equivalent ratios and simplify cannot execute the sharing algorithm in Node 3 — finding the value of one part requires the ratio to be in a form they can work with.

width.minimum: Generate two equivalent ratios for a given ratio; simplify a ratio to its simplest form.
width.typical: Use equivalent ratios to solve scaling problems (e.g. scale up a recipe); verify equivalence using unit rates.
wider: Connect equivalent ratios to the concept of a unit rate (1:n form) and use unit rates for comparison.
Investigate how ratios are used in maps and scale drawings.

modes.reason: Equivalent ratios underpin sharing and all ratio problem types. Students need fluency before applying ratios in multi-step problems.

nodes.label: Sharing in a given ratio
nodes.checkpoint: Students share a quantity in a given ratio and solve related problems.
criteria: Correctly shares a quantity in a two-part ratio.
Identifies the total number of parts in the ratio.
Can work backwards from a share to find the total quantity.

width.minimum: Divide a given quantity in a given two-part ratio (e.g. share $60 in ratio 2:3).
width.typical: Solve sharing problems in two- and three-part ratios; work backwards from a share to find the total.
wider: Investigate profit-sharing problems involving three or more partners in different ratios.
Apply sharing in ratio to real proportional contexts: mixing paint, sharing resources on Country.

modes.reason: Sharing in ratio requires a systematic approach (find total parts, find value of one part, multiply). Students who try to proceed intuitively make errors with non-obvious ratios. An explicit scaffold is necessary.

descriptors.title: Mathematical modelling with rational numbers
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems, involving rational numbers and percentages, including financial contexts; formulate problems, choosing representations and efficient calculation strategies, using digital tools as appropriate; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation, justifying choices made about the representation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply the four operations to rational numbers, work with percentages, and solve ratio problems (from AC9M7N06, AC9M7N08). Students have experience with mathematical modelling in prior years (from AC9M6N09).
descriptors.endpoint: Students formulate, solve and interpret mathematical models involving rational numbers and percentages in practical contexts, justifying representation choices and communicating solutions in terms of the situation.

nodes.label: Formulating a model from a practical problem
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify the mathematical structure of a practical problem and choose an appropriate representation (fraction, decimal, percentage, or ratio) to model it.
criteria: Correctly identifies the operation and representation needed for a given practical problem.
States any assumptions made in setting up the model.
Does not start calculating before identifying the model structure.

width.minimum: Given a practical problem, identify what operation and representation are needed and set up the calculation.
width.typical: Identify when a problem requires a model rather than direct calculation; articulate assumptions made in setting up the model.
wider: Compare how different representations model the same situation (e.g. profit as percentage increase vs dollar value) and discuss what each makes visible.
Investigate how simplifying assumptions affect the model's accuracy.

modes.reason: Formulating a model is the step students most commonly skip, jumping to calculation. An explicit scaffold — identify known, unknown, relationship — is needed before students apply it spontaneously.

nodes.label: Solving and interpreting in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students solve a mathematical model and interpret the result in terms of the original situation, checking reasonableness.
criteria: Expresses the solution in contextually appropriate terms (correct units, reasonable precision).
Checks the reasonableness of the solution using estimation.
Does not present a raw number without contextual interpretation.

width.minimum: Solve a modelled problem correctly and express the answer in contextually appropriate terms.
width.typical: Solve multi-step modelling problems in financial and proportional contexts; use digital tools where appropriate; verify reasonableness with estimation.
wider: Investigate financial modelling: simple budget scenarios involving income, expenses, profit and loss with percentage components.
Model proportion problems using First Nations Australians' contexts (land area proportions, resource allocation).

modes.reason: Interpretation in context is a distinct skill from calculation. Students who can compute correctly frequently give answers without units, in wrong form, or without checking reasonableness. Varied practical contexts build the habit of contextual interpretation.

nodes.label: Justifying representation choices
nodes.checkpoint: Students justify why they chose a particular representation and calculation strategy, and communicate this reasoning clearly.
criteria: Justifies representation choices with reference to the problem context and computation efficiency.
Communicates the solution process, not just the answer.
Can identify a more efficient representation when presented with an inefficient one.

width.minimum: Explain in words why they chose a particular representation (fraction, decimal, percentage) for a given problem.
width.typical: Compare two possible representations for the same problem, evaluate which is more efficient, and justify the choice.
wider: Critique a given solution that uses an inefficient or inappropriate representation — identify the problem and rewrite.
Investigate: when would a percentage model be misleading? (e.g. 50% increase then 50% decrease ≠ original value).

modes.reason: Justification draws on all prior number work simultaneously — representation choices, operation strategies, contextual meaning. The integration and articulation of these is the learning at this node.

descriptors.title: Sample space and probability
descriptors.description: identify the sample space for single-stage events; assign probabilities to the outcomes of these events and predict relative frequencies for related events
descriptors.knowledge: Students can assign probabilities on a 0–1 scale using fractions, percentages and decimals (from AC9M6P01). Students have experience with probability language and listing outcomes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify sample spaces for single-stage events, assign probabilities to outcomes, and use these to predict relative frequencies.

nodes.label: Identifying and listing sample spaces
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify the sample space for a single-stage event and list all possible outcomes systematically.
criteria: Lists a complete sample space for a given single-stage event.
Explains what sample space means.
Verifies completeness (all outcomes accounted for).
nodes.hinge_reason: An incomplete sample space produces wrong probability fractions for all outcomes in Node 2 — if an outcome is missing from the sample space, every other outcome gets an inflated probability and the probabilities cannot sum to 1.

width.minimum: List the sample space for a coin toss and a standard die roll; explain what sample space means.
width.typical: List sample spaces for spinners, lucky dips, and card draws; verify the sample space is complete by confirming all outcomes are mutually exclusive and exhaustive.
wider: Investigate sample spaces with unequal likelihood outcomes — can outcomes still be listed even if not equally likely?
Compare sample spaces for different versions of the same game (6-sided vs 8-sided die).

modes.reason: Systematic, complete listing of a sample space is prerequisite to assigning probabilities. Students who list incomplete sample spaces assign wrong probabilities to all outcomes.

nodes.label: Assigning probabilities to outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students assign theoretical probabilities to outcomes of a single-stage event using P = favourable/total and express these as fractions, decimals or percentages.
criteria: Correctly assigns the probability to each outcome in a sample space.
Verifies that all probabilities sum to 1.
Expresses probability in the most appropriate form for the context.

width.minimum: Assign the probability of each outcome for a fair die roll; express as a fraction.
width.typical: Assign probabilities for events with unequal outcomes (e.g. spinners with unequal sectors); express in fraction, decimal and percentage forms; verify probabilities sum to 1.
wider: Investigate non-fair devices: if a spinner has sectors of 1/4, 1/4, and 1/2, assign probabilities and verify.
Connect probability fractions to relative frequency: a probability of 1/6 means in the long run about 1 in every 6 outcomes.

modes.reason: Students often believe probability only applies to fair devices. Encountering non-fair devices (biased coins, unequal spinners) generalises their understanding.

nodes.label: Predicting relative frequencies
nodes.checkpoint: Students use theoretical probability to predict how often an outcome will occur in a given number of trials.
criteria: Correctly predicts the relative frequency for a given number of trials.
Understands that predictions are expected values, not certainties.
Can adjust predictions for non-fair devices.

width.minimum: Predict the number of times an outcome will occur in 60 trials given its probability.
width.typical: Predict relative frequencies for multiple outcomes; compare predictions to simulated results; explain discrepancies.
wider: Investigate how the accuracy of predictions improves with more trials — connect to AC9M7P02.
Apply relative frequency prediction to real decisions: fairness of a game, likelihood of an event occurring.

modes.reason: Predicting relative frequencies requires connecting probability, multiplication, and the meaning of the sample space — integrating all prior nodes.

descriptors.title: Repeated experiments and simulation
descriptors.description: conduct repeated chance experiments and run simulations with a large number of trials using digital tools; compare predictions about outcomes with observed results, explaining the differences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can assign probabilities and predict relative frequencies (from AC9M7P01). Students have run simulations with increasing trials (from AC9M6P02).
descriptors.endpoint: Students conduct repeated experiments and simulations to observe that relative frequencies approach theoretical probability as the number of trials increases, and explain differences between predicted and observed results.

nodes.label: Running experiments and recording results
nodes.checkpoint: Students conduct repeated chance experiments and record observed frequencies systematically.
criteria: Records observed frequencies in an organised frequency table.
Calculates relative frequency from observed results.
Compares observed relative frequency to theoretical probability.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who record inconsistently cannot generate reliable relative frequencies for Node 2 comparison — without a systematic cumulative record, the convergence pattern of the law of large numbers is invisible in the data.

width.minimum: Conduct a simple chance experiment (e.g. coin toss) for at least 20 trials and record results in a frequency table.
width.typical: Conduct experiments for increasing numbers of trials; record cumulative results; compare observed frequency to predicted frequency at each stage.
wider: Use digital tools to run simulations of the same experiment with 100, 1000, 10000 trials — record and compare results.
Investigate First Nations Australian children's instructive games as probability experiments — record and analyse outcomes.

modes.reason: Systematic data recording is prerequisite to any comparison between experimental and theoretical probability. Students who record inconsistently cannot see the law of large numbers pattern.

nodes.label: Law of large numbers — observed vs predicted
nodes.checkpoint: Students observe that relative frequencies become closer to theoretical probability as the number of trials increases, and explain why short-run results may differ from predictions.
criteria: States that relative frequencies approach theoretical probability as trials increase.
Explains why short-run results can differ significantly from predictions.
Does not commit the gambler's fallacy (thinking past outcomes affect future probabilities).

width.minimum: Explain why 3 heads from 10 coin tosses does not mean the coin is unfair, using the idea that more trials are needed.
width.typical: Use simulation data to show relative frequencies converging toward theoretical probability over many trials; describe the pattern in their own words.
wider: Investigate: how many trials are needed before the relative frequency is consistently within 5% of the theoretical probability?
Apply the law of large numbers to real contexts: insurance companies and casinos rely on this — explain how.

modes.reason: The law of large numbers is counter-intuitive to students who expect short runs to match predictions. Multiple experiments with different devices, each showing the same convergence pattern, build the generalised understanding.

descriptors.title: 2D representations of 3D objects
descriptors.description: represent objects in 2 dimensions; discuss and reason about the advantages and disadvantages of different representations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare parallel cross-sections and recognise their relationship to right prisms (from AC9M6SP01). Students have informal experience with drawings of 3D objects.
descriptors.endpoint: Students represent 3D objects using nets, isometric drawings, and plan/elevation views, and reason about the advantages and disadvantages of each representation.

nodes.label: Nets of prisms and other 3D objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify, draw and construct nets of prisms and other common 3D objects.
criteria: Correctly identifies valid nets for a cube and rectangular prism.
Draws a net that folds correctly to produce a given 3D object.
Does not include overlapping faces in a net.

width.minimum: Identify which nets will fold to make a cube or rectangular prism; draw a net for a triangular prism.
width.typical: Test multiple possible nets for the same object; identify which are valid; construct 3D objects from nets.
wider: Investigate how many valid nets a cube has (11) — systematically find them all.
Design and construct nets for less familiar solids (square pyramid, cylinder).

modes.reason: Students develop spatial reasoning for nets by working with multiple 3D objects. Restricting practice to cubes gives a false sense of mastery that fails with other prisms.

nodes.label: Isometric and plan/elevation drawings
nodes.checkpoint: Students draw and interpret isometric drawings and plan/elevation views (front, back, side, top) of 3D objects.
criteria: Correctly draws at least two views of a 3D object.
Reconstructs a 3D object from its views.
Does not confuse view orientation (e.g. top vs front).
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who produce inconsistent views cannot reason about representation trade-offs in Node 3 — they cannot evaluate whether a net or isometric view is more useful without being able to correctly produce and read both.

width.minimum: Construct at least two views (e.g. top and front) of a given 3D object; interpret an isometric drawing.
width.typical: Draw all standard views of a given object; build an object from its views; use isometric paper to draw 3D objects.
wider: Interpret aerial/isometric views of real buildings or structures and identify the 3D object they represent.
Investigate 2D representations in First Nations Australian art — discuss what spatial information is conveyed.

modes.reason: Interpreting and drawing 2D representations of 3D objects requires systematic reasoning: which face is visible from each view? Students who proceed intuitively produce inconsistent views.

nodes.label: Advantages and disadvantages of different representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students reason about when each type of 2D representation is most useful and what information each preserves or loses.
criteria: States at least one advantage and one disadvantage for two different representations.
Selects an appropriate representation for a given purpose and justifies the choice.
Recognises that no single representation shows all information about a 3D object.

width.minimum: Identify one advantage and one disadvantage of using a net vs an isometric drawing for the same object.
width.typical: Compare representations for a range of objects and purposes; match the representation to the task (e.g. net for construction, isometric for communication).
wider: Investigate professional contexts: architects use plans, packaging designers use nets, engineers use orthographic views — discuss why.
Evaluate: which representation best communicates a given 3D design decision?

modes.reason: Reasoning about representation trade-offs requires familiarity with all representation types simultaneously — this node integrates the prior two nodes.

descriptors.title: Classifying triangles and polygons
descriptors.description: classify triangles, quadrilaterals and other polygons according to their side and angle properties; identify and reason about relationships
descriptors.knowledge: Students have informal familiarity with shape names and basic properties. Students can measure angles and sides.
descriptors.endpoint: Students classify triangles and quadrilaterals using side and angle properties and reason about hierarchical relationships between shape families.

nodes.label: Classifying triangles by sides and angles
nodes.checkpoint: Students classify triangles as scalene, isosceles or equilateral (by sides) and as acute, right-angled or obtuse (by angles), and understand that these classifications are independent.
criteria: Correctly classifies a triangle by both side and angle properties.
Understands that the two classifications are independent.
Does not assume equilateral means right-angled.

width.minimum: Classify a given triangle by both its side and angle properties.
width.typical: Classify a range of triangles; identify that a triangle can be e.g. isosceles and right-angled simultaneously; investigate which combinations are possible.
wider: Construct triangles with given side lengths and determine which combinations are possible (triangle inequality).
Investigate which combinations of side-type and angle-type are possible vs impossible (e.g. can a triangle be equilateral and obtuse?).

modes.reason: Students often treat side classification and angle classification as mutually exclusive. Encountering diverse triangles that require both labels simultaneously resolves this.

nodes.label: Classifying quadrilaterals and their relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students classify quadrilaterals (square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, kite, trapezium) using side and angle properties, and identify hierarchical relationships.
criteria: Correctly classifies any standard quadrilateral using its properties.
States at least two hierarchical relationships between quadrilateral types.
Does not rely on orientation to classify (e.g. recognises a rotated square).
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who classify by appearance rather than properties cannot design reliable classification algorithms in AC9M7SP04 — the algorithm requires specifying testable property conditions, not visual recognition rules.

width.minimum: Classify a given quadrilateral and state the properties used.
width.typical: Describe, compare and contrast all quadrilateral types; explain hierarchical relationships (e.g. all squares are rectangles, not all rectangles are squares).
wider: Construct a hierarchy diagram (Venn or tree) of quadrilaterals showing subset relationships.
Investigate which quadrilateral properties are necessary vs sufficient for classification.

modes.reason: Hierarchical classification requires deliberate reasoning about necessary and sufficient conditions. Students who classify by appearance alone fail with non-standard orientations and confuse the hierarchy.

nodes.label: Classifying other polygons and reasoning about properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students classify polygons by number of sides and by regularity, and reason about properties such as line symmetry and convexity.
criteria: Correctly classifies polygons by name, regularity, and convexity.
Explains what makes a polygon regular.
Can identify whether a polygon is convex or concave and explain the difference.

width.minimum: Name and classify polygons up to at least octagons; distinguish regular from irregular and convex from concave.
width.typical: Reason about properties of specific polygons: angle sums, number of diagonals, symmetries.
wider: Investigate tessellation properties: which regular polygons tessellate alone, and why? Connect to interior angles.
Explore polygon properties in architecture, design, and cultural patterns.

modes.reason: Classifying polygons draws together side properties, angle sum knowledge, and symmetry reasoning simultaneously.

descriptors.title: Transformations on the Cartesian plane
descriptors.description: describe transformations of a set of points using coordinates in the Cartesian plane, translations and reflections on an axis, and rotations about a given point
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plot and read coordinates in all four quadrants of the Cartesian plane (from AC9M6SP02). Students have experienced combinations of transformations to create patterns (from AC9M6SP03).
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe and perform translations, reflections on an axis, and rotations about a given point using coordinates in the Cartesian plane.

nodes.label: Translations using coordinates
nodes.checkpoint: Students translate a set of points on the Cartesian plane and describe the translation using coordinate changes.
criteria: Correctly translates a set of points and records the new coordinates.
Describes the translation in terms of horizontal and vertical movement.
Verifies that the shape is congruent to the original after translation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Fluency with coordinate reading and recording is prerequisite to Nodes 2 and 3 — students who make coordinate errors in translation produce wrong starting points for reflection and rotation, and cannot verify that transformations preserve shape and size.

width.minimum: Translate a simple shape on the Cartesian plane and describe the translation as 'x units right/left, y units up/down'.
width.typical: Perform and describe translations of sets of points in all directions; verify that shape and size are preserved.
wider: Investigate how translations can be described as vector addition: (x, y) → (x+a, y+b).
Explore combinations of two translations — is the order of translation important?

modes.reason: Translation using coordinate notation is foundational to reflections and rotations. Students need fluency with coordinate changes before layer on more complex transformations.

nodes.label: Reflections on axes
nodes.checkpoint: Students reflect a set of points on the x-axis and y-axis and describe the transformation using coordinate rules.
criteria: Correctly reflects a set of points across the x-axis and y-axis.
States the coordinate rule for each reflection.
Does not confuse which coordinate negates for each axis.

width.minimum: Reflect a simple shape on the x-axis and y-axis; record the new coordinates and state the coordinate rule.
width.typical: Apply reflections on both axes; identify the coordinate rule for each; describe patterns in how coordinates change.
wider: Investigate reflections on other lines of symmetry (e.g. y = x) and what happens to coordinates.
Create symmetric patterns by reflecting across both axes and explore rotational symmetry emerging from double reflection.

modes.reason: Students often correctly apply the x-axis rule (negate y) but confuse it for y-axis (negate x). Seeing both reflections in close sequence across multiple figures consolidates the distinction.

nodes.label: Rotations about a given point
nodes.checkpoint: Students rotate a set of points about a given point (origin or other) by 90°, 180° and 270° and describe the rotation using coordinates.
criteria: Correctly rotates points by 90° and 180° about the origin.
Records the new coordinates and identifies the pattern.
Specifies direction of rotation (clockwise/counterclockwise) when describing.

width.minimum: Rotate a simple shape 90° and 180° about the origin; record new coordinates.
width.typical: Perform rotations of 90°, 180° and 270° about the origin and describe the coordinate patterns; apply rotation about a non-origin point.
wider: Investigate the coordinate rule for rotation by 90° about the origin (x,y) → (−y,x) and verify with multiple examples.
Explore the combined effect of reflection and rotation — investigate when two reflections produce a rotation.

modes.reason: Rotation is the hardest transformation for students to reason about from coordinates. An explicit method (plot points, use tracing paper or dynamic software, record new coordinates, identify the pattern) is needed.

descriptors.title: Algorithms for classifying shapes
descriptors.description: design and create algorithms involving a sequence of steps and decisions that will sort and classify sets of shapes according to their attributes, and describe how the algorithms work
descriptors.knowledge: Students can classify triangles, quadrilaterals and polygons by properties (from AC9M7SP02). Students have experience writing step-by-step instructions and using decision trees informally.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design and describe algorithms (using flowcharts or pseudocode) that sort and classify shapes by their attributes.

nodes.label: Designing a classification algorithm
nodes.checkpoint: Students design a step-by-step algorithm (as a flowchart or decision tree) that classifies shapes according to their attributes.
criteria: Produces a flowchart or decision tree that correctly classifies the target shapes.
Includes decision points with clear yes/no branches.
Tests the algorithm on at least two examples and corrects any errors.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who design algorithms without an explicit decision-ordering scaffold produce algorithms with missing branches or ambiguous tests — these cannot be evaluated or described correctly in Node 2, since tracing an incomplete algorithm produces unpredictable outputs.

width.minimum: Create a flowchart that correctly classifies triangles as scalene, isosceles or equilateral.
width.typical: Design and test an algorithm for classifying quadrilaterals; identify and fix errors when the algorithm misclassifies a shape.
wider: Design an algorithm for a broader polygon classification including regularity and convexity.
Compare two algorithms for the same classification task — which is more efficient? Which handles edge cases better?

modes.reason: Algorithm design requires explicit thinking about the order of decisions and what each branch tests. Students who write algorithms informally miss cases and produce ambiguous decision points.

nodes.label: Describing and evaluating algorithms
nodes.checkpoint: Students describe in words how an algorithm works and evaluate its correctness by tracing through it with test cases.
criteria: Correctly traces a classification algorithm with a test input.
Identifies at least one case where a given algorithm fails (if one exists).
Explains in plain language how the algorithm works.

width.minimum: Trace a given classification algorithm with two test shapes and describe each decision made.
width.typical: Evaluate whether a given algorithm is correct, efficient, and handles all cases; identify and fix errors.
wider: Implement the classification algorithm in a simple programming language or flowchart tool.
Investigate the relationship between the number of decision steps and the number of categories — how does complexity scale?

modes.reason: Algorithm evaluation requires seeing both correct and incorrect algorithms to develop critical judgment. Students who only design algorithms rarely develop the ability to critique others'.

descriptors.title: Data acquisition and measures of centre
descriptors.description: acquire data sets for discrete and continuous numerical variables and calculate the range, median, mean and mode; make and justify decisions about which measures of central tendency provide useful insights into the nature of the distribution of data
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interpret and compare distributions using mode and range (from AC9M6ST01). Students have planned and conducted statistical investigations (from AC9M6ST03).
descriptors.endpoint: Students acquire data sets, calculate range, median, mean and mode, and justify which measure best describes a given distribution.

nodes.label: Distinguishing discrete and continuous numerical variables
nodes.checkpoint: Students distinguish discrete from continuous numerical variables and understand how this affects data acquisition.
criteria: Correctly classifies given variables as discrete or continuous.
Explains the key distinction (countable vs measurable).
Identifies appropriate units and precision for a continuous variable.

width.minimum: Classify a set of variables as discrete or continuous and explain the distinction.
width.typical: Identify appropriate methods to acquire data for discrete and continuous variables; consider precision and measurement limitations for continuous data.
wider: Investigate how rounding affects continuous data: when is it appropriate to report a measurement to 1dp vs nearest integer?
Explore data acquisition from secondary sources: what are the limitations of data collected by others?

modes.reason: The discrete/continuous distinction is abstract until students encounter both in varied contexts. Multiple examples from different domains (counting vs measuring) are needed.

nodes.label: Calculating range, median, mean and mode
nodes.checkpoint: Students calculate all four summary statistics for a given data set.
criteria: Correctly calculates range, median, mean and mode for a given data set.
Handles even-count data sets correctly for median.
Recognises and handles data sets with no mode or multiple modes.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who calculate statistics incorrectly cannot reason about which is most appropriate in Node 3 — their comparison is between wrong values, and any justification built on incorrect statistics is meaningless.

width.minimum: Calculate range, median, mean and mode for a small data set with an odd number of values.
width.typical: Calculate all four statistics for data sets with even counts (median as average of two middle values); handle data sets with no mode or multiple modes.
wider: Investigate how the presence of an outlier affects each statistic differently — which is most and least sensitive to outliers?
Compare datasets with the same mean but different ranges and medians — what does each statistic reveal?

modes.reason: Accurate calculation of all four statistics must be fluent before comparison and justification of which is most useful. Errors in calculation undermine all subsequent reasoning.

nodes.label: Justifying which measure is most useful
nodes.checkpoint: Students reason about which measure of central tendency best describes a given distribution, considering outliers, skewness, and the purpose of the summary.
criteria: Identifies which measure best represents a given distribution and justifies the choice.
Explains the effect of outliers on mean vs median.
Selects different measures for different contexts appropriately.

width.minimum: For a given data set, identify which measure is most useful and explain why.
width.typical: Compare two distributions using appropriate measures; explain how outliers affect the mean more than the median; choose appropriate measures for different contexts.
wider: Investigate real contexts where mean is misleading (e.g. average income with extreme wealth) and discuss which measure better represents the population.
Explore how AI systems use descriptive statistics (mean, outlier detection) — connect to practical data science.

modes.reason: Judgment about which statistic is most useful requires encountering distributions where each statistic tells a different story. Skewed distributions with outliers are essential test cases.

descriptors.title: Data displays and distribution
descriptors.description: create different types of numerical data displays including stem-and-leaf plots using software where appropriate; describe and compare the distribution of data, commenting on the shape, centre and spread including outliers and determining the range, median, mean and mode
descriptors.knowledge: Students can calculate range, median, mean and mode (from AC9M7ST01). Students can interpret distributions using mode and range (from AC9M6ST01).
descriptors.endpoint: Students create and interpret stem-and-leaf plots and other numerical data displays, describing and comparing distributions in terms of shape, centre, spread and outliers.

nodes.label: Creating stem-and-leaf plots
nodes.checkpoint: Students construct ordered stem-and-leaf plots from a data set and read values from them accurately.
criteria: Constructs an ordered stem-and-leaf plot with correct stems and leaves.
Orders the leaves within each stem.
Includes a key explaining what the stem and leaf represent.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who construct disordered or incorrect stem-and-leaf plots cannot read summary statistics from them in Node 2 — an unordered display makes median identification impossible and shape description unreliable.

width.minimum: Construct an ordered stem-and-leaf plot for a given data set of 10–15 values.
width.typical: Construct stem-and-leaf plots for larger data sets; split stem-and-leaf plots for side-by-side comparison; use software where appropriate.
wider: Construct a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot to compare two data sets and explain what it shows.
Investigate what stem width to choose for a given data set to make the display useful.

modes.reason: Constructing a correct ordered stem-and-leaf plot is a skill that requires procedural care (ordering leaves, choosing stems). Errors in construction undermine all subsequent interpretation.

nodes.label: Describing distribution shape, centre, spread and outliers
nodes.checkpoint: Students describe the distribution of data in terms of its shape (symmetrical, skewed), centre, spread and the presence of outliers.
criteria: Describes the shape of a distribution using appropriate vocabulary.
Identifies the appropriate measure of centre for the distribution's shape.
Identifies outliers and comments on their effect.

width.minimum: Describe a given distribution using at least three of: shape, centre, spread, outliers.
width.typical: Describe distributions from stem-and-leaf and dot plots; connect features of the display (clusters, gaps, symmetry) to appropriate summary statistics.
wider: Investigate how outliers affect the appearance of a display and which statistics are most affected.
Compare the distribution of the same variable measured in two different groups — what do the differences suggest?

modes.reason: Distribution description requires a vocabulary for varied shapes — symmetrical, positively skewed, negatively skewed, bimodal. Encountering multiple distinct distributions develops this vocabulary.

nodes.label: Comparing distributions
nodes.checkpoint: Students compare two distributions using displays and summary statistics, making statements about differences in shape, centre and spread.
criteria: Makes at least two comparative statements about two distributions (using statistics and display features).
States conclusions in context, not just in mathematical terms.
Does not compare individual values as if they represent the distributions.

width.minimum: Compare two distributions by identifying at least one difference in centre, spread or shape.
width.typical: Systematically compare two distributions using multiple statistics and display features; draw conclusions about what the differences mean in context.
wider: Investigate whether a claim about two groups (e.g. 'boys are taller than girls on average') is supported by the data — use statistics and displays to evaluate.
Explore how sample size affects confidence in comparative claims.

modes.reason: Comparing distributions requires simultaneous application of display reading, summary statistic calculation, and contextual interpretation — the integration of the whole statistics strand at Year 7.

descriptors.title: Statistical investigations
descriptors.description: plan and conduct statistical investigations involving data for discrete and continuous numerical variables; analyse and interpret distributions of data and report findings in terms of shape and summary statistics
descriptors.knowledge: Students have planned and conducted statistical investigations and communicated findings (from AC9M6ST03). Students can create displays and describe distributions (from AC9M7ST01, AC9M7ST02).
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan and conduct statistical investigations with discrete and continuous numerical variables, and report findings in terms of distribution shape and summary statistics.

nodes.label: Planning a statistical investigation
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify a statistical question, plan data collection (including variable type, measurement method and sample), and anticipate potential sources of bias.
criteria: Writes a clear statistical question that can be answered with data.
Identifies the variable type (discrete or continuous) and appropriate measurement method.
Identifies at least one potential source of variability in their data collection.

width.minimum: Write a statistical question, identify the variable type and describe how data will be collected.
width.typical: Plan a full investigation including sample size, data collection method, and at least one potential source of variability or bias.
wider: Compare primary data collection (measurement, survey) with secondary data sources — identify advantages and limitations of each.
Investigate how sample size affects the reliability of conclusions.

modes.reason: Planning requires deliberate reasoning about the investigation process before data is collected. Students who skip planning rarely identify bias and produce poor data.

nodes.label: Conducting, analysing and reporting
