nodes.checkpoint: Students collect data, display it appropriately, analyse the distribution using summary statistics, and report findings in terms of the statistical question.
criteria: Collects, displays and analyses data appropriate to the variable type.
Reports findings that address the original statistical question.
Uses distribution language (shape, centre, spread) in the report.

width.minimum: Collect data, create an appropriate display, calculate summary statistics, and write a brief report answering the statistical question.
width.typical: Conduct a full investigation cycle; choose appropriate displays and statistics for the variable type; report findings including shape, centre, spread and context.
wider: Use secondary data from a public source (e.g. Reconciliation Barometer, ABS) to conduct a statistical investigation on a social or cultural question.
Investigate: does the investigation support or refute a stated claim? Frame the report around evidence for and against.

modes.reason: Conducting and reporting a full investigation integrates all statistics strand skills. The integration and contextual communication are the learning at this node.

Statistical investigation only develops as a transferable skill through conducting multiple investigations in varied contexts. A single investigation produces performance on that topic, not transferable investigation skill.

descriptors.title: Simplify linear expressions
descriptors.description: create, expand, factorise, rearrange and simplify linear expressions, applying the associative, commutative, identity, distributive and inverse properties
descriptors.knowledge: Students can formulate algebraic expressions and apply the distributive property informally (from AC9M7A02). Students understand variables, constants and operations in expressions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students fluently expand, factorise, rearrange and simplify linear expressions, applying algebraic properties explicitly.

nodes.label: Expanding and simplifying linear expressions
nodes.checkpoint: Students expand brackets in linear expressions using the distributive property and collect like terms to simplify.
criteria: Correctly expands brackets including those with negative coefficients.
Collects like terms accurately.
Does not partially distribute (e.g. only multiply the first term).
nodes.hinge_reason: Expansion errors — particularly sign errors with negative coefficients — propagate directly into Node 2 (factorisation requires recognising expanded form) and Node 3 (rearrangement requires reliable expansion to verify). Students who cannot expand fluently cannot check their factorisation or rearrangement by expanding back.

width.minimum: Expand and simplify a linear expression with one set of brackets (e.g. 3(2x + 4) − x).
width.typical: Expand and simplify expressions with multiple brackets and negative coefficients; identify and collect like terms; use algebra tiles or area models to verify.
wider: Investigate the distributive property across subtraction: verify that a(b − c) = ab − ac using substitution and area models.
Explore common student errors in expansion (e.g. 3(x + 2) = 3x + 2) — explain why the error occurs and how to avoid it.

modes.reason: Expanding and collecting like terms is a procedural skill requiring fluency before factorisation and rearrangement. Errors in sign handling with negative coefficients are the primary failure point.

nodes.label: Factorising linear expressions
nodes.checkpoint: Students factorise linear expressions by identifying the highest common factor and express as a product of the HCF and a bracket.
criteria: Identifies the HCF of all terms in a linear expression.
Writes the factorised form correctly.
Verifies by expanding back to the original expression.
nodes.hinge_reason: Factorisation is required within Node 3 rearrangement (isolating a variable from multi-term expressions requires recognising common factors) — students who cannot factorise reliably cannot complete the rearrangement steps that depend on it.

width.minimum: Factorise a linear expression with an integer HCF (e.g. 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3)).
width.typical: Factorise linear expressions with variable and integer common factors; verify by expanding; understand factorisation as the inverse of expansion.
wider: Investigate the relationship between factorisation and GCD from number — connect algebraic HCF to numerical HCF.
Explore factorising expressions with negative leading terms — develop a convention for handling negative HCF.

modes.reason: Factorisation requires an explicit search strategy: identify the HCF of all terms, divide each term, write the bracket. Students who approach factorisation without a structured method miss common factors or introduce errors.

nodes.label: Rearranging linear expressions
nodes.checkpoint: Students rearrange linear expressions and formulas using inverse operations and algebraic properties, maintaining equivalence.
criteria: Correctly rearranges a linear formula to make a specified variable the subject.
Applies inverse operations in the correct order.
Verifies the rearranged formula by substitution.

width.minimum: Rearrange a two-term linear expression to isolate a specified variable.
width.typical: Rearrange multi-term linear formulas to make any variable the subject; apply commutative and inverse properties explicitly; verify by substitution.
wider: Apply rearrangement to real formulas from science and everyday contexts: rearrange distance = speed × time for speed; rearrange area formulas for dimensions.
Investigate how rearrangement connects to solving equations — express the connection between 'rearranging a formula' and 'solving for a variable' explicitly.

modes.reason: Rearranging formulas requires simultaneous application of expansion, factorisation, and inverse operations — integrating all prior nodes in this descriptor.

descriptors.title: Graph and solve linear equations
descriptors.description: graph linear relations on the Cartesian plane using digital tools where appropriate; solve linear equations and one-variable inequalities using graphical and algebraic techniques; verify solutions by substitution
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plot ordered pairs and describe linear relationships on the Cartesian plane (from AC9M7A05). Students can solve one-variable linear equations (from AC9M7A03).
descriptors.endpoint: Students graph linear relations including inequalities, solve linear equations algebraically and graphically, and verify solutions by substitution.

nodes.label: Graphing linear relations including inequalities
nodes.checkpoint: Students graph linear relations of the form y = mx + b and one-variable inequalities on the Cartesian plane, identifying key features.
criteria: Correctly graphs a linear relation from a rule or table.
Identifies gradient and y-intercept from graph and equation.
Correctly represents an inequality including the boundary line convention (solid vs dashed).
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 requires graphical verification of inequality solutions — students who have not worked with inequality graph forms (including boundary line conventions) cannot use graphical methods to verify their algebraic solutions.

width.minimum: Graph a linear relation y = mx + b from a table of values and identify gradient and y-intercept.
width.typical: Graph linear relations and inequalities (x = a, y = a, y ≤ mx + b); identify gradient and intercepts; describe the effect of changing m and b.
wider: Investigate what happens to the graph when m is negative, zero, or undefined — connect each case to a physical or real-world interpretation.
Explore graphing two linear relations on the same axes and identifying the point of intersection — preview of simultaneous equations.

modes.reason: Students who only graph y = mx + b forms often fail with x = a or inequality forms. Exposure to the full range of linear relation types prevents incomplete understanding.

nodes.label: Solving linear equations algebraically
nodes.checkpoint: Students solve linear equations of the form ax + b = cx + d algebraically, including equations requiring expansion, and verify by substitution.
criteria: Solves a linear equation with unknowns on both sides correctly.
Verifies the solution by substitution.
Does not leave the unknown on both sides after the first step.
nodes.hinge_reason: Equation-solving fluency and sign handling are directly required in Node 3 inequality solving — students who make systematic sign errors in equations will apply the same errors in inequalities, including failure to reverse the inequality sign when required.

width.minimum: Solve a two-step linear equation with the unknown on both sides (e.g. 3x + 7 = 6x − 9).
width.typical: Solve linear equations requiring expansion of brackets; solve equations involving fractions; always verify by substitution.
wider: Solve linear equations arising from geometry problems: find the value of x given angle relationships or perimeter conditions.
Investigate equations with no solution or infinitely many solutions — what do these look like graphically?

modes.reason: Solving equations with unknowns on both sides requires procedural fluency and reliable sign handling. This is a high-error-rate skill that needs sustained practice before graphical methods are layered on.

nodes.label: Solving inequalities and using graphical methods
nodes.checkpoint: Students solve one-variable inequalities algebraically and verify using graphical methods; represent solutions on a number line.
criteria: Solves a one-variable inequality correctly including sign reversal where needed.
Represents the solution on a number line with correct open/closed endpoint.
Verifies the solution graphically or by substitution.

width.minimum: Solve a one-variable inequality of the form ax + b < c and represent the solution on a number line.
width.typical: Solve inequalities algebraically including those requiring reversal of the inequality sign when dividing by a negative; represent on number line and verify graphically.
wider: Investigate why dividing by a negative reverses the inequality — use a number line argument to justify.
Explore compound inequalities (a < x < b) and represent their solution sets on a number line.

modes.reason: Inequality solving requires a specific reasoning scaffold around sign reversal — students need an explicit rule and a conceptual justification or they apply it inconsistently.

descriptors.title: Model with linear functions
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve applied problems involving linear relations, including financial contexts; formulate problems with linear functions, choosing a representation; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation, reviewing the appropriateness of the model
descriptors.knowledge: Students can graph linear relations and solve linear equations (from AC9M8A02). Students have experience with mathematical modelling (from AC9M7N09).
descriptors.endpoint: Students formulate linear function models for applied problems, choose appropriate representations, solve and interpret solutions, and review model appropriateness.

nodes.label: Formulating linear models
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify a linear relationship in a practical context, formulate it as a function y = mx + b, and identify the meaning of gradient and intercept in context.
criteria: Correctly identifies gradient and intercept from a practical context.
Formulates the linear function in equation form.
Interprets m and b in terms of the problem context.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires solving and interpreting the model — students who cannot formulate the linear function from context have no model to solve, interpret, or review for appropriateness.

width.minimum: Given a practical context with a constant rate and fixed component, formulate the linear function and identify m and b in context.
width.typical: Formulate linear models for varied contexts (taxi fares, pay rates, motion); identify gradient as rate of change and intercept as fixed value; choose table, graph or equation as appropriate.
wider: Model patterns on Country/Place with linear functions — investigate Indigenous knowledge connections to linear relationships and use the model as a predictive tool.
Compare two linear models on the same axes (e.g. two taxi companies) and find the break-even point algebraically.

modes.reason: Formulating a linear model requires recognising the constant rate structure across varied contexts. Students who only practise with one context type fail to identify the linear structure in novel situations.

nodes.label: Solving, interpreting and reviewing the model
nodes.checkpoint: Students solve a linear model for a given value, interpret the solution in context, and evaluate whether the model is appropriate for the situation.
criteria: Uses the linear model correctly to answer a specific question.
States the solution in contextually appropriate terms.
Identifies at least one limitation or domain restriction of the model.

width.minimum: Use a linear model to answer a specific question; state the solution in context; identify one limitation of the model.
width.typical: Solve practical problems using the model; interpret solutions including units and contextual meaning; review model appropriateness considering domain, linearity assumption, and real-world constraints.
wider: Investigate where a linear model breaks down — at what point does a taxi fare model, pay rate model, or motion model stop being realistic?
Apply linear modelling to a financial context involving different pay structures (base + commission vs flat rate) — model, compare and advise.

modes.reason: Solving, interpreting and reviewing simultaneously requires students to coordinate graphical, algebraic and contextual reasoning — the integration across all three representations is the learning.

descriptors.title: Experiment with linear functions
descriptors.description: experiment with linear functions and relations using digital tools, making and testing conjectures and generalising emerging patterns
descriptors.knowledge: Students can graph linear relations and describe relationships (from AC9M8A02, AC9M7A04, AC9M7A06). Students have used digital tools to vary parameters.
descriptors.endpoint: Students systematically vary parameters of linear functions using digital tools, make and test conjectures, and generalise the effect of parameter changes on the graph.

nodes.label: Effect of gradient parameter on linear graphs
nodes.checkpoint: Students investigate the effect of varying the gradient m in y = mx + b on the graph and generalise the relationship between m and steepness/direction.
criteria: Correctly describes the effect of varying m on the graph.
States a general rule for positive, negative and zero gradient.
Tests the conjecture with at least one new value.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to vary both m and b systematically and generalise about parallel lines — students who have not acquired the conjecture-testing scaffold in Node 1 produce unfounded generalisations in Node 2 or confuse the effects of the two parameters.

width.minimum: Using graphing software, vary m across positive, negative and zero values; describe the effect on the graph.
width.typical: Systematically vary m; compare y = 2x and y = −2x; generalise the connection between the sign and magnitude of m and the graph's steepness and direction.
wider: Investigate what value of m produces a line perpendicular to a given line — discover the relationship m₁ × m₂ = −1 informally.
Explore the case m is undefined (vertical lines x = a) — why can't this be written as y = mx + b?

modes.reason: Making and testing conjectures requires an explicit investigation scaffold: vary one parameter, hold others constant, record observations, propose a general rule, test with a new case. Students who explore without structure draw weak or incorrect generalisations.

nodes.label: Effect of intercept and generalising patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students investigate the effect of varying the y-intercept b, and generalise patterns including the behaviour of parallel lines.
criteria: Correctly states the effect of varying b on the graph.
Identifies that lines with equal gradient are parallel.
States a generalisation supported by evidence from their investigation.

width.minimum: Vary b in y = mx + b; describe the effect on the graph and state what b controls.
width.typical: Vary both m and b systematically; generalise that lines with the same m are parallel; investigate integer solutions to two-variable equations using digital tools.
wider: Investigate how linear functions are used in linear regression models in machine learning — describe what the gradient and intercept represent in this context.
Explore integer solutions to 2x + 3y = 48 — use digital tools to find all solutions and represent them on the Cartesian plane.

modes.reason: Generalising about linear functions requires encountering the pattern across multiple parameter combinations. Students who only investigate one direction miss the interaction between m and b.

descriptors.title: Area and perimeter of composite shapes
descriptors.description: solve problems involving the area and perimeter of irregular and composite shapes using appropriate units
descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply area formulas for triangles, rectangles and parallelograms (from AC9M7M01). Students can calculate circumference of circles (from AC9M7M03).
descriptors.endpoint: Students decompose or compose irregular and composite shapes to find their area and perimeter using appropriate formulas and units.

nodes.label: Decomposing composite shapes for area
nodes.checkpoint: Students decompose a composite shape into known shapes and calculate the total area by summing component areas.
criteria: Correctly identifies a valid decomposition of the composite shape.
Calculates each component area accurately.
Combines areas correctly (adding or subtracting as required).
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires the same dimension-identification discipline for irregular shapes — students who have not internalised the decomposition strategy in Node 1 apply it inconsistently to irregular shapes where the component boundaries are less obvious.

width.minimum: Decompose a composite shape made of two rectangles or a rectangle and triangle; calculate total area.
width.typical: Decompose and calculate area for a range of composite shapes including those with subtracted regions (e.g. shape with a hole); select appropriate decomposition strategy.
wider: Investigate floor plan problems requiring area calculation for irregular rooms — apply to real building design contexts.
Explore shapes requiring both addition and subtraction of areas (e.g. a frame) and generalise the approach.

modes.reason: Decomposition requires an explicit strategy: identify the component shapes, identify dimensions from the diagram, calculate each area, combine. Students who proceed without this strategy make errors in dimension identification.

nodes.label: Perimeter and area of irregular shapes
nodes.checkpoint: Students estimate and calculate the perimeter and area of irregular shapes using measurement approximation strategies.
criteria: Estimates the area of an irregular shape using a systematic method.
Calculates or estimates the perimeter accurately.
States the precision of the estimate and its limitations.

width.minimum: Estimate the area of an irregular shape using a grid overlay; calculate perimeter by summing measured segments.
width.typical: Use increasingly accurate approximation methods (grid, line segments) to estimate area and perimeter; discuss precision and error; apply to practical contexts.
wider: Apply area estimation to a real context: estimate the area of an irregularly shaped land parcel from a map or aerial image.
Investigate how Simpson's rule or similar numerical integration methods formalise the estimation approach — preview of Y11/12 mathematics.

modes.reason: Irregular shape problems require judgment about appropriate estimation methods. Multiple practical contexts (land parcels, natural features, council maps) build the judgment to select appropriate precision.

descriptors.title: Volume and capacity of right prisms
descriptors.description: solve problems involving the volume and capacity of right prisms using appropriate units
descriptors.knowledge: Students can calculate volume of rectangular and triangular prisms using V = Ah (from AC9M7M02). Students understand unit conversion between cubic units and litres.
descriptors.endpoint: Students solve problems involving volume and capacity of right prisms, selecting appropriate units and applying reasoning about optimal dimensions.

nodes.label: Unit relationships between volume and capacity
nodes.checkpoint: Students understand and apply the relationships 1 cm³ = 1 mL, 1000 cm³ = 1 L, 1 m³ = 1000 L, and use these to convert between volume and capacity units.
criteria: Correctly converts between cm³, mL, L and m³.
Selects appropriate units for a given practical context.
Does not confuse cm³ and cm (volume vs length).
nodes.hinge_reason: Unit conversion errors propagate directly into Node 2 — students who confuse cm³ and mL or m³ and L produce answers in the wrong unit or off by a factor of 1000 in practical capacity problems.

width.minimum: Convert between cm³ and mL, and between m³ and L, for given volumes.
width.typical: Apply unit conversion in practical problem contexts; choose appropriate units for the context; explain the relationship between cubic centimetres and millilitres.
wider: Investigate how unit choice affects the numerical value of a measurement — when is it more practical to use litres vs cubic metres in real contexts?
Explore the volume of a cubic metre using 1000 × 1000 mL = 1000 L as a concrete model — connect to large-scale water storage contexts.

modes.reason: Unit conversion between volume and capacity is a precision skill that students frequently get wrong under pressure. Fluency here is prerequisite to problem-solving.

nodes.label: Solving practical volume and capacity problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students solve practical problems involving volume and capacity of right prisms, including optimisation and multi-step contexts.
criteria: Selects and applies the correct formula for the prism type.
Interprets the result in context with appropriate units.
Identifies which measurements are relevant to the problem.

width.minimum: Solve a practical problem requiring volume calculation and capacity interpretation.
width.typical: Apply volume reasoning to optimal packaging, production and dimension problems; interpret capacity in context; select which measurements matter for the problem.
wider: Investigate optimal packaging: for a fixed volume, what dimensions minimise surface area? Explore patterns for rectangular prisms.
Apply volume and capacity to a production context: given a required capacity and one fixed dimension, find the remaining dimension.

modes.reason: Practical volume problems vary significantly in what reasoning is needed — capacity problems, packaging optimisation, and dimension-finding all require recognising the same underlying formula but in different configurations.

descriptors.title: Circumference and area of circles
descriptors.description: solve problems involving the circumference and area of a circle using formulas and appropriate units
descriptors.knowledge: Students understand π and can calculate circumference using C = πd (from AC9M7M03). Students can calculate area of rectangles and triangles.
descriptors.endpoint: Students derive and apply A = πr² to solve problems involving circle area and circumference, including composite shapes with circular components.

nodes.label: Deriving the area of a circle formula
nodes.checkpoint: Students understand why A = πr² using at least one informal derivation method.
criteria: States A = πr² and can explain the formula using at least one informal argument.
Explains why the area must be between 2r² and 4r².
Does not confuse area formula with circumference formula.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who only memorise A = πr² without understanding cannot reliably choose between area and circumference formulas in Node 2 — they conflate the two formulas under pressure, particularly when asked to find radius from area (requiring rearrangement of a formula they don't understand).

width.minimum: State A = πr² and explain informally why it is reasonable (e.g. the area is between 2r² and 4r²).
width.typical: Investigate the area using a square grid or sector rearrangement method; connect the result to A = πr²; verify the formula is consistent with known approximations.
wider: Use the sector rearrangement method — divide circle into increasingly smaller sectors arranged into a near-rectangle — and show why the rectangle's dimensions give πr × r = πr².
Investigate the connection between area and circumference: A = ½ × C × r — explain this geometrically.

modes.reason: Students who only memorise A = πr² without any derivation experience cannot explain why the formula works or recover it when forgotten. Multiple derivation approaches build robust understanding.

nodes.label: Applying circle area and circumference formulas
nodes.checkpoint: Students apply A = πr² and C = 2πr to calculate area and circumference, find radius/diameter given area or circumference, and solve composite shape problems.
criteria: Correctly calculates area given radius or radius given area.
Solves a composite shape problem involving circular components.
Uses an appropriate approximation for π and states it.

width.minimum: Calculate area given radius; find radius given area; solve one practical problem.
width.typical: Apply both formulas in practical contexts; find any unknown (r, d, C, or A) given another; solve composite shape problems including semicircles.
wider: Explore traditional weaving designs by First Nations Australians and investigate the significance and use of circles — calculate areas and circumferences in context.
Investigate composite shapes combining circles with other polygons — e.g. area of a stadium or athletic track.

modes.reason: Circle measurement problems require recognising which formula applies and which quantity is unknown. Varied practical contexts build the judgment to select the right formula and direction of calculation.

descriptors.title: Duration and time zones
descriptors.description: solve problems involving duration, including using 12- and 24-hour time across multiple time zones
descriptors.knowledge: Students can calculate elapsed time and convert between 12- and 24-hour time. Students understand the concept of time zones informally.
descriptors.endpoint: Students solve problems involving duration and time zone conversion, including multi-zone itinerary and scheduling problems.

nodes.label: Converting between time zones
nodes.checkpoint: Students convert times between time zones using UTC offsets and apply 12- and 24-hour time conventions.
criteria: Correctly converts a time between two given time zones.
Handles day changes correctly when conversion crosses midnight.
Uses 24-hour time appropriately to avoid AM/PM ambiguity.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 multi-zone scheduling requires chaining multiple individual time zone conversions — students who cannot reliably handle day changes or offset arithmetic in Node 1 produce cascade errors across the multi-zone itinerary.

width.minimum: Convert a given time from one time zone to another using a UTC offset.
width.typical: Convert between multiple time zones; handle day changes; apply to real contexts (flight arrival times, international calls, Perth vs eastern states).
wider: Investigate why time zones exist and how the International Date Line creates calendar day differences.
Explore daylight saving — how does it affect time zone offsets between Australian states, and why is it not observed uniformly?

modes.reason: Time zone problems vary significantly: some cross midnight, some cross the date line, some involve daylight saving. Multiple real-world contexts are needed to develop reliable conversion reasoning.

nodes.label: Solving multi-zone scheduling and itinerary problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students solve practical problems involving scheduling across multiple time zones, including travel itineraries and virtual meeting planning.
criteria: Correctly plans a meeting or itinerary accounting for all time zone offsets.
Identifies and resolves day-change issues.
Communicates the solution clearly showing local times in each zone.

width.minimum: Plan a meeting time that works for two people in different time zones; show the time in both zones.
width.typical: Plan an international travel itinerary across multiple time zones; calculate local arrival and departure times; identify scheduling challenges for a multi-national team.
wider: Plan an international travel itinerary across at least three time zones in Asia; calculate all local times; identify the best transit options.
Investigate the practical challenge of regular virtual meetings for a company with staff in different Australian states and an international office — propose a fair meeting time.

modes.reason: Multi-zone scheduling requires coordinating UTC offsets, duration calculation, date change reasoning, and 12/24-hour conversion simultaneously — a genuine integration of all time concepts.

descriptors.title: Rates
descriptors.description: recognise and use rates to solve problems involving the comparison of 2 related quantities of different units of measure
descriptors.knowledge: Students can solve ratio problems (from AC9M7N08). Students understand proportional reasoning and unit conversion.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise rates as comparisons of two different quantity types, apply rates to solve conversion and practical problems, and distinguish rates from ratios.

nodes.label: Rates as comparisons of different units
nodes.checkpoint: Students recognise that a rate compares two quantities with different units and express rates in standard form (quantity per unit).
criteria: Correctly identifies and writes a rate from a practical context.
Converts between related rate units.
Distinguishes a rate (different units) from a ratio (same units).
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who only recognise speed as a rate cannot identify the rate structure in Node 2 problems involving pay rates, tax rates, or dilution — they cannot set up the calculation because they don't recognise these as rate problems.

width.minimum: Identify and write rates from practical contexts (e.g. km/h, $/kg); convert between related rate units.
width.typical: Identify constant and average rates in real contexts; apply rates to unit conversion problems; distinguish rates from ratios.
wider: Investigate First Nations Australians' land management practices involving rates — e.g. rate of fire spread under different environmental conditions.
Compare multiple rate units for the same phenomenon (e.g. km/h, m/s, miles/hour) and practise conversion between them.

modes.reason: Rates appear in an enormous variety of contexts. Students who only practise speed calculations fail to recognise pay rates, dilution rates, or interest rates as the same mathematical structure.

nodes.label: Applying rates to practical problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students apply rates to solve practical problems including pay rates, run rates, dilution, taxation, and unit conversions.
criteria: Correctly applies a given rate to solve a practical problem.
Shows the rate calculation clearly with appropriate units.
Interprets the result in context.

width.minimum: Solve a practical problem using a given rate (e.g. calculate cost at a given rate per kg, or distance at a given speed).
width.typical: Apply rates to varied contexts including required run rates in sport, chemical dilution, income tax using rate tables, and currency conversion.
wider: Use taxation rate tables to calculate annual income tax for a given salary — apply marginal rate structure and compute effective rate.
Investigate currency conversion as a rate problem: plan a budget for overseas travel using current exchange rates.

modes.reason: Rate application problems span a very wide range of real-world contexts and problem structures. Breadth of context is the primary driver of transferable rate reasoning.

descriptors.title: Pythagoras' theorem
descriptors.description: use Pythagoras' theorem to solve problems involving the side lengths of right-angled triangles
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify perfect squares, square roots, and right-angled triangles (from AC9M7N01, AC9M7SP02). Students have informal exposure to the 3-4-5 triangle.
descriptors.endpoint: Students state and apply Pythagoras' theorem to find unknown side lengths in right-angled triangles in practical and geometric contexts.

nodes.label: Understanding and stating Pythagoras' theorem
nodes.checkpoint: Students state Pythagoras' theorem (a² + b² = c²) and understand it as a relationship between areas of squares on the sides of a right-angled triangle.
criteria: States Pythagoras' theorem correctly and identifies the hypotenuse.
Verifies the theorem for at least one specific case.
States the converse: if a² + b² = c² then the triangle is right-angled.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 application requires students to identify the hypotenuse and set up a² + b² = c² correctly — students who have only memorised a formula without understanding the area relationship misidentify the hypotenuse or set up the equation incorrectly, producing systematically wrong answers.

width.minimum: State the theorem and identify which side is the hypotenuse; verify the theorem holds for a 3-4-5 triangle.
width.typical: Verify the theorem using area diagrams or proofs from multiple cultural traditions; state the converse; identify Pythagorean triples.
wider: Investigate different applications, demonstrations and proofs of Pythagoras' theorem from multiple cultures: Egypt, Mesopotamia, India, China, and Greece — compare the approaches.
Identify Pythagorean triples systematically: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (7,24,25), (8,15,17) — investigate how to generate new triples from known ones.

modes.reason: Proofs from multiple cultural traditions enrich understanding of the theorem and demonstrate it is not exclusively a Western mathematical result. Multiple verification methods also build confidence before applying the theorem.

nodes.label: Finding unknown side lengths using Pythagoras
nodes.checkpoint: Students apply Pythagoras' theorem to find the hypotenuse or a shorter side in right-angled triangles, including in practical and coordinate geometry contexts.
criteria: Correctly identifies the hypotenuse in a given right-angled triangle.
Finds an unknown side correctly using the theorem.
Applies the theorem to a practical problem context.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 3 triangle classification requires comparing a² + b² with c² — students who cannot fluently apply the theorem to find unknown sides (and who misidentify c as the longest side) apply the classification test to the wrong quantities.

width.minimum: Find the hypotenuse and find a shorter side given the other two sides for at least two examples.
width.typical: Apply the theorem to varied practical problems; identify right-angled triangles within diagrams; apply to distance between two points on the Cartesian plane.
wider: Apply the theorem to 3D problems: find the diagonal of a rectangular prism using the theorem twice.
Investigate how Pythagoras' theorem can determine distance between two points on a Cartesian plane — connect to applications in predictive text and mapping.

modes.reason: Applying Pythagoras requires first identifying the right-angled triangle within a diagram. Students who only practise decontextualised calculations fail to identify the relevant triangle in applied problems.

nodes.label: Classifying triangles using side lengths
nodes.checkpoint: Students use the relationship between a² + b² and c² to classify triangles as right-angled, acute or obtuse.
criteria: Correctly classifies a triangle given three side lengths.
States the rule for each classification (right, acute, obtuse).
Identifies the longest side as c before applying the test.

width.minimum: Given three side lengths, determine whether the triangle is right-angled, acute or obtuse.
width.typical: Apply the classification rule across a range of triangles; explain the reasoning for acute (a² + b² > c²) and obtuse (a² + b² < c²) cases.
wider: Investigate why the inequality changes direction for acute and obtuse triangles — connect to the geometric argument about how the angle affects the opposite side length.
Apply classification to survey and construction contexts: verify whether a corner is square using the converse of Pythagoras.

modes.reason: Triangle classification requires comparing a² + b² with c² and reasoning about the direction of the inequality. Students need an explicit reasoning scaffold to apply this reliably.

descriptors.title: Modelling with ratios and rates
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving ratios and rates, including financial contexts; formulate problems; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation, reviewing the appropriateness of the model
descriptors.knowledge: Students can solve ratio and rate problems (from AC9M7M06, AC9M8M05). Students have modelling experience from prior years.
descriptors.endpoint: Students formulate and solve models for practical problems involving ratios and rates in financial and scientific contexts, review appropriateness and communicate solutions.

nodes.label: Formulating and solving ratio/rate models
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify whether a problem requires a ratio or rate model, formulate it, and solve in context.
criteria: Correctly identifies whether the problem requires a ratio or rate model.
Formulates and solves the model correctly.
Justifies the model choice and interprets the solution in context.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires evaluating model appropriateness — students who have only formulated one model type cannot identify when the chosen model oversimplifies or when a different structure would be more appropriate.

width.minimum: Formulate and solve a practical problem using either a ratio or rate model; state which is appropriate and why.
width.typical: Apply modelling to scales and plans, chemical mixing, currency conversion, and income tax; justify model choice; select efficient calculation strategy.
wider: Investigate radiocarbon dating as a ratio application: model the ratio of carbon-14 to carbon-12 isotopes in organic material to estimate age.
Model the ratio applications in First Nations Australians' string and cordage making — investigate the ratio of fibre lengths and twisting rates involved.

modes.reason: Ratio and rate modelling problems span an unusually wide range of contexts at Year 8. Multiple varied contexts are needed to build the judgment to select the right model structure.

nodes.label: Reviewing model appropriateness
nodes.checkpoint: Students evaluate whether a ratio or rate model is appropriate for a given situation, identify assumptions, and suggest improvements.
criteria: Identifies at least one assumption made in a given model.
Explains how the assumption affects the model's accuracy.
Suggests a reasonable refinement to the model.

width.minimum: State one assumption in a given model and explain how it might limit the model's accuracy.
width.typical: Review the appropriateness of a model for varied practical contexts; identify when a simple ratio/rate model oversimplifies; suggest model refinements.
wider: Compare simple and refined models for the same situation (e.g. constant vs variable exchange rate) — evaluate which is more appropriate and in what circumstances.
Investigate a financial model (income tax brackets) and evaluate where the 'step function' model differs from a smooth rate model — discuss the implications.

modes.reason: Reviewing model appropriateness requires coordinating modelling experience, real-world knowledge, and mathematical reasoning simultaneously — the integration of the whole measurement modelling strand.

descriptors.title: Irrational numbers
descriptors.description: recognise irrational numbers in applied contexts, including square roots and π
descriptors.knowledge: Students can locate non-perfect square roots between consecutive integers and understand π as the constant ratio C/d (from AC9M7N01, AC9M7M03). Students understand the real number line and rational number representation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise irrational numbers in applied contexts, understand that they cannot be expressed as exact fractions, and approximately locate them on the real number line.

nodes.label: Irrational numbers as non-terminating, non-recurring decimals
nodes.checkpoint: Students understand that irrational numbers cannot be expressed as fractions and have decimal expansions that neither terminate nor recur.
criteria: States that irrational numbers cannot be expressed as fractions and have non-terminating non-recurring decimal expansions.
Correctly classifies given numbers as rational or irrational.
Does not confuse 'irrational' with 'very large' or 'impossible to use in calculation'.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate 'irrational' with 'very large' or 'impossible to use' cannot reason correctly in Node 2 about locating irrationals on the number line — they treat approximations as exact values and cannot describe the real number system accurately.

width.minimum: State that √2 and π are irrational; explain what makes a number irrational.
width.typical: Distinguish rational from irrational numbers across a range of examples; use digital tools to explore the decimal expansion of irrational numbers; explain why they cannot be written as exact fractions.
wider: Investigate historical approximations to π in different societies (Egyptian, Chinese, Indian, Greek) and evaluate the accuracy achieved.
Explore the golden ratio φ = (1 + √5)/2 in art and design — verify it is irrational and locate it approximately on the real number line.

modes.reason: The concept of irrationality is abstract — students need multiple concrete examples (√2, √3, π, φ) and contexts to build a stable understanding that goes beyond memorising which numbers are irrational.

nodes.label: Locating irrational numbers on the real number line
nodes.checkpoint: Students approximately locate irrational numbers on the real number line and understand the real number system as including both rational and irrational numbers.
criteria: Correctly locates an irrational number between two consecutive integers on the number line.
Describes the real number system as including both rationals and irrationals.
Does not treat the decimal approximation as the exact value.

width.minimum: Locate √2 and √3 approximately on the real number line by identifying the integers they fall between.
width.typical: Locate a range of irrational numbers (square roots, π) on the number line using digital tools; describe the real number system as the union of rationals and irrationals.
wider: Use digital tools to zoom into the real number line and observe the density of both rational and irrational numbers in any interval.
Investigate applied contexts where irrational numbers arise: hypotenuse lengths from Pythagoras, circumference calculations — connect to where exact values are needed vs approximations.

modes.reason: Locating irrational numbers requires explicit reasoning: identify bounding perfect squares, take their roots, narrow the interval. Without the scaffold students place irrationals arbitrarily.

descriptors.title: Exponent laws
descriptors.description: establish and apply the exponent laws with positive integer exponents and the zero-exponent, using exponent notation with numbers
descriptors.knowledge: Students can write numbers using exponent notation and connect powers of 10 to place value (from AC9M7N02, AC9M7N03). Students understand prime factorisation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students establish and apply the product, quotient, and power-of-a-power rules, and the zero exponent, using numerical examples and exponent notation.

nodes.label: Establishing the exponent laws from expanded form
nodes.checkpoint: Students derive the product of powers, quotient of powers, and power of a power rules from expanded form, and state each rule.
criteria: Derives at least one exponent law from expanded form.
States all three laws and the zero exponent correctly.
Explains why a⁰ = 1.

width.minimum: Derive and state the product rule (aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ) using at least two numerical examples.
width.typical: Derive all three laws from expanded form; state each rule; verify using digital tools; establish that a⁰ = 1 for any non-zero base.
wider: Investigate why a⁰ = 1 using the quotient rule: aⁿ/aⁿ = a⁰ = 1 — connect to the pattern of decreasing exponents.
Explore the pattern extending to negative exponents: what would a⁻¹ mean, following the sequence pattern?

modes.reason: Deriving the laws from expanded form requires an explicit step-by-step process. Students who jump to applying rules without derivation have fragile understanding and apply laws incorrectly to different bases.

nodes.label: Applying exponent laws in combination
nodes.checkpoint: Students apply the exponent laws individually and in combination to simplify numerical expressions, checking that bases are the same before applying.
criteria: Correctly applies each exponent law individually.
Applies laws in combination without confusing different-base expressions.
Does not apply exponent laws when bases differ.

width.minimum: Apply the product and quotient rules to simplify expressions with the same base.
width.typical: Apply all three laws in combination to simplify multi-step numerical expressions; identify when the zero exponent arises naturally; use digital tools to verify.
wider: Investigate expressions where multiple laws apply in sequence — develop a systematic order of operations for exponent simplification.
Explore how exponent laws apply in scientific notation contexts: multiply and divide numbers in scientific notation using the product and quotient rules.

modes.reason: Applying the laws in combination requires procedural fluency with each law before they can be chained. Errors typically arise from applying laws across different bases or confusing additive and multiplicative rules.

descriptors.title: Terminating and recurring decimals
descriptors.description: recognise terminating and recurring decimals, using digital tools as appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can convert fractions to decimals and understand that some fractions produce repeating decimals (from AC9M7N04). Students understand prime factorisation (from AC9M7N02).
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise terminating and recurring decimals and identify from the prime factorisation of the denominator whether a fraction produces a terminating decimal.

nodes.label: Identifying terminating and recurring decimals
nodes.checkpoint: Students distinguish terminating from recurring decimals and use correct notation for recurring decimals.
criteria: Correctly classifies a fraction's decimal expansion as terminating or recurring.
Writes a recurring decimal using correct notation.
Does not confuse recurring with irrational (non-terminating, non-recurring).
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to predict termination from prime factorisation — students who cannot reliably classify a decimal as terminating or recurring by inspection cannot verify whether their prime factorisation prediction is correct.

width.minimum: Classify given fractions as terminating or recurring by division; write recurring decimals using dot or bar notation.
width.typical: Identify terminating, recurring and non-terminating (irrational) decimals; use digital tools to explore the decimal expansion of fractions; apply correct notation.
wider: Investigate the length of the repeating cycle for unit fractions (1/7, 1/11, 1/13) and look for patterns — connect to divisibility.
Explore why 0.999... = 1 using the recurring decimal as an argument — discuss what this tells us about real number representation.

modes.reason: Students often believe all fractions terminate or that recurring means 'goes on forever randomly'. Multiple examples across different denominators resolve these misconceptions.

nodes.label: Predicting termination from prime factorisation of denominator
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify whether a fraction terminates by examining whether the prime factorisation of the denominator contains only factors of 2 and/or 5.
criteria: Correctly predicts whether a fraction terminates from its denominator's prime factorisation.
Explains why the rule works (connection to base 10).
Simplifies fractions first where necessary before applying the rule.

width.minimum: State the rule and apply it to determine whether a given fraction terminates, without performing the division.
width.typical: Apply the rule across a range of fractions including those in non-simplest form; explain why denominators with only 2s and 5s produce terminating decimals.
wider: Investigate why only factors of 2 and 5 produce terminating decimals in base 10 — connect to the structure of our number system and how this would differ in base 12.
Explore mixed examples where simplification first is required before applying the rule.

modes.reason: The connection between prime factorisation and decimal behaviour requires an explicit logical chain that students rarely construct spontaneously. A scaffold linking the denominator structure to the decimal base is needed.

descriptors.title: Four operations with integers
descriptors.description: use the 4 operations with integers and with rational numbers, choosing and using efficient strategies and digital tools where appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can add and subtract integers (from AC9M7N07) and apply the four operations to positive rational numbers (from AC9M7N06). Students understand properties of operations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply all four operations to integers and rational numbers fluently, including multiplication and division of negative numbers, using efficient strategies.

nodes.label: Multiplication and division of integers
nodes.checkpoint: Students establish and apply the sign rules for multiplication and division of integers, including negative × negative = positive.
criteria: Correctly applies sign rules for all combinations of integer multiplication and division.
Explains the sign rule for negative × negative.
Does not confuse multiplication sign rules with addition sign rules.
nodes.hinge_reason: Integer multiplication sign rules are directly required in Node 2 — students who confuse the rules when multiplying integers make the same errors when multiplying negative fractions and decimals, producing systematic sign errors across all rational number operations.

width.minimum: Apply sign rules to calculate products and quotients of integers, including two negative numbers.
width.typical: Establish sign rules using patterns; apply to multi-step calculations; explain why (−1)² = 1 and (−1)³ = −1.
wider: Investigate the pattern (−1)ⁿ for increasing n — connect to the sign rules and predict for any integer exponent.
Explore why negative × negative = positive using a number line or debt/removal model as a conceptual justification.

modes.reason: The sign rules for multiplication are counter-intuitive, especially negative × negative = positive. Multiple representations (pattern, number line, debt model) each resolve a different facet of the misconception.

nodes.label: Efficient strategies for rational number operations
nodes.checkpoint: Students apply all four operations to rational numbers including negative fractions and decimals, selecting efficient strategies and digital tools appropriately.
criteria: Correctly computes with negative fractions and decimals.
Selects an efficient strategy and can justify why.
Does not default to the most laborious method when a simpler one is available.

width.minimum: Calculate results involving mixed negative rational numbers using at least one efficient strategy.
width.typical: Apply commutative, associative and distributive properties to simplify multi-step calculations; select between mental, written and digital strategies based on the numbers involved.
wider: Investigate a complex multi-step problem where choosing the wrong representation (fraction vs decimal vs percentage) leads to significantly more work — compare approaches.
Apply efficient strategies to financial calculations: tax, discount, interest across combined positive and negative quantities.

modes.reason: Fluent application across all four operations with negative rationals requires sustained practice across varied problem types. Efficiency judgments can only develop once the operations themselves are automatic.

descriptors.title: Mathematical modelling with percentages
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving rational numbers and percentages, including financial contexts; formulate problems, choosing efficient calculation strategies and using digital tools where appropriate; interpret and communicate solutions in terms of the situation, reviewing the appropriateness of the model
descriptors.knowledge: Students can model practical problems with rational numbers and percentages (from AC9M7N09). Students can apply four operations to integers and rationals (from AC9M8N04).
descriptors.endpoint: Students formulate and solve practical models involving percentage increase/decrease, financial contexts including tax, and problems with negative quantities; review model appropriateness and communicate solutions.

nodes.label: Modelling percentage increase and decrease
nodes.checkpoint: Students model situations involving percentage increase and decrease, including mark-ups, discounts, and GST, and explain why the result is an increase or decrease.
criteria: Correctly models a percentage increase or decrease problem.
Explains why the change is an increase or decrease.
Uses an efficient multiplier strategy where appropriate.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 financial modelling includes percentage-based tax and interest calculations — students who cannot reliably apply percentage increase/decrease across varied contexts cannot set up the financial models that depend on this reasoning.

width.minimum: Model a percentage increase or decrease problem (e.g. discount, mark-up) and explain why the result is higher or lower.
width.typical: Apply percentage modelling to mark-ups, discounts, GST, and market trends; explain the direction of change; use multiplier approach for efficiency.
wider: Investigate successive percentage changes — why does a 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease not return to the original? Develop a general model.
Model environmental or population contexts involving percentage change over extended time periods — connect to exponential growth informally.

modes.reason: Percentage increase and decrease problems span a wide range of structures and contexts. Students who only practise one type (e.g. discount) fail to recognise the same structure in other contexts (e.g. tax, population change).

nodes.label: Modelling financial and real-world contexts
nodes.checkpoint: Students formulate and solve models for financial problems including personal income tax, and interpret and communicate solutions including review of model appropriateness.
criteria: Formulates a model correctly from a financial or real-world context.
Interprets the solution with appropriate units and contextual meaning.
Reviews whether the model captures the situation accurately.

width.minimum: Model a simple financial problem (e.g. tax bracket, pay rate) and interpret the solution in context.
width.typical: Apply modelling to income tax, comparing taxation brackets; model weather/environmental contexts with positive and negative quantities; review whether the model is appropriate for the situation.
wider: Model personal income tax across multiple tax brackets — calculate effective tax rate and compare to marginal rate.
Investigate modelling of sea depth or temperature changes using negative quantities — apply to real environmental data.

modes.reason: Financial modelling requires simultaneous application of percentage operations, negative number handling, and communication of results in context — the integration of all prior number strand work at Year 8.

descriptors.title: Complementary events
descriptors.description: recognise that complementary events have a combined probability of one; use this relationship to calculate probabilities in applied contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can assign probabilities to single-stage events and verify they sum to 1 (from AC9M7P01). Students understand the sample space.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise complementary events, use P(A) + P(not A) = 1 to find probabilities, and apply this to practical contexts including AI applications.

nodes.label: Recognising complementary events
nodes.checkpoint: Students recognise complementary events as pairs that together cover all outcomes, and state that P(A) + P(not A) = 1.
criteria: Correctly identifies the complement of a given event.
States P(A) + P(not A) = 1 and verifies it for a specific case.
Does not confuse complementary events with mutually exclusive events.
nodes.hinge_reason: Confusion between complementary and mutually exclusive events causes systematic errors in Node 2 — students who cannot reliably identify complements apply P(not A) = 1 − P(A) to the wrong events.

width.minimum: Identify the complement of a given event and verify that P(A) + P(not A) = 1 for a specific example.
width.typical: Identify complementary pairs across varied contexts (dice, spinners, weather); state the relationship; distinguish complementary from mutually exclusive events.
wider: Investigate events that are not easily described by name — construct the complement explicitly from the sample space.
Explore whether two events can be both complementary and mutually exclusive — discuss what this tells you about the sample space.

modes.reason: Recognising complementary events requires reliable identification before the relationship can be applied strategically. Students who confuse complementary with mutually exclusive make systematic errors in node 2.

nodes.label: Using the complement relationship to calculate probabilities
nodes.checkpoint: Students use P(not A) = 1 − P(A) to calculate probabilities in applied contexts, including cases where finding the complement is more efficient than direct calculation.
criteria: Correctly calculates P(not A) given P(A) and vice versa.
Identifies at least one context where finding the complement is more efficient.
Applies the complement relationship correctly to a practical problem.

width.minimum: Given P(A), find P(not A); apply to a practical problem where the complement is given and the event probability is required.
width.typical: Apply the complement relationship to a range of practical contexts; recognise when finding the complement is the more efficient strategy; apply to simple 'at least one' problems.
wider: Investigate how AI applications use complementary event probabilities when assessing binary outcomes — e.g. spam vs not spam, fraud vs not fraud.
Explore P(at least one) = 1 − P(none) for simple cases — apply to problems where direct calculation would require listing many outcomes.

modes.reason: The strategic insight — that finding the complement is sometimes easier — only develops across varied problem types. Students who only practise direct complement calculation miss the efficiency judgment that makes the relationship powerful.

descriptors.title: Combinations for two events
descriptors.description: determine all possible combinations for 2 events, using two-way tables, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams, and use these to determine probabilities of specific outcomes in practical situations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can list sample spaces and assign probabilities for single-stage events (from AC9M7P01). Students understand complementary events (from AC9M8P01).
descriptors.endpoint: Students represent all combinations for two events using two-way tables, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams, and calculate probabilities of compound events.

nodes.label: Representing two-event combinations
nodes.checkpoint: Students represent all possible combinations for two events using two-way tables, tree diagrams and Venn diagrams.
criteria: Correctly lists all combinations for a two-event situation.
Represents combinations accurately using at least one method.
Identifies the advantage of each representation for different questions.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot select an appropriate representation for a given probability question cannot access Node 2 — calculating compound event probabilities requires first constructing a valid representation of the sample space.

width.minimum: Represent all combinations for two events using one of: two-way table, tree diagram, or Venn diagram.
width.typical: Represent the same two-event situation using all three methods; identify which representation is most useful for different probability questions.
wider: Explore First Nations Australian children's instructive games with two-event outcomes — e.g. Battendi from the Ngarrindjeri Peoples — represent combinations and discuss fairness.
Investigate mutually exclusive events using Venn diagrams: show that the circles don't overlap and explain what this means.

modes.reason: Each representation (table, tree, Venn) makes different probability questions easy or hard. Students need experience with all three to develop judgment about which to use for a given question.

nodes.label: Calculating compound event probabilities
nodes.checkpoint: Students use representations to calculate probabilities of compound events using 'and', 'or' (inclusive and exclusive), and 'at least' language.
criteria: Correctly calculates P(A and B) and P(A or B) from a representation.
Distinguishes inclusive and exclusive 'or' in context.
Uses the representation systematically rather than guessing.

width.minimum: Calculate P(A and B) and P(A or B) from a two-way table or Venn diagram.
width.typical: Calculate probabilities using all event language types (and, or, at least, not); distinguish inclusive and exclusive or; apply to practical situations.
wider: Investigate the addition rule P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) informally — verify using a two-way table.
Apply compound probability to real situations: the probability of a randomly selected student studying both maths and music, or either subject.

modes.reason: Compound probability calculation requires careful interpretation of event language before selecting a calculation method. Students who skip the interpretation step frequently calculate the wrong compound event.

descriptors.title: Simulations of compound events
descriptors.description: conduct repeated chance experiments and simulations, using digital tools to determine probabilities for compound events, and describe results
descriptors.knowledge: Students can conduct simulations for single-stage events and understand the law of large numbers (from AC9M7P02). Students can calculate compound event probabilities (from AC9M8P02).
descriptors.endpoint: Students use digital tools including generative AI to simulate compound events, compare simulated relative frequencies to theoretical probabilities, and describe results.

nodes.label: Setting up and running compound event simulations
nodes.checkpoint: Students use digital simulation tools to simulate two-event compound scenarios and record results systematically.
criteria: Sets up and runs a digital simulation for a compound event.
Records results in an organised frequency table.
Selects an appropriate number of trials for the simulation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires a collected dataset — students who cannot set up and run a simulation have no results to compare to theoretical probabilities and cannot access the second node at all.

width.minimum: Use a digital tool to simulate rolling two dice for at least 100 trials and record results in an organised frequency table.
width.typical: Simulate compound events using multiple tool types (random number generators, online simulators, generative AI); record outcomes systematically; select an appropriate number of trials.
wider: Use generative AI to construct and run a probability simulation — describe what the tool does and evaluate whether its outputs are trustworthy.
Compare results from different simulation tools for the same compound event — investigate whether tool choice affects the outcomes.

modes.reason: Setting up simulations across different tool types builds capacity to work with varied digital environments. Students who only use one tool type cannot generalise their simulation skills.

nodes.label: Using simulation results to determine and describe probabilities
nodes.checkpoint: Students compare simulated relative frequencies to theoretical probabilities for compound events and describe what the results reveal.
criteria: Calculates relative frequency from simulation results correctly.
Compares observed relative frequency to theoretical probability.
Explains discrepancies using the concept of sampling variation.

width.minimum: Calculate the relative frequency of a compound event from simulation results and compare to its theoretical probability; explain any difference.
width.typical: Use simulation results to determine probabilities for compound events; compare observed to theoretical; describe results including whether events appear complementary; connect to the law of large numbers.
wider: Investigate whether long-run simulations confirm that two events are complementary — use this as an empirical check on theoretical calculations.
Explore how the number of trials affects the closeness of simulated to theoretical probability — connect to AC9M7P02's law of large numbers.

modes.reason: Drawing conclusions from simulation results requires explicit reasoning: calculate the relative frequency, compare to theoretical, explain the discrepancy in terms of trial size and chance variation. Students who only record results without this reasoning step do not meet the 'determine probabilities' requirement.

descriptors.title: Congruence and similarity
descriptors.description: identify the conditions for congruence and similarity of triangles and explain the conditions for other sets of common shapes to be congruent or similar, including those formed by transformations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can classify triangles, perform transformations, and understand that transformations preserve congruence (from AC9M7SP02, AC9M7SP03). Students can identify equal angles and sides.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify and apply the conditions for triangle congruence (SSS, SAS, AAS, RHS) and similarity (AA, SAS, SSS), and explain these conditions for other shapes including those formed by transformations.

nodes.label: Congruence conditions for triangles
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify and apply the four conditions for triangle congruence (SSS, SAS, AAS, RHS) and explain why each is sufficient.
criteria: States all four congruence conditions correctly.
Identifies which condition applies to a given pair of triangles.
Explains why SSA is not a valid congruence condition.
nodes.hinge_reason: Congruence conditions are the prerequisite for Node 2 (similarity conditions) and directly feed AC9M8SP02 — students who cannot identify and apply congruence conditions cannot access similarity reasoning or establish quadrilateral properties via congruent triangles.

width.minimum: State the four congruence conditions and identify which applies to a given pair of triangles.
width.typical: Apply congruence conditions to prove triangles congruent; explain why each condition is sufficient; investigate whether SSA is a valid condition.
wider: Investigate why SSA is not a sufficient congruence condition — construct two non-congruent triangles with the same SSA combination.
Apply congruence proofs to geometric contexts: show two triangles formed by diagonals of a rectangle are congruent.

modes.reason: Congruence proofs require an explicit three-step scaffold: identify the condition, state the matching pairs, conclude congruence. Students who proceed informally miss required elements and cannot generalise.

nodes.label: Similarity conditions for triangles
nodes.checkpoint: Students identify and apply the conditions for triangle similarity (AA, SAS, SSS) and understand similarity as a scaled version of congruence.
criteria: Identifies similar triangles and states the condition used.
Correctly calculates a missing side using the scale factor.
Maintains consistent matching of corresponding sides.
nodes.hinge_reason: Similarity conditions feed directly into AC9M8SP04 where students design algorithms to classify shapes as congruent, similar, or neither — thin treatment of similarity conditions means the algorithm design task in SP04 cannot be completed.

width.minimum: State the AA condition and use it to identify similar triangles; calculate a missing side using the scale factor.
width.typical: Apply all three similarity conditions; calculate scale factors; use similarity to find unknown side lengths in practical contexts.
wider: Investigate indirect measurement using similarity: measure the height of a building or tree using shadow lengths and similar triangles.
Apply similarity to map scale problems — connect the mathematical similarity to AC9M8M07 ratio modelling.

modes.reason: Similarity in practical contexts (maps, shadows, enlargements) requires recognising the similar triangle structure in non-obvious configurations. Multiple contexts build this recognition.

nodes.label: Congruence and similarity in other shapes and transformations
nodes.checkpoint: Students explain the conditions for congruence and similarity in other common shapes and connect congruence to transformations.
criteria: States conditions for congruence and similarity for a given shape type.
Connects congruence to rigid transformations and similarity to enlargement.
Correctly identifies whether two given shapes are congruent, similar, or neither.

width.minimum: Explain what must be equal for two rectangles to be congruent; explain what makes two rectangles similar but not congruent.
width.typical: Apply congruence and similarity reasoning to quadrilaterals and other polygons; connect congruence to translations, reflections and rotations; connect similarity to enlargement.
wider: Compare angle and side measurements of shapes under each transformation type — systematically determine what changes and what stays the same.
Investigate: is every square similar to every other square? Is every rectangle? Justify using the conditions.

modes.reason: Connecting congruence/similarity to transformations integrates the spatial reasoning from Y7 transformations with the new congruence/similarity concepts — a genuine cross-topic integration.

descriptors.title: Properties of quadrilaterals
descriptors.description: establish properties of quadrilaterals using congruent triangles and angle properties, and solve related problems explaining reasoning
descriptors.knowledge: Students can classify quadrilaterals and state their properties (from AC9M7SP02). Students can identify congruent triangles (from AC9M8SP01).
descriptors.endpoint: Students establish properties of quadrilaterals by reasoning with congruent triangles and angle facts, and solve multi-step problems with full geometric justification.

nodes.label: Establishing quadrilateral properties via congruent triangles
nodes.checkpoint: Students use diagonal decomposition into triangles and congruence arguments to establish properties of specific quadrilaterals.
criteria: Uses a congruence argument to establish at least one quadrilateral property.
States each step with a geometric reason.
Does not assert properties without justification.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires applying established quadrilateral properties to solve multi-step problems — students who have not established those properties with justification have no valid properties to draw on, reducing Node 2 to guessing or memorisation.

width.minimum: Show that the diagonals of a rectangle bisect each other using congruent triangles.
width.typical: Establish properties of parallelograms, rhombuses and rectangles using congruent triangles and angle facts; state each property with justification.
wider: Establish properties of a kite using congruent triangles — which diagonal is the axis of symmetry? Prove using the congruence argument.
Apply quadrilateral properties to construction designs: car jacks, scissor lifts, folding umbrellas — identify which property makes the design functional.

modes.reason: Geometric proof via congruent triangles requires an explicit scaffold: decompose the quadrilateral, identify the congruence condition, state matching elements, conclude the property. Students without this structure produce informal and incomplete arguments.

nodes.label: Solving problems using quadrilateral properties
nodes.checkpoint: Students use established quadrilateral properties to find unknown angles and lengths, providing full geometric reasoning.
criteria: Finds unknown angles or lengths using quadrilateral properties correctly.
States a geometric reason for each step.
Solves at least one multi-step problem without prompting for each step.

width.minimum: Find an unknown angle or side in a quadrilateral using at least one established property.
width.typical: Solve multi-step problems combining quadrilateral properties, parallel line angle facts, and triangle angle sums; give reasons for every step.
wider: Investigate which quadrilateral properties are preserved under each transformation type — connect to the congruence and similarity work from AC9M8SP01.
Design a problem requiring at least three geometric reasoning steps using quadrilateral properties — write the full solution with reasons.

modes.reason: Solving multi-step quadrilateral problems requires drawing on the full repertoire of angle properties, congruence conditions, and quadrilateral-specific facts simultaneously.

descriptors.title: 3D coordinate systems
descriptors.description: describe the position and location of objects in 3 dimensions in different ways, including using a three-dimensional coordinate system with the use of dynamic geometric software and other digital tools
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plot and describe positions on the Cartesian plane (from AC9M7SP03). Students understand transformations in 2D using coordinates.
descriptors.endpoint: Students describe positions in 3D using latitude/longitude/altitude, three-dimensional coordinates, and other spatial reference systems.

nodes.label: Extending the coordinate system to three dimensions
nodes.checkpoint: Students extend the 2D Cartesian plane to three dimensions by adding a third axis (z), and plot and read coordinates in the first octant.
criteria: Plots a point given 3D coordinates in the first octant.
Reads the coordinates of a plotted point.
Identifies which axis extends the 2D plane to 3D.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires interpreting practical 3D reference systems including latitude/longitude/altitude — students who have not built spatial intuition for the third axis cannot map between the abstract coordinate system and these real-world applications.

width.minimum: Plot and read coordinates (x, y, z) for simple positions in the first octant using dynamic geometry software.
width.typical: Describe and locate objects using 3D coordinates; compare 2D and 3D coordinate systems identifying what is the same and what differs.
wider: Construct 3D shapes using 3D design software that uses a three-dimensional coordinate system — connect the coordinates to the vertices of the shape.
Explore geospatial technologies used by First Nations Australian communities to describe position and transformation on Country.

modes.reason: The extension from 2D to 3D coordinates is conceptually demanding — multiple representations (software, verbal description, diagrams) and real-world contexts help students build spatial intuition for the third axis.

nodes.label: Describing positions in real-world 3D systems
nodes.checkpoint: Students describe positions in practical 3D reference systems including latitude/longitude/altitude and multi-storey coordinate systems.
criteria: Correctly describes a position using a practical 3D reference system.
Interprets a 3D coordinate in a real-world context.
Connects the three coordinates to three independent dimensions of location.

width.minimum: Describe the position of an object using latitude, longitude and altitude; interpret a 3D coordinate location in a practical context.
width.typical: Apply 3D coordinate systems to aircraft/drone location, multi-storey buildings, and map-based systems; connect the abstract system to familiar real-world applications.
wider: Investigate how 3D printers use a three-dimensional coordinate system to build objects layer by layer — describe the relationship between the coordinate path and the physical object.
Explore games based on 3D coordinate systems — describe how player position and movement are represented.

modes.reason: 3D spatial reasoning develops through varied practical contexts — aircraft, buildings, games, and printing all use the same underlying coordinate structure but present it very differently.

descriptors.title: Algorithms for congruence and similarity
descriptors.description: design, create and test algorithms involving a sequence of steps and decisions that identify congruency or similarity of shapes, and describe how the algorithm works
descriptors.knowledge: Students have designed classification algorithms for shapes (from AC9M7SP04). Students know the conditions for congruence and similarity (from AC9M8SP01).
descriptors.endpoint: Students design, test and describe algorithms (flowcharts or pseudocode) that classify triangles as congruent, similar, or neither, based on given measurements.

nodes.label: Designing a congruence/similarity classification algorithm
nodes.checkpoint: Students design a step-by-step algorithm that correctly classifies two triangles as congruent, similar, or neither, using the appropriate conditions.
criteria: Designs an algorithm that correctly classifies triangles using at least two conditions.
Includes clear decision points with yes/no branches.
Tests the algorithm with at least two examples and corrects any errors.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires tracing and evaluating an algorithm — students who have not designed one themselves lack the understanding of decision branching and condition ordering needed to identify errors or describe logic in Node 2.

width.minimum: Design a flowchart that correctly classifies two triangles as congruent or not using at least two conditions (SSS and SAS).
width.typical: Design and test an algorithm covering all congruence and similarity conditions; handle edge cases (e.g. insufficient information); describe how the algorithm works.
wider: Evaluate two different algorithms for the same classification task — compare their efficiency and edge case handling.
