Extend the algorithm to classify quadrilaterals as congruent or similar — identify what additional conditions are needed.

modes.reason: Algorithm design requires systematic reasoning about decision order — which condition to test first, what information is needed, and how to handle each branch. Without explicit structure students produce incomplete or ambiguous algorithms.

nodes.label: Evaluating and describing algorithms
nodes.checkpoint: Students trace through a given algorithm with test cases, identify errors or limitations, and describe in plain language how it works.
criteria: Correctly traces an algorithm with given inputs.
Identifies at least one error or limitation in a given algorithm.
Describes the algorithm's logic in plain language.

width.minimum: Trace a given congruence/similarity algorithm with two test inputs; identify whether the algorithm is correct.
width.typical: Evaluate a given algorithm for completeness and accuracy; fix identified errors; describe the algorithm's decision logic in plain language.
wider: Implement a classification algorithm in a simple programming language — test it with generated sets of triangle measurements.
Investigate: what is the minimum number of decision steps needed to distinguish all five outcomes (SSS congruent, SAS congruent, AAS congruent, RHS congruent, similar, neither)?

modes.reason: Evaluating an algorithm requires simultaneously applying geometric knowledge, logical reasoning, and computational thinking — an integration of the space and digital strands.

descriptors.title: Data collection techniques
descriptors.description: investigate techniques for data collection including census, sampling, experiment and observation, and explain the practicalities and implications of obtaining data through these techniques
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan and conduct statistical investigations and identify variable types (from AC9M7ST03, AC9M7ST01). Students understand sampling informally.
descriptors.endpoint: Students distinguish census from sampling, identify appropriate collection techniques for different situations, and explain the practicalities, limitations and bias implications of each.

nodes.label: Census vs sampling and collection technique selection
nodes.checkpoint: Students distinguish census from sampling and identify when each is appropriate; describe the main data collection techniques.
criteria: Correctly distinguishes census from sampling.
Identifies an appropriate collection technique for a given context and justifies the choice.
Explains at least one practical limitation of sampling.
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot evaluate collection techniques for appropriateness cannot identify sources of bias in Node 2 — the bias evaluation depends on first understanding what the technique does and who it includes or excludes.

width.minimum: State the difference between census and sampling; identify which is appropriate for a given situation and explain why.
width.typical: Compare census, sampling, experiment and observation as data collection techniques; evaluate each for practicality, cost, and appropriateness in varied contexts.
wider: Investigate how decisions concerning sampling relate to training AI systems — explain why biased sampling in training data leads to biased AI outputs.
Explore how digital measuring devices and simulations change the practicalities of data collection compared to manual methods.

modes.reason: Judgment about appropriate data collection technique requires encountering a wide range of contexts — scientific experiments, surveys, social studies, AI training. Students who only consider surveys miss the full range.

nodes.label: Bias in data collection
nodes.checkpoint: Students recognise and explain sources of bias in data collection and describe how bias affects conclusions.
criteria: Identifies a source of bias in a data collection scenario.
Explains the likely direction and effect of the bias.
Suggests a concrete method to reduce the identified bias.
nodes.hinge_reason: Bias identification and evaluation is prerequisite for the entire AC9M8ST02–ST04 investigation chain — students who cannot recognise sources of bias produce unreliable sampling designs, analyses, and inferences in all subsequent statistics standards.

width.minimum: Identify a source of bias in a described data collection process and explain its likely effect.
width.typical: Evaluate data collection designs for potential bias; distinguish sampling bias, response bias, and measurement bias; suggest how to reduce bias.
wider: Investigate a real case of biased data collection and its consequences — connect to ethical implications of data misuse.
Explore how voluntary response bias occurs in online surveys and polls — investigate with a class experiment.

modes.reason: Identifying bias requires a systematic approach: who is included, who is excluded, how is the data collected, what might influence responses? Students who proceed intuitively miss systematic biases.

descriptors.title: Sampling methods and distribution analysis
descriptors.description: analyse and report on the distribution of data from primary and secondary sources using random and non-random sampling techniques to select and study samples
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe and compare distributions using displays and summary statistics (from AC9M7ST01, AC9M7ST02). Students understand random sampling informally.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare random and non-random sampling methods, collect samples, analyse and report on distributions from primary and secondary sources.

nodes.label: Comparing sampling methods
nodes.checkpoint: Students compare simple random, systematic, stratified and convenience sampling methods and evaluate the reliability of each.
criteria: Describes at least three different sampling methods.
Explains the reliability advantage of random over convenience sampling.
Selects and justifies an appropriate sampling method for a given context.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to collect a sample using a valid method and comment on how that method affects the distribution — students who cannot distinguish and evaluate sampling methods cannot make these methodological choices or reflect on their effect.

width.minimum: Describe simple random and systematic sampling; explain which gives a more representative sample and why.
width.typical: Compare simple random, systematic, stratified, quota and convenience sampling; evaluate reliability and bias potential for each; select appropriate methods for different contexts.
wider: Investigate primary and secondary data sources relating to reconciliation between First Nations Australians and non-Indigenous Australians — analyse the sampling methods used and evaluate their representativeness.
Explore stratified sampling: demonstrate how stratification improves representativeness when a population has distinct subgroups.

modes.reason: Understanding the trade-offs between sampling methods requires encountering each in a different context. Students who only know random sampling cannot make informed decisions about stratification or systematic approaches.

nodes.label: Analysing and reporting on sample distributions
nodes.checkpoint: Students collect or obtain a sample, analyse the distribution, and report findings from primary or secondary sources.
criteria: Collects or obtains a sample using a valid method.
Analyses and describes the distribution appropriately.
Comments on how the sampling method may have affected the distribution.

width.minimum: Collect a sample using a specified method; display the distribution and report key features.
width.typical: Analyse distributions from both primary and secondary sources; report on shape, centre and spread; comment on sampling method and its effect on findings.
wider: Compare distributions obtained from the same population using different sampling methods — does method affect the observed distribution?
Investigate a secondary data source (e.g. ABS data) and evaluate the sampling methodology used — how does it affect confidence in the findings?

modes.reason: Reporting on a sample distribution requires integrating sampling method choice, data collection, display creation, statistical description, and contextual interpretation simultaneously.

descriptors.title: Sample size and variation
descriptors.description: compare variations in distributions and proportions obtained from random samples of the same size drawn from a population and recognise the effect of sample size on this variation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe distributions using summary statistics and displays (from AC9M7ST01, AC9M7ST02). Students understand sampling methods (from AC9M8ST02).
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare distributions from multiple samples, recognise natural sampling variation, and understand that larger samples reduce variation.

nodes.label: Sampling variation — same population, different samples
nodes.checkpoint: Students recognise that samples from the same population produce different distributions due to chance, and describe the range of variation.
criteria: Explains that samples from the same population will naturally vary.
Describes the range of variation observed across multiple samples.
Does not conclude that sampling variation means the data is wrong.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires students to investigate how variation changes as sample size increases — students who believe samples from the same population should be identical will misinterpret the Node 2 investigation, concluding that variation means something is wrong rather than recognising it as the expected phenomenon being studied.

width.minimum: Compare two samples from the same population and explain why the distributions differ.
width.typical: Compare multiple samples using digital simulation; describe the variation in means, medians, and proportions across samples; connect to the concept of natural sampling variation.
wider: Investigate First Nations Ranger Groups' use of sampling to track species biodiversity — explain why they use sampling rather than census and how variation affects their conclusions.
Explore how data-driven decision-making uses distributions from multiple samples to identify reliable trends vs noise.

modes.reason: Sampling variation is a counter-intuitive concept — students expect samples from the same population to be identical. Multiple simulation contexts build the understanding that variation is expected and natural.

nodes.label: Effect of sample size on variation
nodes.checkpoint: Students investigate and describe how increasing sample size reduces variation in sample statistics, and apply this to making inferences.
criteria: States that larger samples produce less variation in statistics.
Demonstrates the relationship using simulation data.
Applies the principle to justify a recommendation about sample size in a practical context.

width.minimum: Compare the variation in proportions from small vs large samples from the same population; state which varies less.
width.typical: Use digital simulations to investigate how variation changes as sample size increases; describe the pattern; apply to weather forecasting or other prediction contexts.
wider: Investigate the effect of adding or removing data on measures of central tendency and spread — connect to understanding of sample size sensitivity.
Explore how AI and machine learning systems require large training datasets to reduce variation in model performance — connect to the statistical principle.

modes.reason: The sample size-variation relationship requires students to systematically vary sample size, observe the pattern, and reason about why larger samples reduce variation. An explicit investigation scaffold prevents students drawing conclusions from one or two cases.

descriptors.title: Statistical investigations with samples
descriptors.description: plan and conduct statistical investigations involving samples of a population; use ethical and fair methods to make inferences about the population and report findings, acknowledging uncertainty
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan and conduct statistical investigations (from AC9M7ST03). Students understand sampling methods and variation (from AC9M8ST02, AC9M8ST03).
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan and conduct investigations using ethical and fair sampling methods, make inferences about the population, and report findings while explicitly acknowledging uncertainty.

nodes.label: Planning an ethical investigation with sampling
nodes.checkpoint: Students plan a statistical investigation including ethical and fair sampling methods, anticipate sources of uncertainty, and identify how findings will be used to make inferences.
criteria: Specifies the population, sample, and sampling method.
Identifies at least one ethical consideration and addresses it in the plan.
States what inference will be drawn from the investigation.
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 requires conducting the investigation and reporting with acknowledged uncertainty — without a valid, ethically-designed plan from Node 1, there is no investigation to conduct and no basis for making or communicating inferences.

width.minimum: Plan a statistical investigation specifying: the population, the sampling method, why it is ethical and fair, and what inference is being sought.
width.typical: Design an investigation with explicit ethical consideration; identify potential sources of bias and uncertainty; plan how to communicate uncertainty in the report.
wider: Investigate progress in reconciliation between First Nations Australians and non-Indigenous Australians — evaluate the ethical considerations in sampling and reporting for such sensitive topics.
Explore how businesses use electricity consumption data to draw conclusions about event impacts (e.g. pandemic effects) — evaluate the ethical data use.

modes.reason: Planning an ethical investigation requires explicit reasoning about who is included, who might be harmed by the data collection, and how to minimise bias — students need a planning scaffold that surfaces these considerations.

nodes.label: Conducting, inferring and reporting with uncertainty
nodes.checkpoint: Students conduct the investigation, make inferences about the population from the sample, and report findings while explicitly acknowledging the uncertainty introduced by sampling.
criteria: Makes a valid inference about the population from the sample.
Explicitly acknowledges uncertainty in the report.
Connects the degree of uncertainty to the sample size and method.

width.minimum: Conduct a sample investigation; make one inference about the population; state one source of uncertainty in the conclusion.
width.typical: Conduct a full investigation cycle; make multiple inferences; report findings including confidence language; connect sample size to the degree of uncertainty acknowledged.
wider: Compare the inferences drawn from two different sample sizes for the same population — discuss how the larger sample changes confidence in the inference.
Explore how statistical uncertainty is communicated in public health or environmental reporting — compare with how uncertainty is often omitted in media reports.

modes.reason: Conducting and reporting with acknowledged uncertainty integrates sampling method choice, distribution analysis, inference-making, and communication — the full statistics strand at Year 8.

descriptors.title: Exponent laws
descriptors.description: apply the exponent laws to numerical expressions with integer exponents and extend to variables
descriptors.knowledge: Students can establish and apply exponent laws with positive integer exponents and the zero exponent using numbers (AC9M8N02). They have not yet applied exponent laws to negative integer exponents, or extended the laws systematically to algebraic expressions involving variables.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply all exponent laws to numerical expressions with integer exponents (including negative) and extend these laws to simplify algebraic expressions involving variables.

nodes.label: Negative integer exponents
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate expressions with negative integer exponents and explain why a negative exponent produces a reciprocal.
criteria: Correctly evaluates at least two expressions with negative integer exponents as fractions
Explains using a pattern or sequence why a negative exponent produces a reciprocal
Does not confuse a negative exponent with a negative result
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who read negative exponents as negative numbers produce systematically wrong results in every exponent law application in N2 and N3. This misconception is invisible to students — they produce confident wrong answers.

width.minimum: Evaluate at least two expressions with negative integer exponents (e.g. 5⁻³, 2⁻¹); explain using a sequence pattern (e.g. 5³, 5², 5¹, 5⁰, 5⁻¹…) why 5⁻³ = 1/5³.
width.typical: Evaluate a range of expressions with positive and negative integer exponents; explain the pattern that connects positive and negative exponents using division-by-base sequences; connect decimal representations to negative powers of 10 (e.g. 0.01 = 10⁻²).
wider: Represent decimals in expanded exponential form (e.g. 0.475 = 4×10⁻¹ + 7×10⁻² + 5×10⁻³) and connect to place value
Connect negative exponents to SI unit prefixes (e.g. milli- = 10⁻³, micro- = 10⁻⁶, nano- = 10⁻⁹) and explore scientific measurement contexts
Investigate how negative exponents appear in compound interest formulas and other financial mathematics contexts

modes.reason: Students commonly interpret a negative exponent as a negative number (reading 5⁻³ as −125 or −1/125). Seeing the pattern through multiple bases — with the sequence 5², 5¹, 5⁰, 5⁻¹, 5⁻² making the reciprocal structure visible — resolves the misconception more reliably than restating the rule.

nodes.label: Exponent laws with numerical expressions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply all exponent laws (product, quotient, power of a power, power of a product, zero exponent) to simplify numerical expressions with integer exponents and explain why each law works.
criteria: Correctly names and applies at least three distinct exponent laws to simplify a multi-step numerical expression
Justifies at least one step using first-principles counting of factors
Correctly handles the zero exponent (any non-zero base to the power 0 equals 1)
nodes.hinge_reason: Fluency selecting the correct law for the correct operation is the direct prerequisite for N3. Students who conflate product and power-of-a-power laws carry the error into algebraic simplification where it is harder to detect.

width.minimum: Apply at least three exponent laws to simplify numerical expressions involving integer exponents; justify each step using the definition of an exponent (repeated multiplication/division).
width.typical: Apply all five exponent laws to numerical expressions; relate each law to first-principles reasoning (e.g. b²×b³ = b⁵ because counting factors gives 2+3=5 factors); simplify multi-law expressions; identify which law applies in each step.
wider: Investigate why (ab)² = a²b² but (a+b)² ≠ a²+b² — connect to the distributive property and preview of binomial expansion
Apply exponent laws to expressions involving SI prefixes in combined calculations (e.g. 3×10⁴ × 2×10⁻⁶)
Explore how the exponent laws underpin logarithm rules (e.g. log(ab) = log a + log b corresponds to the product law) — conceptual connection only

modes.reason: Selecting the correct law and applying it without error requires fluency built through varied practice. Students who can explain the laws conceptually still commonly make errors on multi-step simplifications — particularly confusing product law (add exponents) with power of a power law (multiply exponents).

nodes.label: Extending exponent laws to variables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply exponent laws to simplify algebraic expressions involving variables, including products, quotients and powers of expressions with constants and variables.
criteria: Correctly simplifies at least two algebraic expressions involving exponent laws, including one with multiple variables
Applies the convention x⁰=1 and x¹=x correctly
Uses negative exponents correctly in algebraic expressions (e.g. writes 1/x² as x⁻²)

width.minimum: Apply exponent laws to simplify at least two algebraic expressions involving one variable (e.g. x³ × x², (a²)³, y⁴ ÷ y²); use correct algebraic conventions (e.g. x¹=x, x⁰=1).
width.typical: Apply all exponent laws to simplify algebraic expressions involving products, quotients and powers of constants and variables (including multi-variable expressions); apply conventions for writing simplified expressions (e.g. 1/w = w⁻¹); relate to first-principles expansion using repeated multiplication.
wider: Simplify complex multi-variable expressions (e.g. (2xy)³/xy⁴) and verify using numerical substitution
Investigate how exponent laws apply in algebraic fraction simplification (e.g. 6a³b²/3ab⁵) as a precursor to rational expressions
Connect algebraic exponent laws to the structure of polynomial expressions and powers of binomials

modes.reason: Students often apply the laws correctly to single-variable expressions but make errors when coefficients and multiple variables are combined (e.g. treating (2x)³ as 2x³ instead of 8x³). Working across a range of expression types — single variable, multiple variables, coefficients included — builds reliable application.

descriptors.title: Binomial products and factorisation
descriptors.description: simplify algebraic expressions, expand binomial products and factorise monic quadratic expressions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply exponent laws to numerical and algebraic expressions (AC9M9A01) and manipulate linear expressions using algebraic properties (AC9M8A01). They have not yet expanded products of two binomials or factorised monic quadratic expressions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students expand binomial products and factorise monic quadratic expressions with integer coefficients, recognising expansion and factorisation as inverse operations.

nodes.label: Expanding binomial products
nodes.checkpoint: Students can expand a product of two linear binomials using the distributive property and simplify the result.
criteria: Correctly expands (x+a)(x+b) for integer a and b, including when one or both are negative
Shows all four partial products before collecting like terms
Correctly simplifies the middle term (a+b)x by combining the two linear partial products
nodes.hinge_reason: Four-partial-product distribution across all sign combinations is mechanically prerequisite for N2 pattern recognition. Students who miss the inner/outer products generate wrong expansions and cannot identify the (a+b)/ab pattern.

width.minimum: Expand one binomial product of the form (x+a)(x+b) where a and b are positive integers; show each multiplication step; simplify by collecting like terms.
width.typical: Expand all four sign combinations — (x+a)(x+b), (x+a)(x−b), (x−a)(x+b), (x−a)(x−b) — where a and b are positive integers; use an area model or algebra tiles to visualise the four partial products; simplify each result.
wider: Expand products where a and b are negative integers or fractions and verify results using numerical substitution
Use algebra tiles or area models to visualise expansion and record the four partial products systematically
Expand products of the form (ax+b)(cx+d) as an extension — introduce the generalisation and identify which cases are monic

modes.reason: Correctly distributing across both terms of the second binomial (the 'FOIL' pattern) is error-prone, especially with mixed signs. Students need practice with all sign combinations to build reliable mechanical fluency before moving to pattern recognition.

nodes.label: Generalising the expansion pattern
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the pattern (x+a)(x+b) = x²+(a+b)x+ab and use it to expand binomial products and predict features of the result.
criteria: States the general pattern (x+a)(x+b) = x²+(a+b)x+ab correctly
Correctly predicts the constant term and the coefficient of x for a new binomial product before expanding
Identifies at least one expansion where the middle term cancels (difference of squares)

width.minimum: Expand three different binomial products; identify that the constant term equals a×b and the coefficient of x equals a+b; state the general pattern.
width.typical: Use the general pattern (x+a)(x+b) = x²+(a+b)x+ab to expand binomial products and check results; predict the constant term and middle coefficient before expanding; connect the pattern to the area model (four regions).
wider: Investigate special cases: difference of squares (x+a)(x−a) = x²−a², and perfect square trinomials (x+a)² = x²+2ax+a² — identify these as efficient shortcuts
Explore how the general pattern extends when a or b is itself an algebraic term
Connect the expansion pattern to Pascal's triangle for powers of binomials (conceptual preview)

modes.reason: Students who have only expanded same-sign cases often fail to generalise to mixed-sign cases — they misapply the pattern when a or b is negative. Working across all four sign combinations and then naming the pattern ensures the generalisation is sign-agnostic.

nodes.label: Factorising monic quadratics
nodes.checkpoint: Students can factorise monic quadratic expressions x²+bx+c with integer roots by finding two integers whose product is c and sum is b.
criteria: Correctly identifies the factor pair (two integers with the correct product and sum) for a monic quadratic
Writes the factorised form correctly as (x+p)(x+q)
Verifies the factorisation by expanding and recovering the original expression
nodes.hinge_reason: Sign-restricted factor-pair search (testing only positive pairs) causes the majority of factorisation failures in AC9M9A04 equation solving. Students cannot solve quadratics algebraically without reliable factorisation.

width.minimum: Factorise one monic quadratic x²+bx+c with integer roots; show the factor pair search (find integers with product c and sum b); verify by expanding.
width.typical: Factorise a range of monic quadratics with integer roots including positive, negative and zero constant terms; use systematic factor pair testing; verify each factorisation by expanding back; recognise when a quadratic does not factorise over integers.
wider: Use digital tools to explore the factorisation of x²+mx+n across a systematic range of integer values of m and n — identify which combinations produce integer factor pairs and which do not
Connect factorisation to the null factor law and solving quadratic equations — show how the factorised form locates the x-intercepts
Investigate perfect square trinomials and difference of squares as special cases of factorisation

modes.reason: The factor-pair search is the central hinge: students often test only positive factor pairs even when c is positive (missing negative-negative pairs that sum to a negative b). Working across all sign combinations of b and c systematically — positive b/positive c, negative b/positive c, positive b/negative c, negative b/negative c — resolves this.

Factor pair search becomes fluent only through practice. Students need enough repetitions with varied b and c values to automatise the search process before the cognitive load of connecting to equation solving is added.

nodes.label: Expansion and factorisation as inverse operations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can move fluently between expanded and factorised forms of monic quadratics and explain the relationship between the two operations.
criteria: Correctly factorises a monic quadratic and verifies by expansion
Explains the inverse relationship between expanding and factorising in their own words
Identifies the correct form (expanded or factorised) to use for a given purpose (e.g. factorised to find roots, expanded to add expressions)

width.minimum: Given a monic quadratic, factorise it; given the factorised form, expand it back; explain in words why expansion and factorisation are inverse operations.
width.typical: Simplify algebraic expressions requiring both expansion and factorisation in the same problem; apply factorisation to simplify algebraic fractions (e.g. (x²+5x+6)/(x+2)); explain the inverse relationship between the two operations.
wider: Apply factorisation to simplify algebraic fractions with monic quadratic numerators — connect to rational expression simplification
Investigate how the relationship between factorised and expanded forms maps to the relationship between multiplied and factored integers (e.g. 12 = 3×4 ↔ x²+7x+12 = (x+3)(x+4))
Explore cases where simplification requires both expansion and factorisation in sequence — e.g. simplifying expressions involving sums of products

modes.reason: This node integrates expansion mechanics and factorisation strategy into a unified view of algebraic form. The key understanding — that the same quadratic expression can be written in multiple equivalent forms and that moving between them is purposeful — is the conceptual payoff of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Gradient, midpoint and distance
descriptors.description: find the gradient of a line segment, the midpoint of the line interval and the distance between 2 distinct points on the Cartesian plane
descriptors.knowledge: Students can graph linear relations on the Cartesian plane and solve linear equations (AC9M8A02). They have not yet formally derived gradient from two coordinate pairs, calculated midpoints algebraically, or applied Pythagoras' theorem to find distance between points.
descriptors.endpoint: Students calculate the gradient, midpoint and distance for any two distinct points on the Cartesian plane and apply these in context.

nodes.label: Gradient from two points
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the gradient of a line segment between two given points and explain why gradient is independent of which two points on the line are chosen.
criteria: Correctly calculates gradient (including sign) between two coordinate pairs
Verifies with a third point that gradient is constant along a line
Correctly identifies whether a gradient is positive, negative, zero or undefined from the coordinates
nodes.hinge_reason: Signed gradient errors (wrong subtraction order) propagate into N2 parallel/perpendicular identification, N3 distance calculation setup, and all linear modelling in N5. Every subsequent node uses gradient as an input.

width.minimum: Calculate the gradient of a line segment between two given coordinate pairs using rise/run; verify using a third point on the same line that the gradient is the same.
width.typical: Calculate the gradient of line segments from coordinate pairs using the formula (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁); verify that gradient is independent of point choice using multiple pairs; interpret gradient as a constant rate of change; identify positive, negative, zero and undefined gradients.
wider: Investigate gradients in real-world contexts using superimposed images (e.g. ramps, escalators, playground equipment) — read gradient from images and connect to the linear function rule
Explore how gradient is used in machine learning to describe linear relationships in data (e.g. linear regression) at a conceptual level
Investigate how the gradient of a road or railway is expressed as a percentage or ratio and connect to the mathematical definition

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse the sign of gradient (reading Δy/Δx in the wrong order) or treat it as always positive. Fluency with correct signed gradient across positive, negative, zero and undefined cases requires practice before gradient is used in more complex applications.

nodes.label: Parallel and perpendicular lines
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use gradient to determine whether two lines are parallel or perpendicular.
criteria: Correctly identifies parallel lines by comparing gradients
Correctly calculates the gradient of a line perpendicular to a given line
Verifies the perpendicular relationship using the product m₁×m₂=−1
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who confuse the direction convention for perpendicular gradients (or believe all gradients are positive) fail to apply parallel/perpendicular tests correctly in N5 combined problems and in coordinate geometry proofs.

width.minimum: State that parallel lines have equal gradients; calculate the gradient of two given lines and determine whether they are parallel.
width.typical: Verify using examples that parallel lines have equal gradients and that perpendicular lines have gradients whose product is −1; apply these relationships to identify parallel/perpendicular lines from equations or coordinates; explain why the perpendicular gradient relationship holds.
wider: Use dynamic geometry software to drag a line and observe how the gradient of a perpendicular line changes — visualise the m₁m₂=−1 relationship dynamically
Investigate how perpendicularity is used in coordinate geometry proofs (e.g. proving a quadrilateral is a rectangle using gradient)
Connect the perpendicular gradient relationship to rotation by 90° on the Cartesian plane

modes.reason: Students often memorise 'product is −1' without understanding why. Seeing the relationship through multiple perpendicular pairs — including cases where gradients are fractions — and explaining it geometrically (rotation) builds robust understanding that survives transfer to novel problems.

nodes.label: Distance between two points
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the distance between two points on the Cartesian plane using Pythagoras' theorem.
criteria: Correctly identifies the horizontal and vertical distances between two points as the legs of a right triangle
Applies Pythagoras' theorem to calculate the exact distance
Expresses the distance in simplified surd form where appropriate

width.minimum: Calculate the distance between two coordinate pairs by constructing the right triangle formed by horizontal and vertical distances and applying Pythagoras' theorem.
width.typical: Derive and apply the distance formula d=√[(x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²] from Pythagoras' theorem; calculate distances across a range of coordinate pairs including where points share no coordinate; verify results using the Pythagorean relationship.
wider: Investigate how the distance formula extends to 3D coordinates (d=√[(x₂−x₁)²+(y₂−y₁)²+(z₂−z₁)²]) and apply to a simple 3D example
Connect distance calculations to geographic distance problems — discuss how latitude/longitude coordinates relate to map distances
Investigate how distance calculations are used in nearest-neighbour algorithms in machine learning (conceptual)

nodes.label: Midpoint of a line interval
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the midpoint of a line interval between two given points.
criteria: Correctly calculates the midpoint coordinates by averaging x and y values
Verifies the midpoint by confirming it lies equidistant from each endpoint
Applies the midpoint calculation correctly when coordinates are negative or fractional

width.minimum: Calculate the midpoint of a line interval between two coordinate pairs by averaging the x-coordinates and averaging the y-coordinates; verify by checking the midpoint lies equidistant from each endpoint.
width.typical: Apply the midpoint formula M=((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2) to a range of coordinate pairs; verify using distance calculations; use midpoints to solve geometric problems (e.g. finding the centre of a line segment, the midpoint of a side of a triangle).
wider: Apply midpoint and gradient together to find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of a line segment
Investigate how midpoints are used in geometric proofs (e.g. the midpoint theorem for triangles)
Explore how midpoint calculations are used in computer graphics for interpolation between two positions

nodes.label: Applying coordinate geometry in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply gradient, midpoint and distance in combination to solve problems in context, including interpreting gradient as rate of change.
criteria: Correctly selects and applies at least two coordinate geometry tools to solve a contextual problem
Interprets the calculated values (gradient, distance, midpoint) correctly in the context of the problem
Shows clearly labelled working and uses appropriate units or notation

width.minimum: Solve one problem that requires using at least two of gradient, midpoint and distance from given coordinates; interpret the result in the context of the problem.
width.typical: Solve applied problems combining gradient, midpoint and distance; interpret gradient as a constant rate of change in linear modelling contexts; use coordinate geometry tools together in multi-step problems.
wider: Investigate how coordinate geometry tools (gradient, distance, midpoint) feature in autonomous vehicle navigation and machine learning algorithms — discuss the real-world application at a conceptual level
Apply coordinate geometry to verify geometric properties of shapes (e.g. prove a triangle is isosceles using distance, or a quadrilateral is a parallelogram using midpoints and gradients)
Model a real-world situation as a coordinate geometry problem (e.g. planning the path of a cable between two points) and solve using appropriate tools

modes.reason: This node brings gradient, midpoint and distance together into combined problem-solving. The integration challenge is selecting the appropriate tool — students who can calculate each formula individually often struggle to determine which is needed when the problem does not name a technique.

descriptors.title: Quadratic functions and equations
descriptors.description: identify and graph quadratic functions, solve quadratic equations graphically and numerically, and solve monic quadratic equations with integer roots algebraically, using graphing software and digital tools as appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can experiment with linear functions and relations using digital tools, making and testing conjectures (AC9M8A04). They have not yet encountered quadratic functions as a distinct family, identified quadratic relationships from tables of values, or solved quadratic equations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify and graph quadratic functions, interpret their key features, and solve monic quadratic equations with integer roots algebraically, graphically and numerically.

nodes.label: Identifying quadratic relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify quadratic functions from tables of values (using second differences) and from the form of an equation.
criteria: Correctly calculates first and second differences for a given table of values
Correctly identifies a quadratic relationship when second differences are constant
Correctly classifies at least three function equations as quadratic or non-quadratic

width.minimum: Calculate first and second differences for a table of values and use constant second differences to identify a quadratic relationship; identify whether y = ax²+bx+c (a≠0) is quadratic from its equation form.
width.typical: Identify quadratic relationships from tables of values (constant second differences), equations and graphs; distinguish quadratics from linear and other functions; recognise the role of the squared term in determining function type.
wider: Investigate how second differences connect to the coefficient of x² (second difference = 2a) and explain the algebraic reason
Explore real-world data sets and use second differences to determine whether the underlying relationship might be quadratic
Connect the identification of quadratic functions to the classification of polynomial functions by degree

nodes.label: Graphing quadratic functions and identifying key features
nodes.checkpoint: Students can graph quadratic functions and identify their key features: turning point, axis of symmetry, x-intercepts, y-intercept, and whether the function has a maximum or minimum.
criteria: Correctly identifies the turning point coordinates and axis of symmetry equation for a graphed quadratic
Correctly reads x-intercepts from the graph and states 'no real solutions' when the graph does not cross the x-axis
Identifies whether the turning point is a maximum or minimum and explains why based on the direction the parabola opens

width.minimum: Graph one quadratic function y=ax²+bx+c using a table of values or digital tools; identify the turning point, axis of symmetry, and whether it opens upward or downward.
width.typical: Graph a range of quadratic functions using digital tools; identify and interpret the turning point, axis of symmetry, x-intercepts (if they exist), y-intercept, maximum and minimum values; determine when values of the function lie within a given range.
wider: Graph percentages of illumination of moon phases and connect the shape to a quadratic model; discuss this in relation to First Nations Australians' understandings of moon phases
Investigate how changing the coefficient of x² affects the width and orientation of the parabola — connect to parameter variation in AC9M9A06
Explore projectile motion contexts (e.g. paths of thrown objects, water from a hose) and interpret turning point and intercepts physically

modes.reason: Students commonly conflate the x-coordinate of the turning point with the axis of symmetry (confusing a point with a line), or believe all parabolas cross the x-axis. Seeing a range of quadratics — including those with no real roots, those with a double root, and those opening downward — addresses all three misconceptions.

nodes.label: Solving quadratic equations algebraically
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve monic quadratic equations with integer roots algebraically using factorisation and the null factor law.
criteria: Rewrites the equation in the form (x+p)(x+q)=0 before applying the null factor law
Correctly identifies both roots (including cases where roots are zero, equal, or negative)
Verifies at least one solution by substitution back into the original equation
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who apply the null factor law to non-zero RHS (e.g. (x-2)(x+3)=6 → x=2 or x=-3) cannot solve equations reliably in N4 or in AC9M9A05 modelling contexts. The equation must equal zero — this is non-negotiable.

width.minimum: Factorise one monic quadratic equation and apply the null factor law to find the two solutions; verify solutions by substitution.
width.typical: Solve a range of monic quadratic equations with integer roots by factorisation and the null factor law; recognise the connection between the factorised form (x−p)(x−q)=0 and the roots x=p, x=q; verify solutions by substitution and by graphical comparison.
wider: Investigate how the null factor law generalises — why does ab=0 imply a=0 or b=0? What property of real numbers does this rely on?
Solve equations of the form x²=a using square roots, recognising two solutions; connect to the graph
Investigate cases where the quadratic does not factorise over integers and discuss what methods would be needed (preview of quadratic formula)

modes.reason: Students commonly find one solution and stop, or misapply the null factor law (e.g. writing x+3=5 when the equation is (x−2)(x+3)=5 instead of 0). The equation must equal zero before the null factor law applies — seeing this across several cases with explicit checking resolves the error.

nodes.label: Connecting algebraic, graphical and numerical solutions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve quadratic equations using multiple methods and explain the connections between graphical x-intercepts, factorised form roots, and numerical solutions.
criteria: Correctly identifies x-intercepts of a quadratic graph and states these as roots of the equation
Explains why a graph with no x-intercepts means the equation has no real solutions
Solves the same quadratic equation using at least two different methods and verifies agreement

width.minimum: Solve one quadratic equation algebraically; sketch the corresponding graph and identify the x-intercepts; explain how the algebraic roots and graphical intercepts are related.
width.typical: Solve quadratic equations using algebraic (factorisation), graphical (reading x-intercepts) and numerical (trial and improvement, digital tools) methods; recognise that a graph with no x-intercepts corresponds to an equation with no real solutions; relate x²=a to two symmetric solutions on the graph.
wider: Investigate quadratic equations with no real solutions graphically — connect to the concept of complex roots at a purely conceptual level (the parabola misses the x-axis)
Use digital tools to solve quadratic equations numerically and compare precision with algebraic solutions
Investigate how quadratic equations model the path of a thrown object — set up and solve an equation to find when the object reaches a given height or hits the ground

modes.reason: This node connects three previously separate methods (algebraic, graphical, numerical) into a unified understanding of quadratic equations. The integration payoff is recognising that each method gives the same answer and that the method choice depends on context — this is the full descriptor demand.

descriptors.title: Mathematical modelling — change
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve applied problems involving change including financial contexts; formulate problems, choosing to use either linear or quadratic functions; interpret solutions in terms of the situation; evaluate the model and report methods and findings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify and graph quadratic functions and solve quadratic equations (AC9M9A04). They have not yet applied the full mathematical modelling cycle — formulating, choosing a function type, solving, interpreting and evaluating — to applied problems involving change.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use the mathematical modelling cycle to formulate and solve applied problems involving change using linear or quadratic functions, interpreting solutions in context and evaluating the model.

nodes.label: Formulating a model — choosing function type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify whether a situation involving change is better modelled by a linear or quadratic function and justify the choice.
criteria: Correctly identifies whether the rate of change in the context is constant or non-constant
States and justifies the choice of linear or quadratic model with reference to the context
Formulates the mathematical relationship (table, graph or rule) from the given information
nodes.hinge_reason: Function type choice is the gateway decision of the modelling cycle. Students who default to linear models regardless of context cannot formulate quadratic models in N2 and produce models that cannot fit the data.

width.minimum: Given one applied context involving change, identify key features (constant vs non-constant rate of change, turning point, boundary conditions) and state whether a linear or quadratic model is more appropriate; give one reason for the choice.
width.typical: Analyse a range of applied contexts; distinguish situations with constant rates of change (linear) from those with non-constant rates or turning points (quadratic); formulate the mathematical relationship from given data or context description; represent using table, graph or algebraic rule as appropriate.
wider: Investigate situations that appear linear over a small domain but are quadratic over a wider range — discuss the importance of domain in model choice
Explore contexts where neither linear nor quadratic is obviously correct — make an explicit decision and justify, acknowledging model limitations
Connect model choice to the second differences test from AC9M9A04 — apply to contextual data to determine function type

modes.reason: Students commonly default to linear models even for non-linear contexts. Seeing varied contexts — including ones with clear turning points (projectile, area) and ones with constant rates (leakage, temperature cooling) — builds the discrimination needed to make an appropriate choice.

nodes.label: Solving and interpreting the model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve a mathematical model (linear or quadratic) and interpret the solution in the context of the original problem.
criteria: States the solution with correct units and in the language of the original context
Checks the solution for contextual reasonableness (e.g. positive time, valid domain)
Correctly interprets at least one graphical feature (turning point, intercept) in terms of the situation

width.minimum: Solve one formulated problem using the chosen model (linear or quadratic); state the solution in terms of the original context (not just as a mathematical value); check whether the solution is reasonable.
width.typical: Solve applied problems using linear and quadratic models; interpret all mathematically valid solutions for contextual reasonableness (e.g. reject negative time values); interpret features such as turning point, intercepts and gradient in context; use graphs and algebraic methods.
wider: Model financial contexts (profit/loss, trade quotes with call-out fees) using linear functions and interpret the break-even point in context
Model practical measurement situations (area of a rectangle where length is a linear function of width) and find optimal dimensions using the quadratic model
Investigate how the turning point of a quadratic model corresponds to a maximum or minimum in context (e.g. maximum height of a projectile, maximum area for a fixed perimeter)

modes.reason: Students often produce mathematically correct solutions but fail to interpret them contextually — accepting negative values, ignoring domain restrictions, or stating solutions without units or meaning. Explicit scaffolding of the interpret step (What does this value mean? Is it physically possible? What are the units?) is the critical investment.

nodes.label: Evaluating the model and reporting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the limitations of a mathematical model and report their methods and findings clearly.
criteria: Identifies at least one assumption the model makes and explains what happens if it is violated
States the domain over which the model gives reasonable predictions
Reports the method and conclusion in a way that someone unfamiliar with the problem could follow

width.minimum: State one assumption the model makes; identify one situation in which the model would break down or give an unreliable answer; write a brief summary of the method and conclusion.
width.typical: Evaluate the model by identifying assumptions, limitations and the range of the domain over which the model is valid; suggest how the model could be refined; report methods and findings with clear mathematical communication including graphs, equations and contextual interpretation.
wider: Model the hunting techniques of First Nations Australians using quadratic functions; explore the effect of increasing the number of hunters on the prey-catch relationship; evaluate the model's assumptions and limitations
Compare two different models for the same context (e.g. linear vs quadratic for a cooling situation) and evaluate which better fits the data over different time intervals
Investigate a real-world data set and evaluate whether a linear or quadratic model is a better fit, using residuals or visual inspection

modes.reason: Evaluation and reporting integrate the full modelling cycle — formulation, solution, interpretation and critique. Students who can solve and interpret often struggle to evaluate the model itself, treating it as absolute rather than as an approximation. This node develops the critical lens that distinguishes modelling from calculation.

descriptors.title: Parameter variation and function families
descriptors.description: experiment with the effects of the variation of parameters on graphs of related functions, using digital tools, making connections between graphical and algebraic representations, and generalising emerging patterns
descriptors.knowledge: Students can formulate and use linear and quadratic models in applied contexts (AC9M9A05). They have not yet systematically varied parameters across function families to generalise the effect of each parameter on graphical form, nor explored function families beyond linear and quadratic.
descriptors.endpoint: Students generalise the effects of parameter variation on the graphs of linear, quadratic and related function families, connecting graphical transformations to algebraic representations.

nodes.label: Parameter variation in linear functions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the effect of varying the parameters a and b in y=ax+b on the graph, and explain what each parameter controls.
criteria: Correctly describes the effect of increasing or decreasing a on the steepness and direction of the line
Correctly describes the effect of increasing or decreasing b as a vertical shift
States a generalisation about what each parameter controls

width.minimum: Use digital tools to vary a in y=ax+b while holding b fixed, and then vary b while holding a fixed; describe what changes on the graph in each case.
width.typical: Systematically vary both parameters in y=ax+b using digital tools; describe the effect of each (a controls gradient/steepness and direction, b controls vertical translation); generate and test a generalisation; connect back to gradient and y-intercept.
wider: Investigate what happens when a=0 (horizontal line) and when b=0 (line through origin) — discuss these as boundary cases of the general linear family
Explore how parameter variation in y=ax+b connects to real-world modelling — e.g. in a hire cost model C=mx+b, interpret what varying m and b independently means in context
Connect y=ax+b to y=m(x−x₁)+y₁ (point-gradient form) and investigate how both represent the same family from different starting points

nodes.label: Parameter variation in quadratic functions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the effect of varying the parameters in y=a(x−h)²+k on the graph, and explain how each parameter produces a specific transformation.
criteria: Correctly identifies the turning point (h, k) from the completed square form
Correctly predicts the direction of horizontal translation for y=(x−h)² (shift right when h>0)
States the effect of a negative value of a (reflection in the x-axis) with a correct example
nodes.hinge_reason: The horizontal-translation direction confusion (y=(x-3)² shifts right, not left) is the most durable misconception in function transformation work. Students who carry this into N3 misread every transformed function graph across all families.

width.minimum: Use digital tools to vary a, h and k separately in y=a(x−h)²+k; describe what each parameter does to the graph of y=x².
width.typical: Investigate transformations of y=x² — vertical stretch/compression (a), reflection (negative a), horizontal translation (h), vertical translation (k); connect the completed square form to the turning point (h, k); generate and test generalisations about each parameter's effect.
wider: Investigate the relationship between y=ax²+bx+c (expanded form) and y=a(x−h)²+k (completed square form) by completing the square for specific cases
Explore how varying the turning point location moves the graph without changing its shape — connect to the concept of a function family defined by a shape and a parameter space
Investigate parabolic shapes in real-world contexts (satellite dishes, parabolic mirrors, bridges) and discuss how the parameters h, k and a correspond to physical features

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse horizontal and vertical translations — in particular, treating y=(x−3)² as a leftward shift rather than rightward. This is a persistent and consequential misconception. Systematic experimentation with multiple values of h, including sign variation, resolves it more reliably than a single worked example.

nodes.label: Generalising across function families
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply parameter variation to at least one additional function family (reciprocal, square root, cube or exponential) and identify patterns that generalise across families.
criteria: Correctly describes the effect of at least one transformation on a function family beyond linear/quadratic
Identifies at least one transformation pattern that appears in two or more different function families
States a generalisation (e.g. 'multiplying by a constant stretches the graph vertically in every family I tested')

width.minimum: Vary the parameters in one function family other than linear or quadratic (e.g. y=a/x, y=aˣ) using digital tools; describe the effect of parameter variation; identify at least one pattern that also appeared in the linear or quadratic family.
width.typical: Experiment with transformations of reciprocal (y=a/x), square root (y=√x), cube (y=x³) and exponential (y=aˣ) functions; identify which transformation behaviours (stretch, reflection, translation) generalise across all families; generate a summary of common patterns.
wider: Compare transformations across all function families explored — identify which parameter plays the 'stretch' role in each and which plays the 'shift' role; construct a generalisation

Investigate how parameter variation in function families provides AI researchers with insights into model behaviour — discuss how varying hyperparameters in neural networks parallels varying function parameters (conceptual)
Investigate the exponential family y=aˣ specifically: how does varying the base a change the growth rate? Connect to compound growth contexts

modes.reason: This node integrates parameter variation across multiple function families into a general principle. The cognitive work is recognising that the same transformation structure (stretch, shift, reflect) appears in every family despite very different function shapes — this generalisation is the descriptor's endpoint.

descriptors.title: Volume and surface area
descriptors.description: solve problems involving the volume and surface area of right prisms and cylinders using appropriate units
descriptors.knowledge: Students can solve problems involving the circumference and area of a circle using formulas (AC9M8M03). They have not yet extended these to three-dimensional objects — finding surface area by unfolding nets, or calculating volumes of right prisms and cylinders.
descriptors.endpoint: Students solve problems involving the surface area and volume of right prisms and cylinders using appropriate formulas and units.

nodes.label: Surface area from nets
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the surface area of a right prism or cylinder by identifying and summing the areas of all faces.
criteria: Correctly identifies all faces of a right prism or cylinder and their dimensions
Calculates the area of each face and sums to give total surface area
Uses appropriate units (cm², m²) and maintains consistency throughout
nodes.hinge_reason: Systematic face-by-face accounting is prerequisite for N3 problem-solving. Students who miss curved faces (cylinder lateral surface) or double-count produce wrong surface areas and cannot reliably select the correct measure in applied problems.

width.minimum: Draw or identify the net of a rectangular prism; calculate the area of each face; sum to find total surface area with appropriate units.
width.typical: Analyse nets of right prisms (rectangular, triangular) and cylinders; identify all faces and their dimensions; calculate the area of each face and sum to find surface area; derive general surface area formulas from nets.
wider: Investigate objects and technologies of First Nations Australians (e.g. woven baskets, bark containers) — analyse their surface structure and estimate the surface area in context
Compare the surface area of different right prisms with the same volume — conjecture which shape minimises surface area and test with calculations
Design packaging for a given object and determine the minimum material required, considering waste from cutting

modes.reason: A common error is double-counting faces or missing curved surfaces (for cylinders). Systematic face-by-face accounting using the net — labelling each face, calculating its area, and summing — prevents these errors. The scaffold is the net itself: it makes every face explicit.

nodes.label: Volume of right prisms and cylinders
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the volume of right prisms and cylinders using V = Ah (cross-sectional area × height).
criteria: Correctly identifies the cross-sectional area as the base of the V=Ah formula
Calculates volume correctly for both right prisms and cylinders
Uses appropriate units (cm³, m³, L) and converts between them where required

width.minimum: Calculate the volume of one right prism and one cylinder using the appropriate formula; state units correctly.
width.typical: Calculate the volume of a range of right prisms (rectangular, triangular) and cylinders; apply the principle V = Ah to connect cross-sectional area to volume; solve practical problems involving volume (e.g. capacity of a tank).
wider: Investigate the relationship between volume and capacity (1 cm³ = 1 mL) in practical measurement contexts
Find different prisms with the same volume but different surface areas; conjecture about which prism shape minimises surface area for a given volume
Investigate the volume of objects in First Nations Australian technology and explore how volume relates to capacity and function

nodes.label: Solving problems with surface area and volume
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply surface area and volume calculations to solve practical problems, including selecting the appropriate measure for the context.
criteria: Correctly identifies whether a problem requires surface area or volume and explains why
Solves the problem using the correct formula with appropriate units
Checks that the answer is reasonable in the context of the problem

width.minimum: Solve one practical problem requiring surface area and one requiring volume; identify which measure is appropriate for each context.
width.typical: Solve a range of practical problems involving both surface area and volume; distinguish contexts requiring surface area (material, wrapping, coating) from those requiring volume (capacity, filling, displacement); apply appropriate formulas and units throughout.
wider: Design a can-cooler for a standard soft-drink can — determine the amount of material needed and find the most cost-efficient way to cut the pieces from a rectangular sheet
Investigate how manufacturers determine dimensions for packaging that minimises material while meeting volume requirements
Explore how surface area to volume ratio affects biological organisms at different scales (e.g. why small animals lose heat faster)

modes.reason: The integration demand is distinguishing when a problem calls for surface area vs volume — a conceptual decision that sits above the calculation mechanics. Students who can calculate both measures often apply the wrong one. This node makes the decision itself the learning.

descriptors.title: Scientific notation
descriptors.description: solve problems involving very small and very large measurements, time scales and intervals expressed in scientific notation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise and use rates to solve problems involving the comparison of related quantities (AC9M8M05). They have not yet represented very large or very small quantities in scientific notation or performed calculations with values in scientific notation.
descriptors.endpoint: Students represent very large and very small measurements in scientific notation, convert between forms, and solve problems using scientific notation.

nodes.label: Converting to and from scientific notation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can convert numbers between decimal form and scientific notation in both directions.
criteria: Correctly converts at least two large numbers and two small numbers to scientific notation
Correctly converts at least two scientific notation values back to decimal form
Uses a coefficient between 1 and 10 in every scientific notation expression
nodes.hinge_reason: Exponent sign errors on very small numbers (0.0004 → 4×10⁴ instead of 4×10⁻⁴) corrupt all calculations in N2 and applied contexts in N3. Reliable bidirectional conversion is the mechanical prerequisite for all subsequent work.

width.minimum: Convert two numbers to scientific notation (one large, one small) and convert two numbers from scientific notation to decimal form; verify by checking the position of the decimal point relative to the power of 10.
width.typical: Convert a range of very large and very small numbers between decimal and scientific notation; explain why scientific notation requires a coefficient between 1 and 10; connect the exponent to place value and decimal point movement.
wider: Investigate examples from science and engineering (geological time scales, molecular masses, astronomical distances) — practise conversion in context
Explore how calculators display numbers in scientific notation and what limits cause the switch from standard to scientific display
Connect scientific notation to SI unit prefixes (nano-, micro-, milli-, kilo-, mega-, giga-) and convert between prefix notation and scientific notation

modes.reason: Students commonly err on the sign of the exponent for small numbers (writing 0.0004 as 4×10⁴ instead of 4×10⁻⁴). This is a precision-required mechanical skill that needs fluency before applications are introduced — repeated practice with both directions, especially for very small numbers, is the remedy.

nodes.label: Calculating with scientific notation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can perform calculations involving numbers expressed in scientific notation by applying exponent laws.
criteria: Correctly multiplies two numbers in scientific notation by multiplying coefficients and adding exponents
Correctly divides two numbers in scientific notation by dividing coefficients and subtracting exponents
Adjusts the result to ensure the coefficient is between 1 and 10 where required

width.minimum: Multiply and divide two numbers in scientific notation by applying the product and quotient exponent laws; express the result in correct scientific notation.
width.typical: Perform a range of calculations (multiplication, division, and simple addition/subtraction with same exponent) with numbers in scientific notation; apply exponent laws correctly; express all results in scientific notation; use digital tools to verify or extend.
wider: Investigate degree of measurement accuracy across different laboratory instruments (measuring cylinder vs pipette) — express readings in scientific notation and compare precision
Solve multi-step problems using scientific notation from science contexts (e.g. calculating the number of molecules in a sample given Avogadro's number and mass)
Explore how floating-point representation in computers uses scientific notation principles and what causes rounding errors in digital calculations

nodes.label: Applying scientific notation in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use scientific notation to solve problems involving very large or very small measurements and time scales.
criteria: Correctly selects and applies scientific notation operations to solve an applied problem
States the answer in scientific notation with appropriate units
Interprets the result meaningfully in the context of the problem (e.g. explains what the order of magnitude means)

width.minimum: Solve one applied problem using scientific notation (e.g. comparing two very large or very small quantities); express the answer in scientific notation with appropriate units.
width.typical: Solve a range of applied problems using scientific notation across science and measurement contexts; compare orders of magnitude; record measurements to the correct degree of accuracy; interpret scientific notation values meaningfully in context.
wider: Investigate time scales in geology or astronomy — compare ages or distances as orders of magnitude and discuss what scientific notation makes tractable that standard notation cannot
Investigate the degree of accuracy provided by different measurement instruments and discuss how this relates to how many significant figures should be recorded
Explore how scientific notation is used in data storage and transmission contexts (e.g. comparing kilobytes, megabytes, gigabytes, terabytes)

modes.reason: Applying scientific notation in context requires integrating conversion, calculation and contextual interpretation — including choosing appropriate precision and units. Students who can convert and calculate often struggle to interpret what a result means in scale terms (e.g. what does 4.6×10⁹ years actually represent?). Contextual application is where the three skills come together.

descriptors.title: Spatial problems — pythagoras, trig and similarity
descriptors.description: solve spatial problems, applying angle properties, scale, similarity, Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry in right-angled triangles
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use Pythagoras' theorem to find unknown side lengths in right-angled triangles (AC9M8M06). They have not yet applied trigonometric ratios in right-angled triangles, or combined similarity, scale, and Pythagoras in multi-concept spatial problems.
descriptors.endpoint: Students solve spatial problems applying angle properties, scale, similarity, Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry in right-angled triangles.

nodes.label: Trigonometric ratios — finding unknown sides
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply sine, cosine and tangent ratios to find unknown sides in right-angled triangles.
criteria: Correctly labels opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse relative to a specified angle
Selects the correct trigonometric ratio for the given information
Calculates the unknown side correctly to an appropriate number of decimal places
nodes.hinge_reason: Correct side labelling (opposite/adjacent relative to the angle, not fixed positions) is prerequisite for every trig ratio application. Students who mislabel sides select the wrong ratio and produce wrong answers in N2 and all applied work.

width.minimum: Identify the opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse relative to a given angle; apply one trigonometric ratio (sin, cos or tan) to find one unknown side; verify using a calculator.
width.typical: Select and apply the appropriate trigonometric ratio (sin, cos, tan) to find unknown sides in right-angled triangles across a variety of configurations; correctly identify which sides are opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse relative to the given angle.
wider: Apply trigonometric ratios to practical contexts (ramps, angles of elevation, surveying) — draw the right-angled triangle and label before calculating
Investigate the relationship between trigonometric ratios for complementary angles (sin θ = cos(90°−θ))
Connect trigonometric ratios to the unit circle (sine = y-coordinate, cosine = x-coordinate for a unit-radius point) as a conceptual bridge to Year 10 work

modes.reason: Correctly identifying opposite and adjacent sides relative to the angle (not relative to the triangle) is a persistent source of error. Fluency in labelling sides — particularly for non-standard triangle orientations — requires varied practice before applying ratios in problem contexts.

nodes.label: Trigonometric ratios — finding unknown angles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply inverse trigonometric ratios to find unknown angles in right-angled triangles.
criteria: Correctly sets up the trigonometric ratio from two known sides
Applies the inverse trigonometric function to find the angle
States the angle in degrees with appropriate precision

width.minimum: Use the inverse trigonometric function on a calculator to find an unknown angle given two sides; state the angle in degrees to one decimal place.
width.typical: Find unknown angles in right-angled triangles using inverse trig functions (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹); apply across a range of configurations; verify by checking that angle sum is 180°.
wider: Apply inverse trig to find angles in practical contexts (angle of inclination of a ramp, bearing problems, roof pitch)
Investigate angles of elevation and depression — solve problems requiring identification of the correct right triangle from a real-world sketch
Explore how trigonometric ratios and their inverses are used in autonomous vehicle navigation algorithms (conceptual)

nodes.label: Similarity, scale and proportion in triangles
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply similarity and scale factor to solve problems involving corresponding sides and areas of similar triangles.
criteria: Correctly identifies corresponding sides in similar triangles and the scale factor
Correctly applies the scale factor to find an unknown side
Correctly applies k² (not k) when finding the ratio of areas of similar figures
nodes.hinge_reason: Applying k rather than k² for area scaling is a persistent error that undermines N4 multi-concept problems whenever area scaling is part of the solution.

width.minimum: Identify corresponding sides in two similar right-angled triangles; use the scale factor to find one unknown side length.
width.typical: Apply similarity and scale factor to find unknown sides in similar triangles; establish the relationship between scale factor and the ratio of areas (area scales as k²); use proportional reasoning to solve practical scale problems (e.g. estimating heights from photographs).
wider: Design and use a Biltmore stick (based on similar triangle principles) to estimate the height of a tree; connect to rates and proportional reasoning
Investigate proportional estimation using photographs — take a photograph with a known reference object and use scale to estimate an unknown measurement
Explore the triangle inequality and generalise the relationship between Pythagoras' theorem and inequalities for acute (c²<a²+b²) and obtuse (c²>a²+b²) triangles

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse scale factor for length with scale factor for area — applying the same multiplier to both. Working across multiple examples where length and area scale differently (k and k²) resolves this conflation.

nodes.label: Solving multi-concept spatial problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve spatial problems requiring a combination of Pythagoras' theorem, trigonometry, similarity and/or scale.
criteria: Draws a labelled diagram identifying all known and unknown quantities
Selects and applies at least two appropriate tools in the correct sequence
States the solution with appropriate units and precision

width.minimum: Solve one spatial problem that requires using at least two of the tools from this descriptor (e.g. find a distance using Pythagoras and then an angle using trig); show the setup and working.
width.typical: Solve applied spatial problems combining multiple tools — Pythagoras, trig ratios, similarity, scale, angle properties; draw labelled diagrams; work across surveying, design and real-world geometry contexts.
wider: Apply Pythagoras and trigonometry to surveying problems — e.g. determine the height of a building or the distance across a river using indirect measurement
Investigate how autonomous vehicles use geometric algorithms involving angles, distances and scale for spatial navigation (conceptual)
Investigate applications of spatial reasoning in First Nations Australian navigation, construction or astronomical contexts

modes.reason: Multi-concept spatial problems require selecting and sequencing the right tool — students who can apply each tool separately often struggle to decide which to use first, or in what order, in an unfamiliar problem. This node makes that decision-making the learning.

descriptors.title: Measurement error
descriptors.description: calculate and interpret absolute, relative and percentage errors in measurements, recognising that all measurements are estimates
descriptors.knowledge: Students can represent and operate with very large and very small values in scientific notation (AC9M9M02). They have not yet formally distinguished between absolute error, relative error and percentage error, or applied these to interpret measurement accuracy.
descriptors.endpoint: Students calculate and interpret absolute, relative and percentage errors in measurements, recognising that all measurements are estimates.

nodes.label: All measurements are estimates
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain why all measurements are estimates and identify lower and upper bounds for a given measurement.
criteria: States that all measurements are estimates and gives a reason related to instrument precision or reading
Correctly calculates lower and upper bounds for a measurement given its precision
Identifies the half-unit uncertainty corresponding to the precision of a given instrument
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who believe exact readings are possible cannot correctly identify bounds in N2/N3 or interpret error meaningfully. The foundational concept — all measurements are estimates — must be established before error quantification is meaningful.

width.minimum: State that all measurements involve some degree of uncertainty; give one reason why; identify the lower and upper bounds for a measurement given to a specified precision (e.g. 4.5 cm measured to the nearest mm → 4.45 to 4.55 cm).
width.typical: Explain why measurements are estimates due to instrument limitations and reading imprecision; identify lower and upper bounds for measurements at different precision levels; connect precision to the instrument being used (e.g. ruler vs calliper).
wider: Investigate the precision of different laboratory instruments (measuring cylinder vs pipette, ruler vs micrometer) and compare the bounds they produce
Explore how measurement precision is communicated using significant figures and connect to scientific notation
Investigate examples where measurement precision has practical consequences (e.g. engineering tolerances, medical dosages)

modes.reason: Students often believe that a measurement is exact if they read it carefully. Seeing multiple contexts where instrument limits — not reader error — introduce unavoidable uncertainty establishes the conceptual foundation that all measurements are estimates.

nodes.label: Absolute and relative error
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate and distinguish absolute error and relative error for a measurement.
criteria: Correctly calculates absolute error as |measured value − exact value|
Correctly calculates relative error as absolute error ÷ exact value
Explains in their own words why relative error allows comparison across different scales

width.minimum: Calculate the absolute error for one measurement (|measured − actual|); calculate the relative error as the ratio of absolute error to the exact value; explain the difference between the two.
width.typical: Calculate absolute and relative errors for a range of measurements; explain that relative error gives a meaningful comparison independent of scale; identify contexts where each measure is more informative.
wider: Compare absolute and relative errors for measurements of very different scales (e.g. a small chemical mass vs a large geological time span) — discuss why relative error is more meaningful for comparison
Investigate how AI regression models use absolute and relative error metrics (MAE, MAPE) to evaluate prediction accuracy — connect to the mathematical definitions
