Explore contexts where only the absolute error matters (e.g. medical dosage) vs contexts where relative error is the right measure (e.g. manufacturing tolerance as a percentage)

nodes.label: Percentage error
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate and interpret percentage error, using absolute value where appropriate.
criteria: Correctly calculates percentage error using the formula (|measured − exact| / exact) × 100
States the percentage error with % units and explains what it means
Identifies at least one context where using absolute value in the formula is important

width.minimum: Calculate the percentage error for one measurement; explain what the percentage error value means in the context of the problem.
width.typical: Calculate percentage errors across a range of practical contexts (attendance estimates, budget variances, scientific measurements); apply the absolute value formula for percentage error; discuss when using absolute value is appropriate and when direction of error matters.
wider: Investigate percentage error in budget or planning contexts — explore whether overestimating or underestimating has different consequences in specific situations
Connect percentage error to the concept of percentage change — identify the structural similarity and the key difference
Investigate how recommendation systems and regression models report percentage error (MAPE) and discuss what a given MAPE value means for prediction quality

modes.reason: Students often apply percentage error correctly in one context but fail to generalise — particularly around when absolute value is needed. Working across contexts where the direction of error matters differently resolves this and builds transferable application.

descriptors.title: Mathematical modelling — proportion, rates and ratio
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving direct proportion, rates, ratio and scale, including financial contexts; formulate the problems and interpret solutions in terms of the situation; evaluate the model and report methods and findings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can calculate and interpret absolute, relative and percentage errors in measurements (AC9M9M04). They have not yet applied the full mathematical modelling cycle to applied problems involving direct proportion, rates, ratio and scale across diverse real-world contexts.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply the mathematical modelling cycle to solve practical problems involving direct proportion, rates, ratio and scale, interpreting solutions in context and evaluating the model.

nodes.label: Identifying and formulating proportion and rate relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify whether a situation involves direct proportion or a rate, represent it mathematically, and formulate it as a model.
criteria: Correctly identifies the constant of proportionality and writes the mathematical relationship
Defines variables clearly and states units
Represents the relationship in at least one form (equation, table or graph)
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify the constant of proportionality and write the mathematical relationship cannot formulate any model for N2 or N3. Formulation is the entry gate for the entire modelling cycle.

width.minimum: Identify one situation as involving direct proportion or a rate; write the mathematical relationship; define the variables and state the constant of proportionality.
width.typical: Distinguish direct proportion (y=kx) from other rate relationships; formulate problems from context descriptions — including financial (pro rata pay, exchange rates), scientific (Hooke's law) and practical (unit conversion) contexts; represent using equation, table or graph.
wider: Explore fire management techniques of First Nations Australians involving proportion — model the rate of fire spread in different fuel types relative to wind speed, temperature and humidity; formulate the relationship and identify variables
Investigate image editing and social media distortion — model how non-uniform scaling breaks proportional relationships and formulate the distortion as a ratio
Model building/construction standards (staircase rise-to-tread ratio, escalator gradient) — formulate compliance conditions as proportion relationships

modes.reason: Students often recognise proportional relationships in familiar contexts (speed = distance/time) but fail to identify them in unfamiliar ones. Working across diverse contexts — pay rates, Hooke's law, scaling, fire spread — builds the pattern-recognition needed for the formulation phase of modelling.

nodes.label: Solving and interpreting the model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve a proportion or rate model and interpret the solution in the context of the original problem.
criteria: Correctly solves the proportion or rate equation
States the solution with units in the language of the original context
Checks whether the solution is contextually reasonable

width.minimum: Solve one formulated proportion or rate problem; state the solution in the language of the context with correct units; check for contextual reasonableness.
width.typical: Solve a range of proportion and rate problems across financial, practical and scientific contexts; interpret solutions contextually; recognise when a solution is outside the valid domain of the model.
wider: Model rate of fire spread and interpret what the model predicts under different weather conditions — discuss the practical implications for land management decisions
Investigate heartbeat rate and caloric burn rate problems — model, solve and discuss the physiological context
Apply exchange rate modelling to financial planning — solve a practical multi-step problem involving currency conversion and compare to real exchange rate data

modes.reason: Students commonly solve proportion equations mechanically but fail to check whether the answer makes sense in context — accepting physically impossible results or omitting units. Explicit scaffolding of the interpret step prevents these errors.

nodes.label: Evaluating and reporting the model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the limitations of a proportion or rate model and report methods and findings.
criteria: States at least one assumption underlying the proportion model
Identifies a context or domain boundary where the model would not apply
Reports the method and conclusion clearly enough for someone unfamiliar with the problem to follow

width.minimum: Identify one assumption the model makes; state one context in which the model would give unreliable predictions; write a brief report of the method and conclusion.
width.typical: Evaluate models by identifying assumptions, domain limitations and contexts where direct proportion is an approximation; suggest refinements; report methods and findings with clear mathematical communication.
wider: Compare linear (direct proportion) and non-linear models for the same real-world situation — evaluate when direct proportion is a reasonable approximation and when it is not
Investigate cases where social media image distortion compounds across multiple edits — model the cumulative effect and evaluate what the model reveals
Evaluate a published proportion-based claim (e.g. from a media report) — check whether the data supports a proportional relationship and discuss limitations

modes.reason: Evaluation and reporting integrate the full modelling cycle. The key integration demand is moving from 'here is my answer' to 'here is how reliable my answer is and what it means' — connecting mathematical result to contextual judgement.

descriptors.title: Real number system
descriptors.description: recognise that the real number system includes the rational numbers and the irrational numbers, and solve problems involving real numbers using digital tools
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise terminating and recurring decimals using digital tools (AC9M8N03). They have not yet encountered the formal distinction between rational and irrational numbers as a system, represented the full hierarchy of real number subsets, or used the real number line to solve problems involving irrational values.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise that the real number system includes rational and irrational numbers; represent the relationships between subsets of real numbers; and solve problems involving real numbers including substitution into formulas.

nodes.label: Subsets of the real number system
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent the hierarchy of number subsets — natural numbers, integers, rationals, irrationals — and explain what distinguishes each from the others.
criteria: Correctly classifies at least four different numbers into the appropriate subsets of the real number system
Explains the distinguishing property of rational numbers (expressible as p/q for integers p, q, q≠0) in their own words
Identifies that integers are rational, not a separate category outside rationals
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reliably classify numbers into subsets carry category errors into every subsequent node — misidentifying irrationals as rationals corrupts exact-form reasoning, number line placement and formula substitution.

width.minimum: Label a diagram showing the nesting of natural numbers, integers, rational and irrational numbers within the reals; give one example of a number belonging to each subset.
width.typical: Represent the relationships between all subsets using a diagram; explain what it means for one set to be a subset of another; classify given numbers (e.g. −3, 2/5, √7, π, 0.333…) into the correct subset and justify.
wider: Investigate whether √4 is rational or irrational and explain why not all square roots are irrational
Explore how the discovery of irrational numbers (e.g. the diagonal of a unit square) challenged ancient Greek mathematical assumptions about number
Investigate the difference between algebraic irrationals (e.g. √2) and transcendental irrationals (e.g. π) at a conceptual level

modes.reason: Students commonly believe all decimals are rational (identifying 0.333… as 'just a long decimal') or that all square roots are irrational. Classifying a range of examples across all subsets — including edge cases like √4, −0, 0.1̄ — resolves these conflations and builds robust category understanding.

nodes.label: Exact and approximate representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between exact representations of irrational numbers (e.g. √2, π) and their decimal approximations, and explain why decimal approximations are not equal to the exact value.
criteria: Correctly identifies a given decimal value as an approximation of an irrational and states which irrational it approximates
Explains why no finite decimal expansion can exactly equal an irrational number
Writes an exact form (e.g. √3) and a correct decimal approximation for the same value, labelling which is which

width.minimum: State that √2 and π cannot be written as exact terminating or recurring decimals; write a decimal approximation of √2 to 4 decimal places and explain what 'approximation' means in this context.
width.typical: Distinguish between exact forms (e.g. √5, π, 3π/2) and decimal approximations across several examples; explain that no finite or recurring decimal can equal an irrational; recognise when a problem calls for an exact answer vs a decimal approximation.
wider: Investigate what happens when calculators display irrational numbers — discuss what the display shows and what it omits
Explore contexts in which exact form is required (e.g. engineering tolerances, symbolic computation) vs contexts where approximation is sufficient
Investigate how mathematicians establish that a number is irrational — explore the classic proof that √2 is irrational (proof by contradiction) at a conceptual level

nodes.label: Real number line and inequalities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can locate real numbers (including irrationals) on the number line and represent solution intervals for linear inequalities.
criteria: Correctly locates at least two irrational numbers approximately on a number line relative to known values
Solves a linear inequality and represents the solution interval correctly on a number line
Uses correct inequality notation and open/closed circle conventions when marking solution intervals
nodes.hinge_reason: Inequality sign-flip errors (when dividing by a negative) and mis-mapping solutions to number line intervals propagate directly into AC9M9A-strand inequality work. Students who cannot represent solution intervals correctly cannot proceed with inequality reasoning.

width.minimum: Locate √2 and π approximately on a number line by comparing to known benchmarks; represent the solution to one linear inequality (e.g. 2x+7<0) as an interval on the number line.
width.typical: Locate a range of rational and irrational values on the number line using benchmarks and approximations; use a real number line to represent solution intervals for inequalities of the forms ax+b<c and ax+b>c; interpret number line representations of solutions.
wider: Use geometric constructions to locate irrational numbers exactly on the number line (e.g. √2 as the diagonal of a unit square, √5 as the hypotenuse of a 1-2 right triangle)
Investigate compound inequalities (e.g. a<x<b) and represent solution sets on the number line
Connect number line representations of solution intervals to graphical solutions of linear inequalities in two variables

modes.reason: Students often solve inequality mechanics correctly but make errors when negative coefficients require the inequality sign to flip, or when translating an algebraic solution interval into a number line diagram. Scaffolding the reasoning — why does dividing by a negative flip the sign? — prevents a persistent procedural error.

nodes.label: Solving problems with real numbers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve problems by substituting real numbers (including irrationals) into formulas, expressing solutions in both exact and approximate decimal form as appropriate.
criteria: Correctly substitutes real number values into a formula and simplifies
Expresses the answer in exact form where appropriate (e.g. 9π cm²) and as a decimal approximation correct to 2 decimal places
Uses correct units and explains the choice between exact and approximate form

width.minimum: Substitute given real number values into a formula (e.g. A=πr²) to calculate a result; express the answer in exact form (e.g. 25π) and as a decimal approximation; use positive and negative rational numbers to solve one practical problem.
width.typical: Solve a range of problems requiring substitution of real numbers into formulas; choose between exact and approximate forms based on context; use positive and negative rational numbers (including financial contexts); apply digital tools to verify or extend manual calculations.
wider: Investigate problems where keeping exact form throughout a multi-step calculation prevents cumulative rounding error — compare the final result of exact vs approximated intermediate steps
Explore financial planning contexts using positive and negative rational numbers (e.g. budgeting with income and expenses) — model a simple scenario algebraically
Investigate the use of exact real number expressions in engineering or architecture contexts where precision matters

modes.reason: This node integrates the earlier concepts — number classification, exact vs approximate representation, and real number line reasoning — into applied problem-solving. Students need to coordinate: identifying which type of real number is involved, deciding whether to leave answers in exact form, and substituting correctly into formulas.

descriptors.title: Compound events
descriptors.description: list all outcomes for compound events both with and without replacement, using lists, tree diagrams, tables or arrays; assign probabilities to outcomes
descriptors.knowledge: Students can conduct repeated chance experiments and simulations using digital tools to determine probabilities for compound events (AC9M8P03). They have not yet systematically listed all outcomes for compound events using structured methods, or formally distinguished with-replacement from without-replacement sampling.
descriptors.endpoint: Students list all outcomes for compound events with and without replacement using systematic methods and assign probabilities to all outcomes.

nodes.label: Systematic listing of compound event outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can list all outcomes for a two-step compound event using a systematic method (list, tree diagram, table or array).
criteria: Lists all outcomes using a systematic method (tree diagram, table or array)
Verifies completeness by confirming the count matches the expected number of outcomes
Represents the outcome space clearly with no duplicates or omissions
nodes.hinge_reason: Systematic and complete listing (no missing or duplicate outcomes) is prerequisite for correct probability assignment in N3. Students who miss outcomes assign probabilities that do not sum to 1 and cannot detect the error.

width.minimum: List all outcomes for one two-step compound event using a tree diagram or table; confirm that all outcomes have been found by checking the total count matches the product of possibilities at each stage.
width.typical: List all outcomes for a range of two-step and three-step compound events using appropriate methods (lists, tree diagrams, tables/arrays); choose the method suited to the structure of the experiment; verify completeness by counting.
wider: Investigate systematic listing for events with equal-probability outcomes (fair coins, dice) and compare to events with unequal probabilities (biased spinner)
Investigate the connection between the total number of outcomes and multiplication — explain why a two-step experiment with m and n outcomes at each stage has m×n total outcomes
Explore how systematic listing underpins combinatorial counting and preview the concept of factorial notation

modes.reason: Systematic and complete listing — without missing or duplicating outcomes — requires careful procedural practice. Students commonly miss outcomes when listing without a structured method. Building the habit of using tree diagrams or arrays, and checking totals, is the key mechanical fluency for this node.

nodes.label: With and without replacement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how replacing or not replacing changes the sample space and the probabilities assigned to outcomes.
criteria: Correctly adjusts the sample space and branch probabilities when replacement is removed
Explains why without-replacement probabilities change at each stage
Correctly assigns probabilities to at least three outcomes in a without-replacement tree diagram
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who apply with-replacement probabilities in without-replacement contexts (or vice versa) assign wrong branch probabilities in N3 tree diagrams. The structural distinction must be secure before probability assignment.

width.minimum: List outcomes for one compound event first with replacement, then without; compare the two sample spaces and explain how one outcome's probability changes.
width.typical: Compare the sample space and probabilities for compound events with and without replacement across a range of contexts; explain the structural reason for the difference (without replacement: each draw reduces the available outcomes); assign correct probabilities to branches of tree diagrams in both cases.
wider: Investigate how card drawing problems (with and without replacement) change probabilities and relate this to real card games
Explore how with/without replacement affects the fairness of random selection processes (e.g. selecting team leaders, committee members)
Connect the without-replacement structure to combinations — discuss informally how the probability of specific ordered sequences compares to unordered selections

modes.reason: Students commonly apply with-replacement probabilities even in without-replacement contexts, or vice versa, because they focus on the type of event rather than the sampling structure. Explicitly contrasting identical scenarios under both conditions — same container, same items, only the replacement rule changes — makes the structural difference salient.

nodes.label: Assigning probabilities to compound event outcomes
nodes.checkpoint: Students can assign probabilities to all outcomes of a compound event and verify that probabilities sum to 1.
criteria: Assigns correct probabilities to all outcomes of a compound event
Multiplies probabilities along branches correctly to find the probability of a specific compound outcome
Verifies that all outcome probabilities sum to 1

width.minimum: Assign probabilities to all outcomes of one compound event (with or without replacement); verify the probabilities sum to 1.
width.typical: Assign probabilities to all outcomes of compound events with and without replacement; calculate the probability of a specific compound outcome by multiplying along branches; verify total probability sums to 1; apply to solve probability problems.
wider: Use repeated trials of First Nations Australian children's instructive games (e.g. Gorri) to calculate probabilities of winning and not winning compound events — compare assigned theoretical probabilities to experimental results
Assign probabilities to multi-stage compound events (three draws, selecting 3 cards) and calculate the probability of a specific sequence
Investigate symmetry in compound event probability — show that different orderings of the same outcome types (e.g. HT vs TH) have equal probability

modes.reason: Assigning correct probabilities integrates the systematic listing of outcomes with the with/without replacement distinction and the multiplication of probabilities along branches. Students who have done each step separately often make errors at the integration point — particularly forgetting to adjust denominator values in without-replacement scenarios.

descriptors.title: Relative frequencies and compound probability
descriptors.description: calculate relative frequencies from given or collected data to estimate probabilities of events involving "and", inclusive "or" and exclusive "or"
descriptors.knowledge: Students can list all outcomes for compound events with and without replacement and assign probabilities (AC9M9P01). They have not yet used relative frequencies from data to estimate probabilities involving compound logical connectives ('and', inclusive 'or', exclusive 'or'), or used Venn diagrams and two-way tables for this purpose.
descriptors.endpoint: Students calculate relative frequencies to estimate probabilities of compound events involving 'and', inclusive 'or' and exclusive 'or', using Venn diagrams and two-way tables.

nodes.label: Relative frequency as a probability estimate
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate relative frequencies from data and explain how they estimate theoretical probability for compound events.
criteria: Correctly calculates relative frequency as (number of times event occurred) ÷ (total number of trials)
States that larger samples give more reliable relative frequency estimates
Uses a relative frequency to make a probability estimate for a future event

width.minimum: Calculate relative frequencies for two events from a given data set; explain why a larger data set gives a more reliable probability estimate.
width.typical: Calculate relative frequencies for a range of events from given or collected data; connect long-run relative frequency to theoretical probability; use relative frequencies to make probability estimates and predictions.
wider: Investigate how large population data sets (e.g. census data, health surveys) are used to estimate population-level probabilities — discuss the role of sample size in reliability
Design and test an algorithm to calculate relative frequencies from a generated data set — evaluate reliability as the data set grows
Connect relative frequency to the frequentist interpretation of probability — contrast with classical (equally likely outcomes) probability

nodes.label: Compound events: 'and', inclusive 'or', exclusive 'or'
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between 'and', inclusive 'or' and exclusive 'or' events and represent them using Venn diagrams or two-way tables.
criteria: Correctly distinguishes inclusive 'or' (A ∪ B) from exclusive 'or' (A or B but not both) on a Venn diagram
Correctly identifies the region for 'A and B' (intersection) on a Venn diagram
Calculates the correct frequency/probability for each compound event type from a given data set
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who conflate inclusive and exclusive "or" assign wrong probability regions on Venn diagrams, corrupting compound probability estimates in N3. The everyday/mathematical "or" distinction must be established before estimation.

width.minimum: Define 'and' (intersection), inclusive 'or' (union including overlap) and exclusive 'or' (union excluding overlap) for two events; represent one compound event of each type on a Venn diagram.
width.typical: Use Venn diagrams and two-way tables to represent and calculate frequencies for events involving 'and', inclusive 'or' and exclusive 'or'; correctly identify which region of the Venn diagram corresponds to each compound event; use these to estimate probabilities from data.
wider: Investigate the addition rule for probability: P(A or B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A and B) — verify using Venn diagrams and explain why the intersection must be subtracted
Connect Venn diagram regions to set notation (intersection ∩, union ∪, complement) as a foundation for formal probability
Investigate real data contexts with overlapping categories (e.g. students who play sport AND music) using two-way tables and calculate all relevant compound probabilities

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse inclusive and exclusive 'or' — in everyday language 'or' is often exclusive, but in probability it is usually inclusive. Working across contexts where the distinction matters — and where both interpretations are plausible — resolves this conflation.

nodes.label: Estimating compound event probabilities from data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use relative frequencies from data to estimate probabilities of compound events ('and', 'or') and use these to make predictions.
criteria: Correctly calculates relative frequencies for both 'and' and 'or' compound events from the same data set
Uses a Venn diagram or two-way table to organise the data before calculating
Makes a reasonable prediction based on the estimated probability and explains the reasoning

width.minimum: Use relative frequencies from a given data set to estimate the probability of one compound event involving 'and' and one involving 'or'.
width.typical: Calculate relative frequencies for a range of compound events from given or collected data; use Venn diagrams or two-way tables as tools; use estimates to make predictions; compare estimates to theoretical probabilities where these can be calculated.
wider: Design, test and refine an algorithm to calculate relative frequencies for compound events from a generated data set; evaluate reliability as the number of trials increases
Investigate a real survey data set with two categorical variables and calculate all four compound probabilities (A and B, A and not B, not A and B, not A and not B) — use a two-way table
Connect relative frequency estimates to decision-making contexts — discuss when a probability estimate is reliable enough to base a decision on

modes.reason: Estimating compound event probabilities from data integrates relative frequency calculation, compound event identification and Venn diagram/two-way table representation. Students who can do each step separately often make errors when they must identify the correct compound event region and then calculate the relative frequency for it.

descriptors.title: Chance experiments and simulations
descriptors.description: design and conduct repeated chance experiments and simulations, using digital tools to compare probabilities of simple events to related compound events, and describe results
descriptors.knowledge: Students can calculate relative frequencies from data to estimate probabilities of compound events involving 'and', inclusive 'or' and exclusive 'or' (AC9M9P02). They have not yet designed and conducted their own simulations using digital tools to compare simple and compound event probabilities.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design and conduct repeated chance experiments and simulations using digital tools, comparing simple and compound event probabilities and describing results.

nodes.label: Designing a chance experiment or simulation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design a chance experiment or simulation that will generate data to compare the probability of a simple event to a related compound event.
criteria: Specifies the outcome space, what is recorded, and the number of trials
Correctly models the probability structure (with/without replacement, equal/unequal probabilities)
Explains how the simulation replicates the real event

width.minimum: Design one simulation (manual or digital) to investigate a compound probability question; state what data will be recorded and how the simulation replicates the real event.
width.typical: Design experiments and simulations for a range of compound probability questions; specify the number of trials; identify what data to collect; ensure the simulation correctly models the probability structure (correct outcome space, with/without replacement as appropriate).
wider: Design a simulation to investigate a counterintuitive probability result (e.g. probability that at least two people in a group share a birthday for small group sizes) and explain the design rationale
Investigate how real-world simulations are used in risk modelling and forecasting — discuss what makes a simulation a reliable model
Compare manual (physical) and digital simulation approaches — discuss the advantages of digital tools for large numbers of trials

nodes.label: Conducting the experiment and comparing probabilities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can conduct a repeated chance experiment or simulation using digital tools, compare results for simple and compound events, and describe results.
criteria: Conducts the simulation with a sufficient number of trials (at least 50) using a digital tool
Correctly calculates relative frequencies for both the simple and compound events
Compares the two results and describes what the comparison reveals

width.minimum: Conduct a simulation with at least 50 trials using a digital tool; calculate the relative frequency of a simple event and one related compound event; compare the two results.
width.typical: Conduct repeated simulations with sufficient trials to see convergence; compare probabilities of simple and compound events (with and without replacement); describe results including what the simulation reveals about the relationship between simple and compound probabilities; compare experimental and theoretical probabilities.
wider: Use repeated trials of First Nations Australian children's instructive games (e.g. Gorri) to calculate probabilities of winning and not winning — compare experimental results from simulation to theoretical predictions derived from systematic listing
Conduct two versions of the same experiment (with and without replacement) using digital tools and compare the effect on compound event probabilities
Investigate how increasing the number of trials affects the closeness of experimental to theoretical probability — connect to the law of large numbers conceptually

modes.reason: Students commonly interpret small-sample simulation results as definitive (confusing experimental variability with theoretical probability). Running simulations under different conditions — varying trial counts, with/without replacement — builds understanding of when and why experimental results diverge from theoretical expectations.

nodes.label: Describing and evaluating results
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe simulation results, compare experimental to theoretical probabilities, and explain any discrepancies.
criteria: States the experimental probability and the corresponding theoretical probability
Explains why the two values are unlikely to be identical for a finite number of trials
Identifies what aspect of the design or trial count could be changed to reduce the discrepancy

width.minimum: Compare one experimental (simulation) probability to the corresponding theoretical probability; explain one reason why the results might differ.
width.typical: Compare experimental probabilities from simulation to theoretical probabilities; describe the relationship between simple and compound event probabilities revealed by the simulation; explain why experimental and theoretical results differ, and what would reduce the discrepancy.
wider: Evaluate the reliability of simulation results across different trial counts — present results from 10, 50, 200 and 1000 trials and discuss convergence
Discuss and evaluate the use of simulation in real-world contexts (e.g. insurance risk modelling, weather forecasting) — assess what makes a simulation trustworthy
Connect simulation results to the design of fair games and discuss what probability results reveal about whether a game is fair

modes.reason: Describing and evaluating results integrates the full investigation cycle: design, conduct, compare and explain. The integration challenge is connecting what the simulation shows to what it means probabilistically — moving from 'I got 0.48' to 'this is consistent with a theoretical probability of 0.5 because...' This is the descriptor's full demand.

descriptors.title: Trigonometric ratios
descriptors.description: recognise the constancy of the sine, cosine and tangent ratios for a given angle in right-angled triangles using properties of similarity
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify conditions for congruence and similarity of triangles (AC9M8SP01). They have not yet used similarity to establish that side-length ratios in right-angled triangles are constant for a given angle, or named and used sine, cosine and tangent.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise that sine, cosine and tangent ratios are constant for a given angle in right-angled triangles and explain this using properties of similarity.

nodes.label: Sides of a right-angled triangle relative to an angle
nodes.checkpoint: Students can correctly identify the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides for a specified angle in a right-angled triangle.
criteria: Correctly labels hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent for a specified angle in at least three different triangle orientations
Explains that opposite and adjacent are defined relative to the angle, not absolute positions
Correctly re-labels when the specified angle changes within the same triangle
nodes.hinge_reason: Correct side labelling relative to the specified angle (not absolute position) is prerequisite for every trig ratio calculation in N2 and N3 and all applied work in AC9M9M03. Every wrong label produces a wrong ratio and a wrong answer.

width.minimum: Label the hypotenuse, opposite and adjacent sides relative to a specified angle in two different right-angled triangles (different orientations).
width.typical: Identify opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse correctly across a range of right-angled triangle orientations and for different specified angles; explain that 'opposite' and 'adjacent' are relative to the angle, not fixed sides of the triangle.
wider: Investigate what happens to the labels when the specified angle changes — show that opposite and adjacent swap when the complementary angle is used
Connect the labelling convention to the definitions of sin, cos and tan before formal calculation
Draw right-angled triangles in multiple orientations (not just with the right angle at bottom-right) and practise labelling for different angles

modes.reason: Correct labelling of sides relative to the angle — particularly in non-standard orientations — is a prerequisite for correct ratio application. This is a precision-required identification skill; errors here propagate to every trig calculation.

nodes.label: Constancy of ratios — similarity argument
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain using properties of similarity why the ratio of two specified sides is constant for a given angle, regardless of triangle size.
criteria: Calculates the same ratio (e.g. opposite/hypotenuse) for at least two similar triangles with the same angle and shows the values are equal
Explains why the ratio is constant using the property of similar triangles
Confirms that the ratio changes when a different angle is used

width.minimum: Draw two similar right-angled triangles with the same acute angle; measure corresponding sides; calculate the ratio opposite/hypotenuse for both triangles and show it is the same.
width.typical: Investigate nested similar triangles (or multiple similar triangles) to verify that the ratio of corresponding sides is constant for a given angle; explain this using the definition of similar triangles (corresponding sides in proportion); do this for at least two different ratios (e.g. opp/hyp and adj/hyp).
wider: Connect the constancy argument to the formal definition of similarity — corresponding sides in similar triangles are proportional by the scale factor
Investigate how the constancy property breaks down for non-similar triangles (i.e. different angles) — confirm that the ratio changes when the angle changes
Connect the sine ratio to the altitude of a unit-hypotenuse triangle and the cosine to the base, developing geometric intuition for the ratios

modes.reason: The similarity argument is the conceptual core of this descriptor and the most common point where understanding breaks down — students accept the constancy empirically without understanding why. Scaffolding the argument (similar triangles → corresponding sides proportional → ratio is constant) builds the 'why' alongside the 'what'.

nodes.label: Naming the ratios: sine, cosine, tangent
nodes.checkpoint: Students can name the sine, cosine and tangent ratios and connect each to the appropriate pair of sides in a right-angled triangle.
criteria: States the correct ratio definition for each of sin, cos and tan
Correctly evaluates each ratio for a right-angled triangle with given side lengths
Correctly connects the tangent ratio to the gradient of a line

width.minimum: State the definitions of sin θ = opp/hyp, cos θ = adj/hyp, tan θ = opp/adj; evaluate each ratio for a given triangle using measured or given side lengths.
width.typical: Define and apply all three trigonometric ratios; connect tangent to the ratio of opposite to adjacent; relate the tangent of the angle a line makes with the x-axis to the gradient of the line; evaluate ratios for several angles using calculators and tables.
wider: Connect the tangent ratio to gradient — investigate that the angle a line makes with the positive x-axis has tan θ = gradient of the line
Investigate how the values of sine, cosine and tangent change as the angle increases from 0° to 90°, identifying boundary cases (sin 0°=0, cos 0°=1, tan 90° undefined)
Explore historical and cultural contexts for trigonometry — how did ancient astronomers and surveyors use these relationships before the formal ratio notation existed?

descriptors.title: Enlargement transformation
descriptors.description: apply the enlargement transformation to shapes and objects using dynamic geometry software as appropriate; identify and explain aspects that remain the same and those that change
descriptors.knowledge: Students can design, create and test algorithms that identify congruency or similarity of shapes (AC9M8SP04). They have not yet applied the enlargement transformation systematically, or generalised the relationships between scale factor and changes to length, area and volume.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply the enlargement transformation to shapes and objects and explain which properties are invariant and which change, including the relationships between scale factor, length, area and volume.

nodes.label: Invariant and changing properties under enlargement
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify which properties of a shape are preserved under enlargement (angles, shape) and which change (side lengths, perimeter, area).
criteria: Correctly applies enlargement transformation and identifies the image dimensions
Lists at least two properties that are invariant (angles, shape) and two that change (lengths, area)
Uses the scale factor correctly to calculate new dimensions

width.minimum: Apply one enlargement transformation to a polygon using a given scale factor; list two properties that remain the same and two that change.
width.typical: Apply enlargement transformations to a range of 2D shapes with various scale factors (including <1 for reduction); identify invariant properties (angles, shape, orientation) and changing properties (lengths, perimeter, area); verify using measurement and ratio.
wider: Investigate how scale drawings and map scales use enlargement transformations — relate scale factor to real-world dimensions
Explore digital zoom and image resizing — discuss how uniform and non-uniform scaling relate to enlargement and distortion
Connect enlargement to the conditions for similarity established in AC9M8SP01 — confirm that enlargement always produces similar shapes

nodes.label: Scale factor relationships for length, area and volume
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generalise the relationships between scale factor k and the scaling of length (×k), area (×k²) and volume (×k³).
criteria: States and applies the correct scaling relationships: lengths ×k, areas ×k², volumes ×k³
Verifies the area scaling relationship (×k²) for at least two different scale factors
Explains in their own words why area scales as k² (two dimensions each scaled by k)
nodes.hinge_reason: Applying k rather than k² for area (and k rather than k³ for volume) is a near-universal error. Students who carry it cannot correctly solve any problem in AC9M9M03 or AC9M9SP03 that involves scaled areas or volumes.

width.minimum: Calculate the area of a shape and its image after enlargement by scale factor k for at least two values of k; identify that area scales by k².
width.typical: Investigate and generalise the relationships: lengths scale by k, areas scale by k², volumes scale by k³; verify using numerical examples for whole and rational scale factors; explain why the exponent increases for each dimension.
wider: Investigate biological scaling — why animals of different sizes have proportionally different limb thicknesses (surface area grows as k², volume as k³, requiring thicker bones)
Explore how the k² area relationship applies to similar figures beyond squares and cubes (e.g. similar triangles, similar irregular polygons)
Investigate how the k³ volume relationship applies to 3D objects (e.g. scale models of buildings or aircraft) and what this means for material use

modes.reason: Students consistently apply k rather than k² when asked about areas of enlarged figures (and k rather than k³ for volumes). The misconception is resistant because k feels intuitively correct. Multiple examples across different shapes and scale factors — verifying k² each time — is more effective than re-explaining the rule.

descriptors.title: Geometric algorithms
descriptors.description: design, test and refine algorithms involving a sequence of steps and decisions based on geometric constructions and theorems; discuss and evaluate refinements
descriptors.knowledge: Students can apply the enlargement transformation and identify invariant properties of similar shapes (AC9M9SP02). They have not yet designed and iteratively refined algorithms grounded in geometric constructions and theorems.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design, test and refine algorithms based on geometric constructions and theorems, representing them using pseudocode or flowcharts and evaluating refinements.

nodes.label: Representing a geometric process as an algorithm
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent a known geometric construction or theorem application as a step-by-step algorithm using pseudocode or a flowchart.
criteria: Writes a step-by-step algorithm with clear, unambiguous steps
Correctly identifies at least one decision step (with two branches) and at least one computation step
Uses pseudocode or flowchart notation consistently

width.minimum: Write a pseudocode or flowchart algorithm for one geometric process (e.g. applying the triangle inequality to test whether three lengths can form a triangle); identify each step as either a computation or a decision.
width.typical: Represent at least two different geometric processes as algorithms (e.g. triangle inequality check, Pythagorean triple generation, angle bisection); use pseudocode or flowchart notation correctly; distinguish sequential steps from decision branches.
wider: Represent a geometric construction (e.g. bisecting an angle using compass and straightedge) as a precise step-by-step algorithm and discuss what makes each step unambiguous
Investigate how geometric algorithms underpin computer graphics — describe conceptually how a rotation or reflection of a polygon could be implemented algorithmically
Compare pseudocode and flowchart representations of the same algorithm — discuss the trade-offs in clarity and detail

nodes.label: Testing an algorithm with cases
nodes.checkpoint: Students can test an algorithm using specific inputs, identify failure cases, and describe what the algorithm does correctly and incorrectly.
criteria: Tests the algorithm with at least three cases including at least one edge or boundary case
Records inputs and outputs systematically
Correctly identifies at least one case where the algorithm fails or produces an unexpected result
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who test only typical cases and miss edge cases cannot identify failure modes — and therefore cannot refine the algorithm in N3. Refinement without prior test failures is superficial or impossible.

width.minimum: Test one algorithm using at least three input cases (including at least one edge case or failure case); record the output for each; identify any case where the algorithm gives an incorrect or unexpected result.
width.typical: Design and execute a test plan with at least three cases (typical, boundary, edge/failure); record expected and actual outputs; identify which cases the algorithm handles correctly and which it does not; explain what makes an edge case or boundary case significant.
wider: Test an algorithm for generating Pythagorean triples — explore what happens at the boundary (n=1, m=1) and for non-integer or negative inputs
Test an angle bisection algorithm against a variety of angles including 0°, 180° and obtuse angles — identify where the algorithm assumptions break down
Develop an algorithm and test it against a data set to evaluate whether it produces correct results for all valid inputs

modes.reason: Students commonly test only 'typical' cases (the algorithm works for the obvious input) and miss edge cases. Scaffolding the reasoning about what makes a good test — including boundary and failure cases — is the key investment before algorithm refinement is possible.

nodes.label: Refining and evaluating the algorithm
nodes.checkpoint: Students can refine an algorithm based on test results and evaluate the refinement, explaining what changed and why it improves the algorithm.
criteria: Makes a specific, justified refinement to the algorithm based on a test failure
Retests with the previously failing case and confirms the refinement resolves it
Evaluates the refined algorithm: states what it now handles correctly and any remaining limitations

width.minimum: Make one refinement to an algorithm based on a failure case identified during testing; explain what the refinement changes and why; retest with the previously failing case.
width.typical: Refine an algorithm to handle failure cases, improve efficiency or increase generality; retest after refinement; discuss and evaluate the refinement — explain what the algorithm now does that it did not before, and any remaining limitations.
wider: Develop an algorithm for animating a geometric construction (e.g. step-by-step angle bisection or perpendicular bisector) and evaluate it using multiple test cases, refining until it handles all valid inputs correctly
Investigate how software developers approach algorithm refinement — discuss the concept of debugging as a structured process of identify-fix-retest
Evaluate two different algorithms for the same geometric task and compare their efficiency, correctness and generality

modes.reason: Refinement and evaluation integrate design, testing and geometric reasoning into the full algorithm development cycle. The integration challenge is connecting the geometric insight (why this theorem or construction works) to the algorithmic fix (how to handle the edge case in code/pseudocode). This is the descriptor's full demand.

descriptors.title: Analysing survey reports
descriptors.description: analyse reports of surveys in digital media and elsewhere for information on how data was obtained to estimate population means and medians
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare distributions from random samples and recognise the effect of sample size on variation (AC9M8ST03). They have not yet critically analysed survey reports for methodology, or evaluated whether reported means and medians are reliable estimates of population parameters.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse survey reports to evaluate how data was obtained and assess the reliability of claims about population means and medians.

nodes.label: How data is obtained — sampling methods in survey reports
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify from a survey report how data was obtained and explain how the sampling method could affect the representativeness of the sample.
criteria: Identifies the sampling method from the report description
States at least one way the sampling method could limit representativeness or introduce bias
Connects the sampling method to the reliability of the reported statistic
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who only evaluate sample size (not sampling method) cannot assess representativeness in N2 and cannot critically analyse reports. The method-vs-size distinction is the conceptual foundation for all statistical evaluation in this descriptor.

width.minimum: Read one survey report and identify the sampling method used; explain one way the method could introduce bias or limit representativeness.
width.typical: Analyse survey reports from media sources; identify sampling methods (random, convenience, voluntary response); explain how each method affects representativeness; link sampling method to the reliability of any statistical claims about the population.
wider: Analyse reports on public opinion surveys about environmental issues (e.g. land clearing, wind farms) — evaluate the sampling method and discuss the reasonableness of inferences
Investigate how technological and social changes (e.g. decreased landline usage, caller ID avoidance) create new sampling biases in phone surveys
Explore how NLP tools are used to analyse large volumes of survey data and discuss limitations of automated analysis

modes.reason: Students commonly evaluate surveys only on surface features (large sample = trustworthy) without examining how the sample was obtained. Working across multiple report types — polls, media surveys, research reports — builds the discrimination between sample size and sampling method quality.

nodes.label: Evaluating statistical claims — means and medians
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate a claim about a population mean or median by linking it back to how the data was collected and what the data displays show.
criteria: Links a specific statistical claim in a report to the sampling method and data collection process
Assesses whether the claim is adequately supported by the evidence described
Identifies at least one reason why the reported mean or median might not accurately represent the full population

width.minimum: Identify one claim about a population mean or median in a survey report; explain whether the sampling method and sample size support or undermine that claim.
width.typical: Evaluate statistical claims in survey reports by linking claims to displays, reported statistics and sampling information; assess whether the reported mean or median is a reasonable estimate of the population parameter given how the data was obtained.
wider: Analyse reports from the ABS or other government sources on Australian population data and compare to similar data from other countries (e.g. age distributions in Australia, Cambodia, Tonga) — evaluate whether comparisons are valid given how the data was collected
Investigate statistical reports on Australia's trade with Asia-region countries — evaluate whether the reported statistics support the claims made
Explore how different ways of computing an average (mean vs median) can produce different impressions from the same data set

modes.reason: Students who only evaluate reports from one domain (e.g. political polls) apply a narrow template and fail to transfer evaluation skills to scientific, environmental or health reports. Working across diverse report types — different fields, different claim styles, different audiences — builds flexible critical reading that generalises.

descriptors.title: Sampling methods and representation bias
descriptors.description: analyse how different sampling methods can affect the results of surveys and how choice of representation can be used to support a particular point of view
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse survey reports for information on how data was obtained and evaluate claims about population means and medians (AC9M9ST01). They have not yet systematically compared how different sampling methods affect results, or examined how visualisation choices support a particular viewpoint.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse how sampling methods affect survey results and how representation choices can be used to support a particular point of view.

nodes.label: How sampling method affects results
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain how at least two different sampling methods produce different results for the same population and why.
criteria: Correctly describes the mechanism by which each sampling method could introduce bias
Gives a specific example of a population or group that each method would over- or under-represent
Explains why random sampling is generally preferred for population inference

width.minimum: Compare random sampling and convenience sampling for the same hypothetical survey; explain one way each method could produce different results.
width.typical: Compare at least two sampling methods (e.g. random, voluntary response, convenience, systematic); explain the biases each can introduce; use examples to show how different methods applied to the same population would likely produce different results.
wider: Investigate cultural bias in sampling: explore potential under-representation of First Nations Australians in statistical reports and what sampling methods could address this
Investigate how decreased landline usage and caller ID avoidance systematically exclude certain demographic groups from phone surveys — discuss what populations are being missed
Explore online survey platforms and discuss which demographic groups they systematically over- or under-represent

nodes.label: How representation choices support a point of view
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how choices about data visualisation can be used to support a particular viewpoint and assess the strength and fairness of different representations.
criteria: Identifies at least one specific visualisation feature that could create a misleading impression
Explains how changing that feature would affect the viewer's interpretation
Assesses whether the representation fairly represents the data or is designed to support a predetermined conclusion

width.minimum: Identify one feature of a data visualisation (e.g. truncated axis, cherry-picked range) that makes the data appear to support a particular conclusion; explain how changing this feature would change the impression.
width.typical: Analyse multiple data visualisations (including infographics) for features that could be used to mislead or emphasise a particular point of view; identify strengths, weaknesses and possible biases; discuss how the same data could be presented differently to support a different viewpoint.
wider: Compare two visualisations presenting the same data with different design choices — evaluate which more accurately represents the data and why
Investigate how infographics in media selectively use data to support arguments — find a real example and critically analyse it
Explore how statistical visualisation choices affect public opinion on policy issues (e.g. climate data, health statistics) — discuss the ethical implications of misleading visualisation

modes.reason: Students commonly identify only the most obvious manipulation (truncated axis) but miss subtler choices (selective time range, inappropriate graph type, misleading scale). Analysing visualisations from multiple real media sources surfaces a range of techniques and builds genuine visual literacy.

descriptors.title: Comparative data distributions
descriptors.description: represent the distribution of multiple data sets for numerical variables using comparative representations; compare data distributions with consideration of centre, spread and shape, and the effect of outliers on these measures
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse how sampling methods affect survey results and how representation choices support a point of view (AC9M9ST02). They have not yet formally described and compared distributions across multiple data sets using shape, centre, spread and outlier effects simultaneously.
descriptors.endpoint: Students represent and compare multiple data distributions considering centre, spread, shape and the effect of outliers.

nodes.label: Describing distribution shape
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the shape of a data distribution using appropriate terminology (symmetric, positively skewed, negatively skewed, bimodal).
criteria: Correctly identifies symmetric, positively skewed and negatively skewed distributions from graphs
Explains where the 'tail' is in each skewed distribution and which direction it points
Identifies a bimodal distribution and gives a plausible explanation for why two peaks might occur
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who confuse positive and negative skew (or cannot identify bimodal) cannot describe comparative distributions in N3 using shape — a required component of the full comparison.

width.minimum: Identify and label at least two different distribution shapes from graphs (e.g. one symmetric, one skewed); explain what each term means in terms of where the data is concentrated.
width.typical: Describe and distinguish symmetric, positively skewed, negatively skewed and bimodal distributions from graphs; explain what each shape reveals about where data is concentrated and what real-world contexts produce each shape.
wider: Investigate real health data (e.g. disease incidence rates, life expectancy distributions) and describe distribution shape — discuss what the shape reveals about the population
Explore why certain measurements tend toward symmetric distributions (e.g. heights of a population) while others are skewed (e.g. household income, reaction times)
Investigate bimodal distributions in real contexts — discuss what a bimodal shape might indicate about an underlying population

modes.reason: Students commonly confuse positive and negative skew (associating 'positive' with a long tail pointing right but struggling with the direction when the axis is unlabelled or when the tail extends left). Seeing multiple real-data examples, connecting shape to context, resolves the label-direction confusion.

nodes.label: Comparative representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent two or more data sets using the same comparative display type to allow direct comparison.
criteria: Constructs a correctly labelled comparative representation with aligned scales
Reads at least two summary statistics (e.g. median, range) directly from the representation
Identifies which data set has greater centre and greater spread from the display

width.minimum: Construct a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot or parallel dot plot for two data sets; ensure the scales are aligned for direct comparison.
width.typical: Construct and interpret back-to-back stem-and-leaf plots, parallel box plots and comparative histograms; align scales correctly; read summary statistics directly from comparative representations.
wider: Construct and compare two or more representations of the same data pair (e.g. back-to-back stem-and-leaf and parallel box plots) — discuss what each representation reveals and obscures
Explore comparative data from NIAA 'Closing the Gap' reports — construct appropriate comparative representations and discuss what they show
Investigate health trend data across demographic groups using grouped histograms and evaluate what the comparison reveals

nodes.label: Comparing distributions — centre, spread, shape, outliers
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare two or more distributions considering centre, spread, shape and the effect of outliers on each measure.
criteria: Compares two distributions using at least three of: centre, spread, shape, outliers
Correctly explains that outliers affect the mean more than the median
States the comparison in contextually meaningful terms (not just as numerical facts)

width.minimum: Compare two data distributions by stating which has greater centre and greater spread; identify one outlier and explain its effect on the mean vs median.
width.typical: Compare distributions using centre (mean, median), spread (range, IQR), shape (skew, symmetry) and outlier effects; explain how outliers affect the mean more than the median; make contextually meaningful statements about what the comparison reveals.
wider: Investigate the effect of a single extreme outlier on the mean, median and range of a data set — calculate each before and after removing the outlier and compare
Compare distributions of two populations (e.g. age distributions in two countries) and discuss what the similarities and differences reveal in context
Explore how choosing mean vs median can be used to support different impressions of the same data set — connect to the representation bias discussion in AC9M9ST02

modes.reason: Comparing distributions holistically — using centre, spread, shape and outliers together rather than one at a time — is the descriptor's full demand. Students who have learned each measure separately often give fragmented comparisons ('the mean is higher' without reference to spread or shape). Integration means forming a coherent overall comparison.

descriptors.title: Choosing data displays
descriptors.description: choose appropriate forms of display or visualisation for a given type of data; justify selections and interpret displays for a given context
descriptors.knowledge: Students can represent and compare multiple data distributions using comparative representations (AC9M9ST03). They have not yet systematically matched display type to data type and purpose, or justified visualisation choices for a given audience and context.
descriptors.endpoint: Students choose appropriate data displays for given data types, justify their selections, and interpret displays in context.

nodes.label: Matching display type to data type
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the data type (categorical nominal/ordinal, numerical discrete/continuous) and select an appropriate display type.
criteria: Correctly classifies the data type as categorical (nominal/ordinal) or numerical (discrete/continuous)
Selects an appropriate display type and names it
Justifies the selection with reference to the data type
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot classify data type (categorical vs numerical, discrete vs continuous) cannot make justified display choices in N2 — justification requires naming the data type as the reason.

width.minimum: Classify one data set as categorical or numerical, discrete or continuous; select and justify an appropriate display type for it.
width.typical: Classify a range of data sets by type; match display types to data types (bar chart for categorical nominal, histogram for numerical continuous, dot plot or stem-and-leaf for small discrete numerical data sets); justify choices based on data type.
wider: Investigate non-standard display types such as infographics and assess what data type and purpose they are suited for — evaluate one real infographic
Compare the same data displayed in two different but plausible formats and evaluate which communicates more effectively for the intended audience
Use digital tools including generative AI to produce multiple display options for the same data set and critically evaluate each

modes.reason: Students commonly apply bar charts to all categorical data and histograms to all numerical data, without distinguishing discrete vs continuous or nominal vs ordinal. Working across a range of data types — including ordinal categorical (survey scales), numerical discrete (count data) and numerical continuous (measurement data) — builds accurate discrimination.

nodes.label: Justifying and interpreting displays in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can justify a display choice with reference to purpose and audience, and interpret key features of a display in context.
criteria: Justifies a display choice with reference to both data type and purpose/audience
Correctly interprets at least two features of the display in the language of the context
Evaluates whether the display communicates the key message clearly and fairly

width.minimum: Choose a display for a given data set and purpose; justify the choice with reference to both the data type and the audience; interpret one key feature of the display in context.
width.typical: Choose and justify display types for a range of contexts, considering data type, audience and purpose; interpret displays by identifying and explaining key features (trend, centre, spread, proportion) in context; compare and interpret stacked bar charts, area charts and line graphs for part-whole and trend data.
wider: Evaluate a non-standard visualisation (e.g. infographic from a news source) — assess purpose, audience and how well it communicates the statistical question
Use generative AI to produce display options for a data set, then critically evaluate which form is most appropriate for the intended purpose and audience
Investigate how stacked bar charts and area charts represent part-whole relationships and when line graphs are more appropriate for trend data

modes.reason: Justifying display choices requires integrating data type knowledge, audience awareness and purpose — not just selecting a graph type in isolation. Students who can classify data but cannot articulate why a display works for a specific audience and purpose have not reached the descriptor's full demand.

descriptors.title: Statistical investigations
descriptors.description: plan and conduct statistical investigations involving the collection and analysis of different kinds of data; report findings and discuss the strength of evidence to support any conclusions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan and conduct statistical investigations using samples, make population inferences acknowledging uncertainty (AC9M8ST04). They have not yet applied this across different kinds of data (primary and secondary, quantitative and qualitative), or evaluated the strength of evidence to support conclusions.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan and conduct statistical investigations across different data types, report findings, and evaluate the strength of evidence supporting their conclusions.

nodes.label: Planning the investigation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can pose a statistical question and plan a data collection strategy appropriate to the question, identifying potential sources of bias.
criteria: Poses a statistical question that can be investigated with data
Identifies an appropriate data source (primary or secondary) and justifies the choice
Identifies at least one potential source of bias in the planned data collection

width.minimum: Pose one statistical question; identify whether primary or secondary data is more appropriate; describe one data collection method and one potential source of bias.
width.typical: Pose a clear statistical question; plan data collection including source (primary or secondary), method, sample size and sampling strategy; identify potential sources of bias and how to minimise them; consider ethical and fair data collection practices.
wider: Pose statistical questions in relation to reconciliation and First Nations Australian communities; plan data collection from multiple sources, considering relationships between variables and cultural sensitivity in data collection

Plan a multi-variable investigation (e.g. factors affecting location for a tropical fruit plantation) using secondary data from multiple sources; identify what data is available and what its limitations are
Investigate how ABS and other government agencies plan large-scale data collection — evaluate the methods they use and the potential sources of error

nodes.label: Collecting and analysing data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collect or access data appropriate to the investigation and analyse it using suitable representations and summary statistics.
criteria: Collects or accesses data that is relevant to the stated statistical question
Represents the data using an appropriate display type
Calculates at least one relevant summary statistic and states what it means for the investigation

width.minimum: Collect or access data for the investigation; represent it using an appropriate display; calculate at least one summary statistic relevant to the question.
width.typical: Collect or access data from appropriate sources; clean and organise data as needed; represent using appropriate displays for the data type; calculate relevant summary statistics (centre, spread); identify patterns or relationships in the data relevant to the investigation question.
wider: Access and analyse secondary data from the ABS or equivalent databases; compare data from multiple sources and evaluate consistency
Plan and conduct a consumer research investigation with attention to sampling techniques, data cleaning and the difference between primary and secondary data quality
Investigate multi-variable data (e.g. rainfall, land prices, farming costs across multiple regions) and analyse relationships between variables

modes.reason: Students often analyse data without maintaining a connection to the original question — reporting statistics and graphs without explaining what they mean for the investigation. Scaffolding the reasoning loop (What did I find? What does this mean for my question?) keeps the analysis purposeful.

nodes.label: Reporting findings and evaluating evidence
nodes.checkpoint: Students can report investigation findings and evaluate the strength of evidence supporting their conclusions.
criteria: States at least one finding supported by specific data evidence
Evaluates the strength of that evidence (strong/moderate/weak) and explains why
Identifies at least one limitation of the investigation that affects confidence in the conclusion

width.minimum: State one finding from the data analysis; explain what evidence supports it; identify one limitation of the evidence.
width.typical: Report investigation findings clearly with supporting data evidence; distinguish between strong and weak evidence; discuss what the data does and does not support; acknowledge uncertainty and limitations; identify how the investigation could be improved.
wider: Report findings from an investigation into a socially significant topic (e.g. reconciliation data, health disparities) — discuss the strength of evidence carefully and consider what further data would be needed to support stronger conclusions
Compare conclusions drawn from investigations using different data sources or methods for the same question — discuss how data collection choices affect conclusions
Evaluate the strength of statistical evidence in a published report and compare to the strength of evidence from the student's own investigation

modes.reason: Reporting and evaluation integrate the full investigation cycle — question, data, analysis and conclusion. The integration challenge is producing a conclusion that is honest about what the evidence supports and what it does not, rather than overstating findings. This distinguishes mature statistical reasoning from mechanical data processing.

descriptors.title: Expand, factorise and simplify
descriptors.description: expand, factorise and simplify expressions and solve equations algebraically, applying exponent laws involving products, quotients and powers of variables, and the distributive property
descriptors.knowledge: Students can expand binomial products and factorise monic quadratic expressions (AC9M9A02). They have not yet applied exponent laws to algebraic terms with positive and negative integral exponents, nor factorised non-monic quadratics or used the completed square form.
descriptors.endpoint: Students expand, factorise and simplify algebraic expressions and solve equations algebraically, applying exponent laws for products, quotients and powers of variables with positive and negative integral exponents, and the distributive property including completed square form.

nodes.label: Exponent laws for algebraic terms
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply exponent laws (product, quotient, power of a power) to simplify algebraic expressions involving positive integral exponents.
criteria: Student correctly applies at least two distinct exponent laws to simplify a given algebraic expression
Student can identify which exponent law applies when given a mixed expression
nodes.hinge_reason: Exponent law errors propagate directly into N2 (negative exponents) and N3 (expansion) — students who confuse product and power rules produce systematic algebraic errors in all subsequent manipulation work.

width.minimum: Apply each of the three exponent laws to simplify monomial expressions with positive integral exponents (e.g. x³ × x², x⁵ ÷ x², (x²)³).
width.typical: Apply product, quotient and power laws to simplify multi-term algebraic expressions; handle combinations of laws in a single expression; verify results by expanding.
wider: Investigate what happens when exponent laws are applied inconsistently or laws are confused — identify the error and correct it
Connect exponent laws for algebraic terms to the same laws for numerical bases, confirming the rules are the same structure

modes.reason: Exponent law errors (especially confusing product and power rules) are persistent and procedural. Students need fluency through practice before tackling negative exponents or multi-law expressions.

nodes.label: Negative integral exponents
nodes.checkpoint: Students can apply exponent laws to expressions involving negative integral exponents and express results with positive exponents.
criteria: Student correctly rewrites expressions with negative exponents in equivalent positive exponent form
Student can derive the negative exponent meaning from the quotient law rather than reciting a rule

width.minimum: Simplify algebraic expressions involving negative integral exponents, converting between negative exponent form and fraction form (e.g. x⁻² = 1/x²).
width.typical: Apply all exponent laws to expressions containing both positive and negative integral exponents; simplify and solve linear equations that involve negative exponents; move fluently between equivalent forms.
wider: Investigate how negative exponents arise naturally from the quotient law (x² ÷ x⁵ = x⁻³) and explain why a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ without memorising as a definition
Explore how negative exponents appear in scientific notation for very small quantities and connect algebraic manipulation to measurement contexts

modes.reason: The connection between negative exponents and reciprocals is non-obvious and frequently confused. Students benefit from having the reasoning chain made explicit (quotient law → zero exponent → negative exponent) rather than memorising a rule.

nodes.label: Expansion using the distributive property
nodes.checkpoint: Students can expand products of binomials and trinomials using the distributive property, including special products (difference of two squares, perfect square trinomials).
criteria: Student correctly expands a binomial product with no errors including sign handling
Student identifies whether a quadratic expression is a difference of two squares or perfect square trinomial
nodes.hinge_reason: Sign errors in expansion cascade directly into N4 — students who cannot reliably expand binomials cannot recognise factorisation as the inverse, nor complete the square form.

width.minimum: Expand a product of two binomials using the distributive property; identify difference of two squares and perfect square patterns.
width.typical: Expand products of binomials and trinomials; apply special product patterns fluently; expand expressions with multiple terms; verify by substituting numerical values.
wider: Investigate the geometric interpretation of expansion (area model) and use it to verify algebraic results
Explore how the distributive property scales: connect expanding (a+b)(c+d) to expanding products with more terms, developing a general pattern

modes.reason: Sign errors in expansion (especially with negative terms) are a frequent and persistent source of algebraic error. Fluency requires practice, not just understanding.

nodes.label: Factorisation of quadratic expressions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can factorise monic and non-monic quadratic expressions, including using the completed square form.
criteria: Student correctly factorises a non-monic quadratic expression by an appropriate method
Student converts a monic quadratic to completed square form and explains what each part represents
Student explains why factorisation and expansion are inverse operations

width.minimum: Factorise monic quadratic expressions (ax² + bx + c where a=1) by finding factor pairs; explain the relationship between factorisation and expansion.
width.typical: Factorise monic and non-monic quadratic expressions using systematic methods (factor pairs, grouping, or completing the square); complete the square for a monic quadratic; explain the inverse relationship between factorisation and expansion.
wider: Investigate the completed square form y = a(x-h)² + k as a lens for understanding the vertex form of a quadratic — connecting algebraic manipulation to graphical features
Explore cases where quadratic expressions cannot be factorised over the integers (discriminant negative) and discuss what this means algebraically and graphically
