modes.reason: Students frequently treat factorisation methods as disconnected procedures. Wider contexts — including completed square form, connections to graphing, and non-factorisable cases — help students see factorisation as a coherent algebraic transformation rather than a set of tricks.

Completing the square requires coordinating expansion, factorisation and the relationship between algebraic form and geometric meaning. This is the node where prior procedural skills integrate into a unified understanding.

nodes.label: Solving equations algebraically
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve equations algebraically by applying exponent laws and factorisation, including quadratic equations.
criteria: Student solves a quadratic equation by factorisation with correct solutions including sign handling
Student verifies solutions by substitution into the original equation

width.minimum: Solve a quadratic equation by factorisation; solve a simple equation involving an algebraic exponent law manipulation.
width.typical: Solve quadratic equations using factorisation, completing the square, or the quadratic formula where appropriate; apply exponent laws to solve equations involving variable exponents; verify solutions by substitution.
wider: Investigate how different solution methods for quadratic equations (factorisation, completing the square, quadratic formula) are related and when each is most efficient
Explore equations that reduce to quadratic form through substitution (e.g. u = x²) and solve them using factorisation techniques

modes.reason: Students need a range of equation-solving approaches (factorisation, completing the square) and the judgement to select the most appropriate one for a given equation. Repertoire, not just one method, is the goal.

descriptors.title: Linear inequalities and simultaneous equations
descriptors.description: solve linear inequalities and simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables; interpret solutions graphically and communicate solutions in terms of the situation
descriptors.knowledge: Students can find gradient, midpoint and distance between points on the Cartesian plane (AC9M9A03). They have not yet solved linear inequalities or simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables, nor interpreted solution regions graphically or communicated solutions in everyday context language.
descriptors.endpoint: Students solve linear inequalities and simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables, interpret solutions graphically including solution regions, and communicate solutions in terms of the situation using appropriate context language.

nodes.label: Solving linear inequalities
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve a linear inequality in one variable algebraically and represent the solution on a number line.
criteria: Student correctly reverses the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number
Student represents the solution set correctly on a number line, including open/closed circle distinction

width.minimum: Solve a one-variable linear inequality by isolating the variable; correctly reverse the inequality sign when multiplying or dividing by a negative number; represent the solution on a number line.
width.typical: Solve linear inequalities in one variable involving multiple steps; handle all four inequality types; represent solutions on number lines; verify solutions by substitution.
wider: Investigate why multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality direction using a concrete number line argument — building reasoning rather than rule-following
Explore compound inequalities (a < x < b) and their graphical representations, connecting to interval notation

modes.reason: The reversal rule for negative multiplication is a genuine misconception point — students who only see examples with positive divisors develop a fragile understanding. Multiple inequality types and both positive/negative operations are needed to stabilise the concept.

nodes.label: Graphing linear inequalities in two variables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can graph the solution region for a linear inequality in two variables in the Cartesian plane and verify a point's membership using substitution.
criteria: Student correctly identifies and shades the solution region for a given linear inequality in two variables
Student verifies whether a specified point satisfies the inequality using substitution

width.minimum: Graph the boundary line for a linear inequality in two variables; shade the correct half-plane; verify using a test point (e.g. (0,0)).
width.typical: Graph solution regions for linear inequalities in two variables using both solid and dashed boundary lines; verify regions using test points; represent constraints from practical problems as inequalities and graph their regions.
wider: Investigate the feasible region formed by two or more simultaneous linear inequalities — identify its vertices and discuss what the region represents in a practical context
Explore how graphical regions correspond to integer solution sets for budget or resource constraints, connecting continuous and discrete representations

modes.reason: Students frequently shade the wrong half-plane, especially when rearranging inequalities changes the orientation. The test-point method needs to be taught as a reliable verification strategy, not an afterthought.

nodes.label: Solving simultaneous linear equations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve a pair of simultaneous linear equations in 2 variables using algebraic methods (substitution or elimination).
criteria: Student correctly solves a pair of simultaneous linear equations and verifies the solution in both equations
Student can apply both substitution and elimination, selecting an appropriate method for the given pair
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot solve simultaneous equations reliably cannot proceed to N4 — contextual formulation and interpretation both require a correct algebraic solution to reason about.

width.minimum: Solve a pair of simultaneous linear equations using either substitution or elimination; verify the solution by substituting into both equations.
width.typical: Solve simultaneous linear equations using substitution, elimination and graphical methods; choose the most efficient method for a given pair; verify solutions; recognise that parallel lines have no solution and coincident lines have infinitely many.
wider: Investigate the strategies inherent in First Nations Australian children's instructive games (e.g. Weme from the Warlpiri Peoples) and their connection to solving simultaneous equations
Explore systems where elimination requires scaling one or both equations and discuss why the solution is preserved under these operations

modes.reason: Sign errors in elimination (especially subtracting equations) are a persistent source of mistakes. Fluency with both substitution and elimination methods requires deliberate practice before contextualised application.

nodes.label: Interpreting and communicating solutions in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can formulate a practical problem as simultaneous equations or inequalities, solve it, and communicate the solution in plain language appropriate to the context.
criteria: Student correctly defines variables and formulates simultaneous equations or inequalities from a described context
Student states the solution in terms of the original context using appropriate everyday language
Student identifies whether the solution makes sense within the context's constraints (e.g. integer values, non-negative quantities)

width.minimum: Define variables for a context problem, write simultaneous equations, solve, and state the answer in everyday terms relevant to the situation.
width.typical: Formulate, solve and interpret simultaneous equations and linear inequalities across multiple practical contexts (pricing comparisons, budget constraints, break-even analysis); use appropriate context language ('break-even point', 'feasible combinations'); interpret graphical solutions within the situation; identify integer constraints where relevant.
wider: Investigate how simultaneous equations model real supply-and-demand or profit-and-loss scenarios; evaluate the assumptions the model makes and discuss when the model breaks down
Explore First Nations Australian children's instructive games as contexts for strategy and constraint analysis, investigating connections to mathematical solution structures

modes.reason: Translation between contextual language and algebraic formulation is a genuine hinge — students who can solve equations but struggle to set them up from context have an incomplete understanding. Multiple context types (pricing, budget, resource allocation) build the translation skill.

This node integrates all prior procedural work (solving inequalities, solving simultaneous equations, graphing regions) into the full problem-solving cycle. Formulation, solution and interpretation must operate together.

descriptors.title: Exponential functions
descriptors.description: recognise the connection between algebraic and graphical representations of exponential relations and solve related exponential equations, using digital tools where appropriate
descriptors.knowledge: Students can experiment with parameter variation on graphs and generalise emerging patterns using digital tools (AC9M9A06). They have not yet worked specifically with exponential relations — identifying them from tables, connecting their algebraic and graphical representations, or solving exponential equations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise exponential relations from tables, equations and graphs; connect algebraic and graphical representations of exponential functions; and solve related exponential equations.

nodes.label: Recognising exponential relations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify an exponential relation from a table of values by recognising a constant multiplicative ratio between consecutive dependent variable values.
criteria: Student correctly identifies an exponential relation from a table by calculating and confirming the constant multiplicative ratio
Student distinguishes an exponential table from a linear table by identifying the structural difference (ratio vs difference)
nodes.hinge_reason: If students cannot identify exponential relations from tables, they cannot ground the graphical features (N2) or representations work (N3) in pattern recognition — both subsequent nodes require students to have the ratio-as-indicator firmly established.

width.minimum: Given a table of values, determine whether the relationship is exponential by checking whether consecutive dependent variable values have a constant ratio; contrast with linear (constant difference) and quadratic (constant second difference).
width.typical: Identify exponential, linear and quadratic relations from tables of values; articulate the distinguishing feature of each (constant ratio, constant first difference, constant second difference); generate tables for given exponential rules and verify the constant ratio property.
wider: Investigate real data sets (e.g. population counts, compound interest balances, radioactive decay measurements) and classify the underlying relationship from table features
Explore what happens to the constant ratio when the base is between 0 and 1 (decay) vs greater than 1 (growth) and predict graph shape from the ratio

modes.reason: Students often confuse exponential with linear or quadratic growth, especially when the exponential starts slowly. Multiple table types (growth, decay, different bases) build the pattern recognition needed to distinguish reliably.

nodes.label: Graphical features of exponential functions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can sketch or interpret the graph of an exponential function, identifying key features including the y-intercept, asymptote, and whether it represents growth or decay.
criteria: Student correctly identifies the y-intercept and horizontal asymptote from an exponential graph or equation
Student states whether an exponential function represents growth or decay and connects this to the base value
nodes.hinge_reason: Asymptote misconceptions block N3 — students who cannot correctly interpret the horizontal asymptote cannot move fluently between algebraic and graphical representations, because the asymptote is the key feature distinguishing the graphical form.

width.minimum: Identify the y-intercept and horizontal asymptote of an exponential graph; state whether the function shows growth or decay; connect the base value to the graph's behaviour.
width.typical: Describe and sketch the graphs of exponential functions y = aˣ for a > 1 (growth) and 0 < a < 1 (decay); identify y-intercept, asymptote, domain and range; use digital graphing tools to investigate the effect of varying the base and coefficient.
wider: Investigate the effect of transformations (vertical stretch, vertical translation) on exponential graphs using digital tools; conjecture and test rules for how parameters affect the graph
Compare exponential growth curves for different bases (e.g. 2ˣ vs 3ˣ vs 10ˣ) and relate the visual rate of increase to the constant ratio in the corresponding tables

modes.reason: The horizontal asymptote concept is frequently misunderstood — students need explicit reasoning about why y → 0 but never reaches 0, and how this connects to the algebraic form. Scaffolding this reasoning prevents persistent errors in interpretation.

nodes.label: Connecting algebraic and graphical representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can move fluently between the algebraic equation and graphical representation of an exponential relation, reading key information from each form.
criteria: Student correctly identifies key graphical features (y-intercept, asymptote, growth/decay) from a given exponential equation
Student writes or identifies the exponential equation corresponding to a given graph

width.minimum: Given an exponential equation, identify the key graphical features; given an exponential graph, write or identify the corresponding equation.
width.typical: Translate between algebraic and graphical representations of exponential functions in multiple directions; use digital tools to verify connections; extract information from graphs to form equations; use equations to predict graphical features before plotting.
wider: Investigate how digital tools with symbolic manipulation reveal that the same exponential relationship can be expressed in multiple equivalent algebraic forms
Explore the connection between the constant ratio in a table, the base in the equation, and the steepness of the graph — building a unified understanding across all three representations

modes.reason: Moving fluently between table, equation and graph is the integration goal — students who can work with each representation individually but cannot translate between them have compartmentalised rather than connected knowledge. This node is where the three representations become one coherent object.

nodes.label: Solving exponential equations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can solve simple exponential equations by writing both sides in terms of a common base and equating exponents.
criteria: Student correctly rewrites both sides of an exponential equation using a common base
Student solves for the exponent and verifies the solution by substitution

width.minimum: Solve a simple exponential equation where both sides can be expressed as powers of the same base (e.g. 2ˣ = 8).
width.typical: Solve exponential equations by expressing both sides with a common base; apply exponent laws where necessary before equating; use graphical methods (intersection) as a check; investigate equations requiring digital tools where exact algebraic solution is not accessible.
wider: Investigate how First Nations Australian Ranger programs' population modelling using exponential equations requires solving for time — connecting equation-solving to meaningful applied problems on Country/Place
Explore how digital tools can solve exponential equations graphically (intersection method) and discuss the relationship between the graphical and algebraic approaches

modes.reason: Students who only see equations with obvious common bases (powers of 2) struggle when different bases appear. Varied base combinations build the flexible base-matching thinking needed.

descriptors.title: Model growth and decay
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve applied problems involving growth and decay, including financial contexts; formulate problems, choosing to apply linear, quadratic or exponential models; interpret solutions in terms of the situation; evaluate and modify models as necessary and report assumptions, methods and findings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can connect algebraic and graphical representations of exponential relations and solve exponential equations (AC9M10A03). They have not yet chosen between linear, quadratic and exponential models for a given applied context, nor evaluated and modified models, nor reported assumptions and findings in a full modelling cycle.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use mathematical modelling to solve applied growth and decay problems by selecting, applying, evaluating and reporting linear, quadratic or exponential models; interpret solutions in terms of the situation; and report assumptions, methods and findings.

nodes.label: Selecting the appropriate model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can determine whether a given growth or decay situation is best modelled as linear, quadratic or exponential by analysing the pattern of change.
criteria: Student correctly classifies a relationship from a table using the appropriate pattern (difference or ratio)
Student justifies the classification by showing the relevant constant pattern in the data
nodes.hinge_reason: Incorrect model selection at N1 means the wrong equation is formulated in N2 — the entire modelling output is invalid if the model type is misidentified.

width.minimum: Classify a relationship as linear, quadratic or exponential using a table of values (constant first difference, constant second difference, constant ratio); justify the classification.
width.typical: Use first differences, second differences and ratios to classify relationships; connect the classification to the appropriate equation form; recognise when contextual descriptions (constant rate, constant percentage change) indicate a model type without needing a table.
wider: Compare multiple representations of the same situation (table, graph, verbal description) and classify the model from each, checking for consistency
Investigate edge cases where the model type is not immediately clear (e.g. growth that starts linear but becomes exponential) and discuss the limitations of simple classification

modes.reason: Students who practise model selection on obvious cases (doubling = exponential, flat rate = linear) fail when the context is ambiguous or described verbally rather than in a table. Multiple context types — financial, biological, physical — build reliable classification.

nodes.label: Formulating and applying the model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can write an equation for a growth or decay model from a described context and use it to answer questions about the situation.
criteria: Student writes a correct exponential model equation identifying initial value and growth/decay factor from a described context
Student uses the equation to calculate a specified value and states it in context-appropriate units

width.minimum: Write an exponential growth or decay equation from a described context (stating initial value and growth/decay factor); use the equation to calculate a value at a specified time.
width.typical: Formulate linear, quadratic and exponential models from contextual descriptions; calculate key values (e.g. population at a given time, balance after n periods); determine doubling time or half-life for exponential models; model compound interest using authentic rates.
wider: Investigate and formulate exponential equations for population growth of native animals on Country/Place with varying reproductive behaviour, discussing what the model's parameters represent ecologically
Model compound interest scenarios using authentic Australian interest rate data; compare compound and simple interest growth over time

modes.reason: Setting up exponential models from verbal descriptions requires explicit scaffolding — students need a clear process for identifying initial value, growth factor (from percentage change), and time variable before they can write the equation reliably.

nodes.label: Interpreting and evaluating the model
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret modelled results in terms of the original situation and evaluate whether the model is appropriate, identifying key assumptions and limitations.
criteria: Student interprets a modelled result in clear context-appropriate language
Student identifies at least one assumption the model makes and explains what would happen if that assumption were violated
Student identifies at least one context in which the model would give unreliable predictions

width.minimum: Interpret a modelled result in plain language relevant to the context; state at least one assumption the model makes; identify one limitation of the model.
width.typical: Interpret results (doubling time, break-even point, half-life, projected value) in context-specific language; evaluate whether the model fits the situation by checking against known data points; identify assumptions (e.g. constant growth rate, no external shocks); discuss limitations of extrapolation.
wider: Investigate how exponential equations are used in carbon dating to estimate the age of First Nations Australians' artefacts — examining the assumptions underlying the method and discussing the social significance of measurement accuracy
Compare model predictions to actual data for a well-documented growth/decay situation and evaluate where the model diverges and why

modes.reason: Model evaluation — identifying assumptions and limitations — is a genuine hinge skill. Students who only evaluate models in one context (e.g. financial) struggle to apply the same critical lens to biological or physical contexts. Multiple context types build transferable evaluation thinking.

Interpretation and evaluation require coordinating the mathematical result with the real-world context, the model's structure, and an understanding of what assumptions were made. This node integrates the modelling cycle into a complete act of mathematical reasoning.

descriptors.title: Experiment with functions and relations
descriptors.description: experiment with functions and relations using digital tools, making and testing conjectures and generalising emerging patterns
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use mathematical modelling with linear, quadratic or exponential models to solve growth and decay problems (AC9M10A04). They have not yet experimented systematically across the range of function and relation types at this year band — including circles, intersections of different function types, and bisection methods — using conjecture and generalisation as the primary inquiry mode.
descriptors.endpoint: Students experiment with functions and relations using digital tools, making and testing conjectures, and generalising emerging patterns across linear, quadratic, exponential and circular representations.

nodes.label: Making and testing conjectures with digital tools
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use a digital graphing tool to explore a function family, formulate a conjecture about an observed pattern, and test it by varying parameters.
criteria: Student states a conjecture as a testable claim (not an observation) about a function family
Student provides evidence from at least two test cases that either supports or contradicts the conjecture
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not structure exploration as conjecture-test cycles cannot do the work of N2–N4 — locating intersections, working with circles, and generalising all require disciplined hypothesis-driven use of digital tools rather than undirected play.

width.minimum: Use a digital tool to observe a pattern in a function family (e.g. varying the coefficient of x²); state a conjecture; test it with at least two additional parameter values.
width.typical: Formulate and systematically test conjectures across multiple function families (linear, quadratic, exponential); vary parameters deliberately rather than randomly; record what changes and what stays constant; refine or reject conjectures based on evidence.
wider: Investigate how digital tools with zoom functionality allow systematic refinement of approximate intersection locations — connecting the visual zoom process to interval bisection as a numerical method
Explore how machine learning uses functions and parameter variation to fit models to data — connecting mathematical experimentation to an emerging applied context

modes.reason: Students often explore digital tools without structuring their exploration as conjecture-test cycles. Explicit scaffolding of the conjecture-test-refine loop is needed before students can use digital tools as genuine mathematical inquiry instruments.

nodes.label: Intersections of functions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use digital tools to locate intersection points of two functions and identify coordinate values, including using zoom or bisection to refine approximations.
criteria: Student locates the intersection of two given functions graphically and states the coordinates
Student can refine an approximate intersection point using a zoom or bisection approach

width.minimum: Locate the approximate intersection of two graphed functions using a digital tool; read off the coordinates.
width.typical: Locate intersections of linear, quadratic and exponential function pairs; apply zoom or bisection methods to refine approximations to specified accuracy; identify intersections of a linear function with a quadratic or a circle; connect intersection points to the algebraic meaning (simultaneous solution).
wider: Apply a bisection algorithm to systematically narrow an interval containing a root of a quadratic, connecting the numerical method to graphical behaviour and developing a general procedure
Investigate how intersections of functions are used to solve equations that cannot be solved by standard algebraic methods — appreciating digital tools as extending algebraic capability

modes.reason: Students who only find intersections of linear function pairs may not recognise the same process applies to quadratic-linear, exponential-linear, or circle-linear intersections. Multiple function pairings are needed to generalise the concept.

nodes.label: Circles and transformations as relations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can work with the unit circle x² + y² = 1 as a relation, apply transformations, and identify key features of the transformed relation.
criteria: Student correctly graphs the unit circle using a digital tool and explains why it is not a function
Student identifies the effect of a given transformation on the circle's centre and radius

width.minimum: Recognise x² + y² = 1 as a circle centred at the origin with radius 1; graph it using a digital tool; identify that it is a relation, not a function.
width.typical: Apply transformations (translation, scaling) to x² + y² = 1; identify the centre and radius of the resulting circle; find intersection points of a circle with a linear function graphically; investigate intervals where a quadratic function is positive or negative.
wider: Explore transformations of the unit circle algebraically, connecting the transformed equation to the geometric centre and radius, and generalising the standard form (x−h)² + (y−k)² = r²
Investigate the difference between functions and relations more broadly — why a circle is a relation but not a function, and how this distinction matters for analysis

modes.reason: The function/relation distinction is a genuine conceptual hinge — students who have only worked with functions may not recognise that y = f(x) is not the only valid form of a mathematical relationship. The circle provides the canonical context for making this distinction clear.

nodes.label: Generalising emerging patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can generalise a pattern observed across multiple function experiments into a stated rule or conjecture that applies across a family of cases.
criteria: Student states a generalisation in clear terms that applies to all tested cases
Student tests the generalisation against at least one case not used to form it and reports whether it holds

width.minimum: State a generalisation (in words or algebraic form) that summarises a pattern observed across at least three cases in a function experiment.
width.typical: Generalise patterns across function families (e.g. the effect of coefficient changes, the relationship between roots and factors); express generalisations algebraically where possible; test generalisations against novel cases; distinguish generalisations that hold from those that break down at boundary cases.
wider: Investigate how the same function family (e.g. exponential) appears across multiple domains (finance, biology, physics) and generalise which structural features drive the shared behaviour
Explore how pattern generalisation in mathematics connects to how machine learning models extract patterns from data — a conceptual parallel rather than a formal equivalence

modes.reason: Generalisation is the culminating act of this descriptor — it requires coordinating observations across experiments, identifying invariant features, and expressing findings in general form. This node is where the exploratory work of prior nodes becomes mathematical knowledge.

descriptors.title: Surface area and volume of composite objects
descriptors.description: solve problems involving the surface area and volume of composite objects using appropriate units
descriptors.knowledge: Students can solve surface area and volume problems for right prisms and cylinders (AC9M9M01). They have not yet worked with composite objects — solids formed by combining or subtracting multiple familiar 3D shapes.
descriptors.endpoint: Students solve problems involving the surface area and volume of composite objects by decomposing them into familiar component solids and applying appropriate units.

nodes.label: Decomposing composite objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the component solids in a composite object and describe how they combine (addition or subtraction of volumes/surfaces).
criteria: Student correctly identifies the component solids of a given composite object
Student identifies which faces become internal when components join and explains why they are excluded from surface area calculations
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot identify which faces become internal when solids join will systematically double-count or include hidden faces in N2 surface area calculations — the decomposition reasoning is the prerequisite for accurate calculation.

width.minimum: Given a composite solid, identify its component prisms or cylinders; state whether surfaces are added, removed, or partially removed when the components join.
width.typical: Decompose composite objects into components in multiple ways; identify which faces become internal (no longer exterior) when components join; choose the most efficient decomposition for a given problem.
wider: Explore how the same composite object can be decomposed in more than one way and verify that both decompositions give the same result
Investigate real composite structures (e.g. buildings with attached extensions, storage tanks with domed ends) and practise identifying their components from photographs or plans

modes.reason: The internal face problem — faces that disappear when two solids join — is the main source of surface area errors. Students need the reasoning made explicit: when solids share a face, that face is removed from both surfaces, not just one.

nodes.label: Surface area of composite objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the surface area of a composite object by summing exposed faces of component solids.
criteria: Student correctly calculates the surface area of a composite object with no missing or double-counted faces
Student states the answer in appropriate units
nodes.hinge_reason: Surface area calculation errors cascade into N4 — modelling problems requiring surface area (e.g. material cost estimation) produce meaningless results if the calculation step is unreliable.

width.minimum: Calculate the surface area of a composite solid formed from two right prisms or cylinders, correctly excluding internal faces.
width.typical: Calculate surface areas of composite objects formed from multiple components including prisms, cylinders and combinations; estimate surface areas for practical purposes; apply appropriate units and check reasonableness of answers.
wider: Estimate the surface area of composite objects in practical contexts where exact dimensions are unavailable, discussing the accuracy needed for the application
Investigate how surface area to volume ratio changes as objects become more complex, with applications to packaging design or heat transfer

modes.reason: Surface area calculation errors are systematic — missing faces, double-counting, unit errors. Fluency requires deliberate practice across multiple composite configurations before modelling applications.

nodes.label: Volume of composite objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the volume of a composite object by summing or subtracting volumes of component solids.
criteria: Student correctly calculates the volume of a composite object using an appropriate decomposition
Student states the answer in appropriate units and checks reasonableness

width.minimum: Calculate the volume of a composite solid formed from two right prisms or cylinders by addition or subtraction of component volumes.
width.typical: Calculate volumes of composite objects using additive and subtractive decomposition; select the most efficient decomposition; apply appropriate units; estimate volumes for practical contexts.
wider: Investigate how material costs or capacity calculations for real composite structures (e.g. swimming pools, storage tanks, industrial containers) depend on accurate volume calculation
Explore how 3D printing or CNC fabrication requires precise volume calculations for material estimation, connecting measurement to design technology contexts

modes.reason: Volume calculation errors (especially additive vs subtractive decomposition confusion) are systematic. Fluency with volume calculation across multiple composite configurations is needed before modelling applications in N4.

nodes.label: Modelling with composite objects
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use surface area and volume calculations for composite objects to solve a practical problem, stating assumptions and interpreting results in context.
criteria: Student identifies the composite object structure relevant to the practical problem and performs the correct calculation
Student states the result in context-appropriate terms and identifies at least one assumption made
Student checks whether the result is reasonable given the context

width.minimum: Apply surface area or volume calculation to solve a practical problem involving a composite object; state the answer in context-relevant terms.
width.typical: Model practical problems involving composite objects (e.g. rainwater collection from a composite roof, optimal storage container design, supply estimation for an event); identify and state assumptions; interpret and evaluate results; choose between competing designs using calculated values.
wider: Design and evaluate optimal composite container configurations for a given volume constraint (e.g. maximum rainwater storage fitting a given space), modelling multiple configurations and comparing
Investigate how surface area to volume ratio of composite biological structures (e.g. lung alveoli, tree branching) is optimised for function — connecting measurement to real-world design principles

modes.reason: Translating practical problems into composite object decompositions varies substantially across context types. Students who only model one context type (e.g. construction) may not apply the same decomposition thinking to biological or design contexts. Multiple context types build flexible application.

This node integrates decomposition, surface area and volume calculation with the full modelling cycle — formulation, calculation, interpretation and evaluation. It is the integration point for all prior nodes in this descriptor.

descriptors.title: Logarithmic scales
descriptors.description: interpret and use logarithmic scales in applied contexts involving small and large quantities and change
descriptors.knowledge: Students can use mathematical modelling to solve proportion, rate, ratio and scale problems (AC9M9M05). They have not yet encountered logarithmic scales or the concept of order-of-magnitude calibration.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret and use logarithmic scales across applied contexts, explaining why a logarithmic scale is appropriate for certain data and reading values correctly from logarithmic representations.

nodes.label: Order of magnitude and the logarithmic idea
nodes.checkpoint: Students can explain that a logarithmic scale is calibrated in orders of magnitude and describe how equal intervals on a log scale represent multiplicative (not additive) steps.
criteria: Student correctly explains what equal intervals represent on a logarithmic scale (multiplicative, not additive steps)
Student reads a value from a base-10 log scale and expresses it as a power of 10
nodes.hinge_reason: The multiplicative (not additive) calibration of log scales is the foundational concept for all subsequent interpretation work — students who do not grasp this cannot meaningfully read log scale values (N2) or compare quantities across orders of magnitude (N3).

width.minimum: Explain that each step on a logarithmic scale represents a ×10 (or ×2, depending on base) change rather than a fixed additive amount; contrast this with a linear scale.
width.typical: Explain the order-of-magnitude calibration of logarithmic scales; read values from a base-10 log scale; convert between linear and log representations of the same value; explain why 10² and 10³ are one 'step' apart on a log scale despite being 900 apart on a linear scale.
wider: Investigate how the choice of base (base 2, base 10, natural log) changes the scale and appears in different scientific contexts
Explore how scientific notation and logarithmic scales express the same underlying idea — that very large or very small numbers are more usefully described by their order of magnitude

modes.reason: The multiplicative nature of log scales is conceptually unfamiliar — students arrive expecting all scales to be linear. The reasoning chain (each step multiplies rather than adds; equal visual distance = equal ratio) needs explicit scaffolding.

nodes.label: Interpreting logarithmic scales in context
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read and interpret data presented on a logarithmic scale in at least two real-world contexts, explaining what the scale reveals about the data.
criteria: Student correctly reads a value from a logarithmic scale graph and expresses it in appropriate units
Student explains why a logarithmic scale is more appropriate than a linear scale for a given data set

width.minimum: Read and interpret a graph using a logarithmic scale (e.g. Richter scale, decibel scale); explain what a one-unit increase on the scale means in terms of the quantity measured.
width.typical: Interpret logarithmic scales across multiple contexts (Richter, decibel, pH, exponential growth graphs); explain when a log scale is more appropriate than a linear scale (wide range of values, exponential growth, percentage change); compare the same data displayed on linear and log axes.
wider: Investigate dating methods at geological sites significant to First Peoples of Australia, including the Madjedbebe dig — examining how logarithmic scales and scientific notation are used in radiometric dating and discussing the measurement accuracy and social significance of the findings
Investigate how logarithmic scaling is used in machine learning algorithms to compress large value ranges — connecting the mathematical concept to a contemporary data science application

modes.reason: Log scale interpretation is a genuine hinge — students who can read a Richter scale often cannot interpret a pH scale or a log-transformed growth graph because they treat each as a separate skill rather than the same mathematical structure. Multiple contexts stabilise the underlying concept.

nodes.label: Using logarithmic scales for change and comparison
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use logarithmic scales to compare quantities that span multiple orders of magnitude and interpret what differences between scale values mean.
criteria: Student correctly interprets the multiplicative meaning of a difference between two values on a logarithmic scale
Student compares two quantities on a log scale and expresses the comparison as a ratio

width.minimum: Use a logarithmic scale to compare two quantities that differ by at least two orders of magnitude; interpret the comparison in context.
width.typical: Use logarithmic scales to compare quantities across multiple orders of magnitude; interpret differences between scale values in terms of multiplicative ratios; discuss why a 1-unit difference on a Richter or decibel scale represents a ×10 (or ×10 in energy) difference in the quantity; make and interpret predictions using log scale data.
wider: Investigate and compare the logarithmic representation of the same quantity (e.g. sound intensity) on different scale types, explaining how the choice of display affects perception of differences

Explore how logarithmic comparison is used in finance (comparing investment growth over time) and biology (comparing population sizes across species) — applying the same mathematical tool in different domains

modes.reason: Using log scales for comparison integrates reading (node 2) with the order-of-magnitude concept (node 1) into the practical skill of making meaningful comparisons. It is where students move from interpreting individual values to reasoning about differences between them.

descriptors.title: Pythagoras and trigonometry in practical contexts
descriptors.description: solve practical problems applying Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry of right-angled triangles, including problems involving direction and angles of elevation and depression
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise sine, cosine and tangent as constant ratios for a given angle using similarity (AC9M9SP01). They have not yet applied Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry to multi-step practical problems involving bearings, elevation and depression, or decomposition of 3D problems into 2D.
descriptors.endpoint: Students solve practical multi-step problems applying Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry of right-angled triangles, including problems involving direction, bearings, and angles of elevation and depression.

nodes.label: Angles of elevation and depression
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify angles of elevation and depression in a diagram or described situation and set up the correct right-angled triangle for calculation.
criteria: Student correctly identifies and labels the angle of elevation or depression and the relevant sides in a diagram
Student selects and applies the correct trigonometric ratio to solve for an unknown side or angle
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot correctly set up diagrams for elevation/depression problems cannot decompose 3D problems in N3 — the 2D triangle extraction step in N3 requires confident diagram-drawing from N1.

width.minimum: Identify the angle of elevation or depression in a diagram; label the relevant sides (opposite, adjacent, hypotenuse) relative to the angle; select and apply the correct trigonometric ratio.
width.typical: Solve problems involving angles of elevation and depression across multiple contexts (building heights, cliff distances, aircraft angles); draw and label diagrams from verbal descriptions; apply both sin, cos and tan as appropriate; use a clinometer context to connect measurement to calculation.
wider: Investigate how clinometers are used in practical surveying and apply the technique to measure a building or tree height, comparing the measured angle to the calculated result
Explore how elevation and depression problems arise in navigation contexts and connect to angle of inclination in road design or ramp accessibility standards

modes.reason: Students frequently confuse elevation and depression angles, especially when the observer is at height rather than ground level. Multiple problem setups — observer below, observer above, horizontal reference varying — stabilise the concept.

nodes.label: Bearings and direction problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret compass bearings and use trigonometry to solve navigation problems involving direction and distance.
criteria: Student correctly translates a described bearing problem into a labelled right-angled triangle diagram
Student solves for the required distance or angle using appropriate trigonometric ratios

width.minimum: Interpret a three-figure compass bearing; draw a right-angled triangle from a described bearing problem; solve for a distance or angle.
width.typical: Solve navigation problems using bearings including multi-leg journeys; decompose bearings problems into right-angled triangle components; calculate final bearing and distance from a multi-step trip; apply both Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometric ratios as needed.
wider: Explore navigation techniques used by First Nations Australians — including wayfinding using stars, landforms and ecological markers — and investigate connections between these spatial reasoning systems and trigonometric principles
Investigate how bearings problems arise in orienteering course design and plan a multi-leg course specifying bearing and distance for each leg

modes.reason: Converting bearing descriptions to labelled right-angled triangles requires a systematic process that students find non-obvious. The translation from compass direction to triangle orientation needs explicit scaffolding.

nodes.label: Decomposing 3D problems into 2D
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a right-angled triangle embedded in a 3D situation, extract the relevant 2D problem, and solve it using Pythagoras' theorem or trigonometry.
criteria: Student identifies the relevant right-angled triangle within a 3D situation and draws a clear 2D diagram
Student solves the 2D problem correctly and states the answer in context-appropriate terms

width.minimum: Identify a right-angled triangle within a described 3D situation (e.g. a diagonal of a rectangular box, the angle of a ramp); solve for the required measurement.
width.typical: Decompose at least two different types of 3D problems into 2D right-angled triangle sub-problems; apply Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry within each 2D sub-problem; combine results to answer the 3D question; use dynamic geometric software to visualise the decomposition where helpful.
wider: Investigate how autonomous vehicles use Pythagoras' theorem and trigonometry to calculate distance and navigate 3D spaces, including implications of sensor measurement accuracy
Apply trigonometric decomposition to a design problem (e.g. finding the angle a roof truss makes with a horizontal beam given the pitch and span) connecting measurement to construction contexts

modes.reason: The key difficulty in 3D problems is identifying which 2D triangle to extract — this is not obvious and varies with the problem type. Multiple 3D problem types (box diagonal, ramp angle, building height from distance) build the spatial parsing skill.

3D decomposition integrates elevation/depression (node 1), triangle identification and Pythagoras into coordinated 3D spatial reasoning. It is the capstone problem type where all elements operate together.

descriptors.title: Impact of measurement errors
descriptors.description: identify the impact of measurement errors on the accuracy of results in practical contexts
descriptors.knowledge: Students can interpret and use logarithmic scales in applied contexts (AC9M10M02). They have not yet systematically identified sources of measurement error or analysed how errors compound and propagate through calculations to affect accuracy.
descriptors.endpoint: Students identify sources of measurement error and describe their impact on the accuracy of results across practical contexts, including how compounding errors affect repeated or multi-step calculations.

nodes.label: Sources and types of measurement error
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify sources of measurement error in a practical context and distinguish between errors arising from the instrument, the method, and the measurer.
criteria: Student identifies at least two sources of measurement error in a described context
Student distinguishes between instrument error, method error, and human error in a given example

width.minimum: Identify at least two distinct sources of measurement error in a described context; categorise each as instrument-related, method-related, or human error.
width.typical: Identify and categorise sources of measurement error across multiple practical contexts; distinguish systematic errors (consistent bias) from random errors (variable); explain how each type of error affects measured values differently.
wider: Investigate scientific measuring techniques applied to First Peoples of Australia — including radiometric dating and genetic sequencing — and identify the sources of measurement error specific to each technique
Explore how measurement errors in autonomous vehicle sensors (e.g. LIDAR, GPS) arise from the physics of measurement and discuss their safety implications

modes.reason: Students who only identify errors in familiar classroom measurement contexts (ruler parallax, balance inaccuracy) may not recognise the same analytical framework applies to sophisticated scientific or technological measurement. Multiple context types build transferable error analysis.

nodes.label: Impact of individual measurement errors
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe how a measurement error propagates into a calculated result and estimate the size of the impact.
criteria: Student correctly calculates the range of values for a derived quantity given a measurement error margin
Student explains why the impact of a measurement error is larger for some calculations than others
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how individual errors propagate into calculated results is the prerequisite for N3 — students who cannot trace a single error's effect cannot reason about how errors accumulate across iterations.

width.minimum: Given a measurement with a stated error margin, calculate how that error affects a derived result (e.g. if length is off by 1 cm, how does area change).
width.typical: Calculate the effect of measurement error on derived quantities (area, volume, interest, rate); describe how the impact grows as the formula becomes more complex; use bounds (max/min values from error margins) to state ranges for calculated results.
wider: Investigate how truncation versus rounding errors affect the accuracy of financial calculations at scale — e.g. the impact of truncating cent values across millions of customer records
Explore how measurement accuracy in dating methods (e.g. radiocarbon dating) determines the precision of age estimates for historical artefacts and discuss what this means for archaeological claims

modes.reason: The propagation of error through a formula requires systematic reasoning — students need a process (calculate with maximum, minimum, and best-estimate values; compare results) rather than intuitive guessing. Explicit scaffolding prevents underestimation of impact.

nodes.label: Compounding errors in repeated calculations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify how measurement errors compound across repeated or multi-step calculations and describe the effect on accuracy.
criteria: Student explains, with a worked example, how a small error in a single measurement produces a larger error after repeated calculations
Student identifies at least one practical context where accumulated measurement error has meaningful consequences

width.minimum: Given a calculation repeated multiple times (or a multi-step formula), describe how errors accumulate — that repeated rounding or truncation can produce a substantially different final result.
width.typical: Analyse how compounding errors affect accuracy in at least two contexts (repeated interest calculations, multi-step geometric calculations, sequential measurements); estimate the accumulated error after n repetitions; discuss when accumulated error becomes practically significant.
wider: Investigate the social impact of measurement errors in First Peoples of Australia contexts — including how errors in population counts or dating results have influenced policy or historical narratives
Explore how measurement errors in perception and control systems of autonomous vehicles compound across multiple sensor readings and what safeguards are built in to manage accumulated error

modes.reason: Compounding errors appear very differently across contexts — financial truncation produces systematic underpayment, geometric errors grow multiplicatively, sequential sensor errors accumulate directionally. Multiple contexts are needed to generalise the concept.

Understanding compounding errors requires integrating knowledge of individual error impact (node 2) with iterative reasoning about how small errors grow across repetitions. This is the node where error analysis becomes applicable to real multi-step situations.

descriptors.title: Model proportion and scaling
descriptors.description: use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving proportion and scaling of objects; formulate problems and interpret solutions in terms of the situation; evaluate and modify models as necessary, and report assumptions, methods and findings
descriptors.knowledge: Students can identify how measurement errors affect accuracy of results in practical contexts (AC9M10M04). They have not yet used mathematical modelling as a full cycle (formulate, solve, interpret, evaluate, modify) specifically for proportion and scaling problems.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use mathematical modelling to solve practical problems involving proportion and scaling, interpreting and evaluating results in context and reporting assumptions, methods and findings.

nodes.label: Scale factors and conversion
nodes.checkpoint: Students can determine the scale factor between a model and the actual object, and use it to convert measurements in both directions.
criteria: Student correctly calculates a scale factor from given measurements and applies it to find an unknown dimension
Student explains why area and volume scale differently from linear dimensions
nodes.hinge_reason: Scale factor errors cascade through N2 and N3 — students who cannot correctly derive and apply scale factors will misread plans (N2) and formulate incorrect proportion models (N3), invalidating all downstream work.

width.minimum: Calculate the scale factor given one model measurement and one actual measurement; use the scale factor to find an unknown actual or model dimension.
width.typical: Determine scale factors from plans, drawings or physical models; convert dimensions in both directions (model → actual, actual → model); apply scale factors to areas (scale factor squared) and volumes (scale factor cubed); check scale consistency across a drawing.
wider: Estimate the scale of an unfamiliar object (e.g. a toy car, a model building) by measuring a recognisable linear dimension and comparing to a known typical value
Investigate how scale factors apply differently to lengths, areas and volumes — and why a model that is 1:10 in length has a volume ratio of 1:1000

modes.reason: The scaling of areas and volumes (squared and cubed scale factors) is a non-obvious extension of linear scale that students frequently miss. Explicit reasoning about why area scales by k² and volume by k³ prevents rote misapplication.

nodes.label: Reading and using scaled plans
nodes.checkpoint: Students can read dimensions from a scaled plan or elevation drawing and use them to make practical decisions or calculations.
criteria: Student reads a dimension from a scaled plan and correctly converts it to an actual measurement
Student uses plan dimensions to evaluate a practical decision (e.g. 'will this furniture fit?')

width.minimum: Read dimensions from a scaled plan using the stated scale; convert plan measurements to actual measurements.
width.typical: Use plans and elevation drawings to make design decisions (e.g. furniture placement, room modifications); convert between plan and actual dimensions; identify when a proposed change is feasible given the scale; apply appropriate scales for different purposes (1:100 for buildings, 1:50 for rooms).
wider: Investigate compliance with Australian building codes and standards using a scaled plan — e.g. checking whether corridor widths, door clearances, or escalator gradients meet specified standards
Design a modified building plan (e.g. adding a room extension) using an appropriate scale, ensuring all new dimensions are proportionally correct

modes.reason: Reading scaled plans varies across plan types (floor plans, elevation drawings, site plans) and scale conventions. Students who only practise with one plan type may not apply the scale reading process to unfamiliar formats.

nodes.label: Modelling proportion and scaling problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can formulate a practical scaling or proportion problem as a mathematical model, solve it, and interpret the result in context.
criteria: Student correctly formulates a proportion or scaling relationship from a described context and solves for the required quantity
Student states at least one assumption of the model and evaluates whether the result makes sense in context

width.minimum: Formulate a scaling or proportion problem from a practical context; solve using a scale factor or proportion equation; state the result in context-appropriate terms.
width.typical: Apply mathematical modelling to solve proportion and scaling problems across multiple contexts (prototypes, 3D printing, architectural plans); state assumptions; interpret and evaluate results; modify the model when initial assumptions prove inadequate; report methods and findings clearly.
wider: Investigate how AI image generators use proportion and scaling techniques (aspect ratio preservation, object-to-scene ratio) to produce realistic images — critically evaluating outputs for proportion errors

Model a 3D printing or rapid-prototyping scenario: determine scale factor for a given material constraint, calculate dimensions of the scaled model, and evaluate whether the model will fit its intended purpose

modes.reason: Proportion and scaling modelling problems vary considerably in how they're set up across contexts (plans use ratio scales, 3D printing uses dimensional constraints, AI imaging uses aspect ratios). Multiple context types build flexible formulation skills.

The full modelling cycle (formulate, solve, interpret, evaluate, modify, report) integrates scale factors (node 1), plan reading (node 2), and contextual reasoning into complete mathematical modelling practice. This is the integration node for the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Approximations of real numbers
descriptors.description: recognise the effect of using approximations of real numbers in repeated calculations and compare the results when using exact representations
descriptors.knowledge: Students can recognise the real number system including rational and irrational numbers and solve problems (AC9M9N01). They have not yet investigated how approximation errors accumulate and compound across repeated calculations, or compared results from exact versus approximate representations.
descriptors.endpoint: Students recognise the effect of using approximations of real numbers in repeated calculations and compare results with those obtained using exact representations.

nodes.label: Exact vs approximate representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between an exact representation of a real number and an approximation, and identify when approximation introduces error.
criteria: Student correctly identifies which representation of a real number is exact and which is approximate
Student explains what information is lost or changed when an exact irrational number is replaced by a decimal approximation

width.minimum: Give an example of an irrational number that has an exact form (e.g. √2, π) and an approximate decimal form; explain what is lost in the approximation.
width.typical: Distinguish exact from approximate representations for irrational numbers, repeating decimals and fractions; identify where approximation is unavoidable (e.g. decimal display) and where exact form is available; calculate with both forms for a simple expression and compare results.
wider: Investigate how computer systems store real numbers as floating-point approximations and what the consequences are for repeated arithmetic operations
Explore historical examples where exact representation mattered (e.g. Archimedes' bounds on π) and discuss how mathematical culture has handled the tension between exactness and practicality

modes.reason: Students need to encounter exact vs approximate representations across number types (surds, π, repeating decimals) to generalise the concept beyond any single example. One example risks exemplar convergence — students may believe the issue is specific to π rather than a general property of approximation.

nodes.label: Truncation vs rounding
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the difference between truncation and rounding and identify which produces a systematic bias.
criteria: Student correctly applies both truncation and rounding to the same decimal value and obtains different results
Student explains that truncation introduces a systematic bias while rounding does not
nodes.hinge_reason: The truncation/rounding distinction is the prerequisite for N3 — students who do not distinguish between them cannot describe how accumulated error differs between truncation (systematic bias) and rounding (approximate unbiasedness).

width.minimum: Distinguish truncation from rounding for a given decimal value; state that truncation always rounds toward zero and identify this as a systematic bias.
width.typical: Apply truncation and rounding to various decimal values; explain why truncation produces a systematic underestimate (for positive values) while rounding is approximately unbiased; identify contexts where each method is conventionally used.
wider: Investigate the financial impact of systematic truncation: if every transaction is truncated to the nearest cent, what is the accumulated effect across millions of transactions?
Compare how different programming languages and financial systems implement rounding and truncation, and discuss the real-world consequences of different conventions

modes.reason: Students often treat truncation and rounding as equivalent. The distinction — and particularly why truncation introduces bias — requires explicit reasoning about the direction and magnitude of the difference.

nodes.label: Effect of approximation in repeated calculations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can demonstrate, using a worked example, that repeated use of an approximate value produces a different final result than using the exact representation, and describe the nature of the accumulation.
criteria: Student produces a worked example showing the numerical difference between approximate and exact calculations across repeated steps
Student explains why the difference grows with repetition rather than staying constant

width.minimum: Calculate a result using an approximate value repeated across at least two steps and compare it to the result using the exact value; describe the difference.
width.typical: Investigate the effect of approximation in at least two repeated-calculation contexts (e.g. repeated simple interest steps, perimeter of a compound shape involving π, volume of a sphere used in a multi-step problem); quantify the accumulated error; discuss whether the accumulated error matters for the application.
wider: Investigate approximation error accumulation in contexts involving compound shapes with circles — e.g. using π ≈ 3.14 vs exact π across multiple component areas and comparing the cumulative difference

Limited width note: this descriptor has genuinely thin context breadth at Y10 — the core concept (approximation error accumulates in repeated calculation) does not vary dramatically across phenomena. Width directions above extend the contexts modestly; depth of reasoning about when error matters is where the real enrichment lies.

modes.reason: Students who only see approximation error in one context (e.g. rounding π) may not recognise the same accumulation pattern in financial or measurement contexts. Two or three context types stabilise the general principle.

descriptors.title: Conditional probability
descriptors.description: use the language of "if ... then", "given", "of", "knowing that" to describe and interpret situations involving conditional probability
descriptors.knowledge: Students can design simulations comparing simple and compound event probabilities (AC9M9P03). They have not yet used the specific language of conditional probability ('given', 'if...then', 'knowing that') to describe or interpret situations, nor distinguished dependent from independent events using this language.
descriptors.endpoint: Students use the language of conditional probability correctly to describe and interpret situations involving dependent and independent events, using two-way tables, Venn diagrams, arrays and tree diagrams.

nodes.label: The language of conditional probability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can interpret statements using conditional probability language ('given', 'if...then', 'knowing that') and identify what information is being conditioned on.
criteria: Student correctly identifies the conditioning event and the outcome event in a conditional probability statement
Student distinguishes P(A|B) from P(B|A) and explains why they are not generally equal
nodes.hinge_reason: Confusion between P(A|B) and P(B|A) cascades into every subsequent node — students who cannot reliably distinguish the conditioning direction will set up wrong calculations in N2 and reach incorrect independence conclusions in N3.

width.minimum: Correctly interpret a conditional statement using 'given' or 'knowing that' in context; identify what event is the condition and what event is the outcome.
width.typical: Interpret all four conditional probability language forms ('if...then', 'given', 'of', 'knowing that') across multiple contexts; distinguish between 'P(A given B)' and 'P(B given A)'; identify common language errors in interpreting conditional statements.
wider: Investigate the 'prosecutor's fallacy' — confusing P(evidence | innocent) with P(innocent | evidence) — as a high-stakes real-world example of conditional language misinterpretation

Explore how natural language processing systems use conditional probability to predict the next word ('given the previous words, what comes next?') and connect the linguistic and mathematical uses of 'given'

modes.reason: Conditional probability language is a genuine hinge — confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A) is a systematic error with serious real-world consequences (medical testing, legal reasoning). Multiple context types, including reversed conditional statements, are essential to stabilise the distinction.

nodes.label: Representing conditional probability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use two-way tables, Venn diagrams and tree diagrams to represent situations involving conditional probability and read conditional probabilities from these representations.
criteria: Student correctly reads a conditional probability from a two-way table by restricting to the appropriate row or column
Student represents the same conditional probability situation using at least two different representations and verifies consistency
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot correctly restrict to the conditioning row/column in a two-way table will calculate unconditional rather than conditional probabilities — this error propagates directly into N3 independence testing, which depends on accurately computing P(A|B).

width.minimum: Read a conditional probability from a two-way table or Venn diagram; identify the relevant subset of the sample space defined by the condition.
width.typical: Represent conditional probability situations using two-way tables, Venn diagrams, arrays and tree diagrams; read conditional probabilities from each representation; move between representations of the same situation; verify that probabilities are consistent across representations.
wider: Investigate medical testing scenarios using two-way tables (sensitivity, specificity, false positive rate) and interpret conditional probabilities in terms of clinical decision-making
Explore how the same conditional probability problem appears very different depending on which representation is used, and discuss why some representations make conditional probability more intuitive

modes.reason: Reading conditional probabilities from a two-way table requires a systematic process: identify the conditioning row/column, restrict to that sub-total, then read the outcome frequency. Students who skip this restriction process get incorrect unconditional probabilities.

nodes.label: Dependent and independent events
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use conditional probability language and representations to determine whether two events are dependent or independent.
criteria: Student correctly determines whether two events are dependent or independent by comparing P(A|B) and P(A)
Student explains in plain language what it means for two events to be independent in terms of conditional probability

width.minimum: Calculate P(A|B) and P(A) for a given situation; determine whether the events are independent by checking whether conditioning on B changes the probability of A.
width.typical: Use arrays and tree diagrams to represent dependent and independent event probabilities; compare probabilities of dependent and independent events; identify whether conditioning changes the probability (dependent) or not (independent); connect independence to the language 'knowing that B has occurred does not change the probability of A'.
wider: Investigate how conditional probability is used in recommendation systems: 'given that a user watched X, what is the probability they will watch Y?' — and discuss whether the events are truly independent or dependent

Explore real-world cases where events that appear independent are actually dependent (e.g. disease co-occurrence, correlated financial risks) and discuss the consequences of incorrectly assuming independence

modes.reason: The distinction between dependent and independent events requires checking in multiple contexts — students who only practise with card draws may assume independence is rare. Varied contexts (medical, technological, financial) build reliable dependence-testing.

This node integrates conditional language (node 1) and representations (node 2) into the full concept of conditional probability: what it means for one event's probability to depend on another. It connects the linguistic, graphical and numerical aspects into coherent understanding.

descriptors.title: Simulate conditional probability
descriptors.description: design and conduct repeated chance experiments and simulations using digital tools to model conditional probability and interpret results
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe and interpret situations involving conditional probability using language, tables and diagrams (AC9M10P01). They have not yet designed and conducted simulations specifically for conditional probability or dependent event scenarios using digital tools.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design and conduct repeated chance experiments and simulations using digital tools to model conditional probability situations, and interpret simulated frequencies in relation to theoretical probabilities.

nodes.label: Designing simulations for conditional probability
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design a simulation to model a conditional probability situation, specifying how the conditioning will be implemented in the digital tool.
criteria: Student describes a simulation design that correctly encodes the conditional structure of the problem
Student implements the simulation in a digital tool and runs it for a sufficient number of trials

width.minimum: Describe the steps needed to simulate a conditional probability scenario (e.g. drawing without replacement); implement the simulation using a digital tool.
width.typical: Design simulations for dependent event scenarios (with and without replacement); implement using digital tools; identify how the conditioning condition is built into the simulation design; distinguish simulation design for dependent vs independent events.
wider: Investigate simulations for counter-intuitive problems (Monty Hall three-door problem, birthday problem) — design the simulation, run it, and use the results to explain why the intuitive answer is wrong
Design a simulation for a sampling-with-replacement vs without-replacement scenario at different sample sizes, investigating at what population-to-sample ratio the difference becomes negligible

modes.reason: Designing a simulation for conditional probability requires explicit reasoning about how dependency is encoded in the simulation steps. Students who design simulations mechanically without thinking through the dependency structure produce invalid results.

nodes.label: Interpreting simulated results
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare simulated frequencies to theoretical probabilities and explain why they differ for small samples but converge for large samples.
criteria: Student correctly compares a simulated frequency to the theoretical probability and describes the direction and size of the difference
Student explains that increasing sample size reduces the gap between simulated and theoretical probabilities

width.minimum: Compare the simulated frequency from a chance experiment to the theoretical probability; explain why they are not identical.
width.typical: Compare simulated and theoretical probabilities across multiple simulation runs and sample sizes; identify that larger samples produce closer approximations; quantify the convergence using relative frequency; explain why simulation results are not exact.
wider: Investigate how simulation is used to predict infection rates for flu or virus spread — run the simulation with different infection probability assumptions and discuss what the range of outputs means for public health planning
Explore how probability simulations are used in real-world decision-making (supply chain management, insurance pricing) and identify what assumptions are built into each simulation

modes.reason: Interpreting simulation results varies across context — comparing simulated and theoretical for a fair coin is different from interpreting disease spread simulations where theoretical probability is unknown. Multiple contexts build flexible interpretation.

nodes.label: Connecting simulation to real-world decision-making
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify a real-world situation where probability simulation supports decision-making and explain what the simulation contributes that theoretical analysis cannot.
criteria: Student describes a real decision-making context where simulation is used and explains what the simulation provides
Student identifies at least one assumption in the simulation and explains how changing it would affect the result

width.minimum: Describe one real situation where simulation is used for decision-making; explain what problem the simulation is solving.
width.typical: Identify at least two real contexts where probability simulation is used (supply/demand, insurance, disease modelling, queueing); explain what information the simulation provides; discuss what assumptions are built into the simulation and how those assumptions affect its reliability.
wider: Investigate the use of Monte Carlo simulation in finance or engineering and discuss how repeated random sampling builds an approximate probability distribution for an otherwise analytically intractable problem
Analyse a disease spread simulation (e.g. flu or virus infection rate modelling) and discuss the ethical responsibilities involved in communicating probabilistic predictions to the public

modes.reason: Connecting simulation to real-world decision-making integrates simulation design (node 1), result interpretation (node 2), and contextual understanding of why simulation is used. It is the node where probability simulation becomes a reasoning tool rather than a procedural exercise.

descriptors.title: Deductive reasoning and geometric proof
descriptors.description: apply deductive reasoning to proofs involving shapes in the plane and use theorems to solve spatial problems
descriptors.knowledge: Students can establish properties of quadrilaterals using congruent triangles and solve related problems (AC9M8SP02). They have not yet applied formal deductive reasoning to construct proofs — writing logically connected sequences of statements with explicit justification — or used theorems as starting points for solving new spatial problems.
descriptors.endpoint: Students apply deductive reasoning to construct proofs involving shapes in the plane and use geometric theorems to solve spatial problems.

nodes.label: Proof vs demonstration
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between a practical demonstration (showing a result is true in specific cases) and a mathematical proof (showing it must be true in all cases), and explain why the distinction matters.
criteria: Student correctly classifies a given geometric argument as a demonstration or a proof and explains the distinction
Student identifies at least one unstated assumption or generalisation step that would need to be made explicit in a rigorous proof
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not understand why a specific demonstration is insufficient cannot construct a valid proof in N2 — they will produce examples when asked for proofs, not recognising what a general argument requires.

width.minimum: Explain the difference between demonstrating that a result holds in a specific example and proving it holds in all cases; give one example of each for a geometric result.
width.typical: Distinguish proof from demonstration for at least two geometric results; explain why measuring angles in a specific triangle does not prove the angle sum property for all triangles; identify what makes a valid geometric proof (general argument, logical chain, no unstated assumptions).
