wider: Investigate historical cases where a result was widely believed true before a proof was found, and cases where apparent demonstrations turned out to be wrong — building appreciation for why proof matters
Explore how automated theorem provers (ATP) and interactive proof assistants (IPA) provide a formal framework for verifying proofs that is distinct from human demonstration

modes.reason: The proof vs demonstration distinction is conceptually non-trivial and frequently resisted by students who see measurement as sufficient. Explicit reasoning about why a general argument is needed — and what a general argument must include — is essential groundwork.

nodes.label: Constructing deductive proofs
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a deductive proof for a geometric result, writing a sequence of logically connected statements with explicit reasons at each step.
criteria: Student writes a valid geometric proof with each step explicitly justified
Student identifies and corrects an unjustified step when presented with an incomplete proof
nodes.hinge_reason: Proof construction fluency and a working theorem repertoire are both required for N3 — students cannot apply theorems to solve novel problems if they cannot yet deploy those theorems as justified reasons within a proof.

width.minimum: Write a proof for one geometric result (e.g. base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal) using a sequence of statements with stated reasons (given, definition, congruence test, angle property).
width.typical: Construct proofs involving congruent triangles, angle properties, and similarity; write proofs in clear logical sequences with explicit reasons; apply multiple geometric theorems within a single proof; identify when a proof is complete vs when a step is missing or unjustified.
wider: Investigate the proof that the base angles of an isosceles triangle are equal using multiple approaches (congruence, reflection symmetry, circle geometry) and compare what each approach illuminates
Use dynamic geometry software to investigate and then prove a less familiar result (e.g. the angle in a semicircle is 90°, or the perpendicular bisectors of a triangle are concurrent)

modes.reason: Proof writing is a skill that requires repeated practice — students who understand the concept of proof still need to develop fluency with the format (statement → reason chains) and the range of justifications available. Practice across multiple proof types is needed.

Students need a repertoire of geometric theorems and congruence criteria they can deploy as reasons within proofs. Building this repertoire across triangle and quadrilateral contexts is prerequisite for flexible proof construction.

nodes.label: Using theorems to solve spatial problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify which geometric theorem applies to a given spatial problem and use it as a basis for solving or proving a result.
criteria: Student correctly identifies a relevant geometric theorem for a given problem and uses it as a stated reason in the solution
Student solves a multi-step spatial problem requiring at least two distinct theorems

width.minimum: Identify a geometric theorem relevant to a spatial problem; apply it as a reason in solving for an unknown angle or length.
width.typical: Apply multiple geometric theorems to solve multi-step spatial problems involving angles, lengths and congruence; select appropriate theorems from a repertoire; combine similarity, congruence and angle properties in problem-solving; verify answers using logical consistency.
wider: Use dynamic geometry software to investigate the shortest path that touches three sides of a rectangle — formulate, investigate and prove that the path forms a parallelogram
Investigate how logical reasoning and similarity are used in numerical exercises that go beyond congruence (e.g. problems involving scale factors, trigonometric relationships, or circle geometry)

modes.reason: Applying theorems flexibly to novel problems requires exposure to varied problem types. Students who only practise theorem application in congruence contexts may not recognise when similarity or angle properties provide the key step in a new problem.

Using theorems to solve spatial problems integrates proof (node 2) with problem-solving: the ability to identify what is known, what theorem bridges the gap, and how to construct the argument. It is the culminating problem-solving mode of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Networks and network diagrams
descriptors.description: interpret networks and network diagrams used to represent relationships in practical situations and describe connectedness
descriptors.knowledge: Students can describe position and location in 3 dimensions using coordinate systems (AC9M8SP03). They have not yet encountered network diagrams as a mathematical representation of relationships, nor worked with concepts of connectedness, edges, vertices, or graph-theoretic properties.
descriptors.endpoint: Students interpret networks and network diagrams representing relationships in practical situations, describe connectedness, and apply Euler's formula to polyhedra represented as networks.

nodes.label: Network diagrams — structure and vocabulary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify the nodes and edges of a network diagram and explain what each represents in a given practical context.
criteria: Student correctly identifies nodes and edges in a network diagram and explains what each represents in context
Student describes connectedness — what it means for two nodes to be connected — in terms of the practical situation

width.minimum: Given a network diagram for a practical situation, identify the nodes (vertices) and edges; describe in plain language what each represents in the context.
width.typical: Interpret network diagrams for at least three different practical contexts (transport, social, ecological, technological); identify nodes and edges; describe what connectedness means in each context; distinguish directed from undirected networks where relevant.
wider: Represent First Nations Australians' kinship systems using network diagrams and explore the significance of the relationships to Country/Place encoded in the network

Investigate how a home network (LAN), social network, or electrical wiring network can be represented as a network diagram and use it to identify practical issues (e.g. single points of failure, router placement)

modes.reason: Network diagrams look structurally similar across contexts but encode very different relationships. Students who only interpret one type of network (e.g. transport) may not recognise that kinship systems, food webs and computer networks use the same mathematical object. Multiple contexts build generalised network thinking.

nodes.label: Analysing connectedness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can analyse the connectedness of a network, identifying connected components, paths, and constraints such as traversability.
criteria: Student correctly determines whether a given network is connected and justifies the answer
Student traces a valid path between two specified nodes in a network diagram

width.minimum: Determine whether a given network is connected (all nodes reachable from any starting node); identify a path between two specified nodes.
width.typical: Analyse connectedness in practical network contexts; identify connected vs disconnected networks; trace paths between nodes; investigate the Königsberg bridge problem as a classical example of traversability (Eulerian path); identify whether a network has an Eulerian path based on vertex degree.
wider: Investigate food web networks — identify producers, consumers and decomposers as node types; analyse what happens to the network if a key node is removed
Explore metabolic networks or other biological/chemical structures as graph representations and discuss what network properties reveal about the system

modes.reason: The Königsberg bridge problem and Eulerian path reasoning require systematic thinking about vertex degree — students need the odd-degree criterion explained, not just demonstrated. Explicit scaffolding of the reasoning prevents trial-and-error approaches.

nodes.label: Polyhedra as networks and Euler's formula
nodes.checkpoint: Students can represent a polyhedron as a network diagram and verify Euler's formula F + V = E + 2.
criteria: Student correctly draws the network representation of a given polyhedron
Student verifies Euler's formula by correctly counting faces, vertices and edges

width.minimum: Draw the network representation of a simple polyhedron (e.g. cube, tetrahedron); count faces, vertices and edges; verify F + V = E + 2.
width.typical: Represent multiple polyhedra as network diagrams; verify Euler's formula for each; identify exterior and interior faces in the network representation; explain why the formula holds as a topological property rather than a geometric coincidence.
wider: Investigate how Euler's formula connects to planar graph theory and discuss which graphs can be drawn without edge crossings
Explore polyhedra with 'holes' (toruses) and investigate how Euler's formula changes for different topological structures

modes.reason: Representing polyhedra as networks integrates 3D spatial knowledge with graph theory — students must translate between a geometric object and its topological network representation. This is the cross-domain integration point of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Algorithms for spatial problems
descriptors.description: design, test and refine solutions to spatial problems using algorithms and digital tools; communicate and justify solutions
descriptors.knowledge: Students can design, test and refine algorithms based on geometric constructions and theorems (AC9M9SP03). They have not yet applied this capability to the full range of spatial problem types at Y10 — scale models, floor plan optimisation, network routing, and self-similar patterns — or communicated and justified solutions at this level.
descriptors.endpoint: Students design, test and refine algorithmic solutions to spatial problems using digital tools, and communicate and justify their solutions.

nodes.label: Defining and decomposing spatial problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can precisely define a spatial problem and decompose it into sub-problems suitable for algorithmic solution.
criteria: Student states a spatial problem with precise inputs, constraints and success criteria
Student identifies at least two sub-problems and explains how they combine to solve the full problem
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot precisely define a spatial problem before designing an algorithm produce solutions that do not match the actual constraints — N2 algorithm design and N3 testing are both invalidated by an underspecified problem definition.

width.minimum: Define a spatial problem in precise terms (specifying inputs, constraints, and desired output); identify at least two sub-problems that together constitute the full problem.
width.typical: Define and decompose spatial problems across different types (floor plan optimisation, network routing, scale model design); identify which decomposition makes the problem most tractable; specify all constraints and success criteria before designing the algorithm.
wider: Explore how geospatial technologies used by First Nations Australians' communities decompose spatial problems of position and transformation — and compare these problem-solving approaches to computational decomposition methods
Investigate how floor plan problems (e.g. minimising congestion at key areas in a department store) can be formally specified as optimisation problems with defined constraints

modes.reason: Problem decomposition requires systematic thinking — students who jump to algorithm design before the problem is precisely defined frequently produce solutions that do not match the actual constraints. Explicit problem specification before algorithm design needs scaffolding.

nodes.label: Designing algorithms for spatial problems
nodes.checkpoint: Students can design an algorithm (using pseudocode or flowchart) that addresses a defined spatial problem.
criteria: Student produces pseudocode or a flowchart that is unambiguous and complete for the defined spatial problem
Student identifies decision points and loops in the algorithm and explains their role

width.minimum: Write pseudocode or a flowchart for an algorithm that solves a defined spatial problem; the algorithm must specify all steps clearly enough that another person could follow it.
width.typical: Design algorithms for spatial problems across at least two different types (e.g. scale model generation and network routing); express algorithms in pseudocode or flowchart; identify decision points and loops; evaluate the algorithm's completeness before testing.
wider: Design algorithms for producing self-similar (fractal) patterns using recursive pseudocode; trace the algorithm for at least two iterations to verify the pattern
Investigate how computational thinking approaches to weighted network problems (shortest path, minimum spanning tree) can be expressed as algorithms and test them on small networks

modes.reason: Students need experience designing algorithms for multiple spatial problem types — the algorithm structures for scale model generation, floor plan optimisation and network routing are different. A repertoire of problem-type-to-algorithm-structure mappings is the goal.

nodes.label: Testing, refining and justifying
nodes.checkpoint: Students can test an algorithm against multiple cases, identify and fix failures, and communicate why the refined solution addresses the problem.
criteria: Student tests the algorithm against at least two cases and correctly identifies a failure case
Student describes a specific refinement and explains how it addresses the identified failure
Student communicates the solution and justification clearly to a specified audience

width.minimum: Test an algorithm against at least two different input cases; identify one case where it fails or produces unexpected output; describe a refinement to address the failure.
width.typical: Test algorithms against a range of cases including edge cases; systematically identify failure modes; refine the algorithm to address failures; validate the refined version; communicate the solution and justification in clear terms appropriate for the audience.
wider: Investigate how geospatial technologies used by First Nations Australians' communities address spatial problems of position and transformation — considering how these established methods relate to computational verification
Apply the testing process to a self-similar pattern algorithm — validate against multiple iteration depths and compare the algorithmic output to a geometric description of the pattern

modes.reason: Testing and refinement takes very different forms across problem types — testing a floor plan algorithm requires spatial visualisation, testing a network routing algorithm requires tracing paths, testing a fractal algorithm requires iteration tracing. Multiple problem types build the generalised testing mindset.

Testing and justification integrates problem decomposition (node 1), algorithm design (node 2) and communication into the complete design cycle. It is the node where algorithmic thinking becomes a full engineering practice.

descriptors.title: Critique statistical reports
descriptors.description: analyse claims, inferences and conclusions of statistical reports in the media, including ethical considerations and identification of potential sources of bias
descriptors.knowledge: Students can choose and justify appropriate data displays for given contexts (AC9M9ST04). They have not yet systematically analysed statistical claims in media for bias, misleading representations, or ethical considerations — moving from producing displays to critically reading others' statistical arguments.
descriptors.endpoint: Students analyse statistical claims, inferences and conclusions in media reports, identifying misleading representations, potential sources of bias, and ethical considerations.

nodes.label: Identifying misleading representations
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify specific features of a statistical graph or claim that could mislead a reader and explain the mechanism by which the misleading effect works.
criteria: Student identifies a specific misleading feature in a given statistical representation and names it accurately
Student explains the mechanism — how the feature creates a false impression — not just that it exists

width.minimum: Identify at least one specific misleading feature in a given statistical graph or report (e.g. truncated axis, non-zero baseline, cherry-picked time period) and explain how it creates a false impression.
width.typical: Identify multiple types of misleading features across several statistical representations; explain the mechanism for each (how the visual or numerical choice distorts the impression); distinguish between deliberate misleading and ambiguity; recognise when data is not related to the claim being made.
wider: Analyse how the identification of bias is critical in machine learning and deep learning — because biased training data produces systematically unfair or inaccurate AI outputs — connecting statistical critique to contemporary technology

Use the concept of Indigenous data sovereignty to critique and evaluate the Australian Government's 'Closing the Gap' report — examining whose data is collected, how it is framed, and what claims are made

modes.reason: Misleading representations take many forms — broken axes, cherry-picked endpoints, inappropriate scale choices, correlation presented as causation. Students who only practise with broken axes may not recognise other manipulation types. Multiple examples across different misleading techniques are needed.

nodes.label: Evaluating samples and representativeness
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate whether a sample described in a statistical report is likely to be representative of the claimed population.
criteria: Student identifies the sample source and size in a described study
Student gives a specific reason why the sample is or is not likely to be representative of the population

width.minimum: Identify the source and approximate size of a sample in a report; state whether it is likely to be representative of the described population and why.
width.typical: Evaluate sample representativeness across multiple report types; identify sampling bias (self-selection, convenience, non-response); explain how non-representative samples invalidate inferences to the population; connect sample size to reliability of estimates.
wider: Investigate population rates and ethical considerations when presenting statistical data involving infection rates — examining how 'per head of population' framing affects interpretation and what ethical responsibilities reporters have
Use secondary data to predict rates of a health event (e.g. side effects, infection) and discuss the ethical considerations of reporting such predictions to the public

modes.reason: Sample evaluation applies very differently across study types — voluntary surveys, government data collections, medical studies, and social media polls all have different bias mechanisms. Multiple sample contexts are needed to build generalised representativeness reasoning.

nodes.label: Ethical considerations in statistical reporting
nodes.checkpoint: Students can identify ethical considerations in statistical reporting and explain how ethical or political motivations can influence how data is collected, framed, or presented.
criteria: Student identifies at least one ethical consideration in a statistical report that goes beyond technical accuracy
Student explains how an ethical or political framing has shaped a statistical claim or its presentation

width.minimum: Identify at least one ethical consideration in a described statistical report (e.g. who collected the data, who benefits from the conclusion, whose perspective is absent).
width.typical: Identify multiple ethical considerations across different statistical reports; explain how ethical or political framing shapes data collection, display choice, and conclusion drawing; distinguish between statistical error and deliberate misrepresentation; evaluate statistical claims in terms of both technical accuracy and ethical transparency.
wider: Investigate how the concept of Indigenous data sovereignty challenges conventional approaches to government-collected data about First Nations Australians — examining who has the right to collect, use and interpret data about a community

Analyse a specific case of statistical reporting in public health or environmental policy and evaluate the ethical responsibilities of researchers, media and government in communicating uncertainty and risk

modes.reason: Ethical analysis of statistical reporting is a genuine hinge — students need to move beyond 'this graph is misleading' to understanding how statistical choices encode values and power. Multiple context types (health, government, AI) build this more complex critical lens.

Ethical critique integrates technical accuracy analysis (node 1), sample evaluation (node 2), and value judgements about who is served by a statistical claim. It is where statistical literacy becomes critical literacy.

descriptors.title: Boxplots and continuous distributions
descriptors.description: compare data distributions for continuous numerical variables using appropriate data displays including boxplots; discuss the shapes of these distributions in terms of centre, spread, shape and outliers in the context of the data
descriptors.knowledge: Students can analyse statistical claims in media including ethical considerations and sources of bias (AC9M10ST01). They have not yet constructed or interpreted boxplots, calculated five-number summaries, or compared continuous distributions by shape.
descriptors.endpoint: Students compare data distributions for continuous numerical variables using boxplots and other displays, discussing centre, spread, shape and outliers in context.

nodes.label: Five-number summary
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate the five-number summary for a data set and explain what each value represents.
criteria: Student correctly calculates all five values of the five-number summary
Student explains what each value represents (not just its name)
nodes.hinge_reason: Quartile calculation errors propagate directly into N2 — an incorrect five-number summary produces an incorrectly drawn boxplot, making the entire graphical representation misleading.

width.minimum: Calculate minimum, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and maximum for a given data set; state what each of the five values represents.
width.typical: Calculate five-number summaries for multiple data sets; distinguish between median and mean as measures of centre; calculate IQR; identify the quartile boundaries as the values that divide the data into four equal groups.
wider: Investigate different conventions for calculating quartiles (inclusive vs exclusive median methods) and compare results on the same data set
Explore how the five-number summary connects to the concept of percentiles more generally — Q1 is the 25th percentile, Q3 is the 75th percentile

modes.reason: Quartile calculation errors (especially confusion about whether to include or exclude the median when finding Q1 and Q3) are systematic. Fluency with the calculation procedure needs practice before interpretation work.

nodes.label: Constructing and interpreting boxplots
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a boxplot from a five-number summary and interpret the key features in the context of the data.
criteria: Student correctly constructs a boxplot from a five-number summary with accurate scale and labelling
Student correctly identifies the median, IQR and any outliers from a given boxplot
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who misread boxplot features (interpreting box width as frequency, misidentifying the median position) cannot make valid distribution comparisons in N3 — the comparison task depends on correctly reading the features being compared.

width.minimum: Draw a boxplot from a given five-number summary; identify and label the five key positions; describe what the box and whiskers represent.
width.typical: Construct boxplots from raw data sets; interpret box width (IQR as spread measure), whisker length, and outlier positions; describe distributions in terms of centre and spread using boxplot features; identify outliers using the 1.5 × IQR rule; connect the visual representation to the five-number summary.
wider: Investigate how the identification and handling of outliers is a critical step in machine learning — comparing statistical outlier detection criteria to how data scientists decide whether to include or exclude outliers from model training
Explore how boxplots are used in scientific research to compare experimental vs control group distributions and identify practically significant differences

modes.reason: Students frequently misread boxplots — interpreting box width as frequency rather than spread, or misidentifying the median position. Explicit reasoning about what each feature encodes is essential before comparison work.

nodes.label: Comparing distributions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can compare two or more distributions using boxplots, describing similarities and differences in centre, spread, shape and outliers in context.
criteria: Student compares two distributions using boxplots, commenting on centre, spread, shape and outliers with context-appropriate language
Student explains what the distributional difference reveals about the underlying context

width.minimum: Compare two distributions using side-by-side boxplots; describe at least two differences in terms of centre and spread using context-appropriate language.
width.typical: Compare multiple distributions using boxplots and other displays (histograms, dot plots, cumulative frequency graphs); describe shape (symmetry, skew, modality); discuss what the shape reveals about the data-generating process; use digital tools to explore different display types for the same data; evaluate which display best addresses a given question.
wider: Compare the distribution shapes of the same variable across different subgroups (e.g. performance across different schools, biological measurements across different species) and discuss what the comparison reveals
Investigate how the same data appears very different on different display types (boxplot, histogram, dot plot) and evaluate which display answers a given statistical question most effectively

modes.reason: Describing distribution shape (symmetric, skewed, bimodal) requires seeing these shapes in varied contexts — biological data is often right-skewed, social data often bimodal. Multiple data contexts build the shape-recognition vocabulary and connect shape to real-world phenomena.

Distribution comparison integrates five-number summary knowledge (node 1), boxplot construction and reading (node 2), and contextual interpretation into the full statistical comparison act. It is the endpoint of this descriptor's learning progression.

descriptors.title: Scatterplots and association
descriptors.description: construct scatterplots and comment on the association between the 2 numerical variables in terms of strength, direction and linearity
descriptors.knowledge: Students can compare continuous distributions using boxplots discussing centre, spread, shape and outliers (AC9M10ST02). They have not yet constructed scatterplots or described association between two numerical variables in terms of strength, direction and linearity.
descriptors.endpoint: Students construct scatterplots and comment on the association between two numerical variables in terms of strength, direction and linearity.

nodes.label: Constructing and reading scatterplots
nodes.checkpoint: Students can construct a scatterplot from a bivariate data set and read individual data points accurately.
criteria: Student correctly plots a set of bivariate data points on labelled axes with appropriate scale
Student can read the approximate coordinates of a specified point from the scatterplot

width.minimum: Plot a set of (x, y) data points on correctly labelled axes; read the approximate coordinates of plotted points.
width.typical: Construct scatterplots from data sets in multiple contexts; choose appropriate scales and axis labels; identify the explanatory and response variable; use digital tools to construct and explore scatterplots.
wider: Investigate the relationship between two variables of spear throwers used by First Peoples of Australia using real data — construct the scatterplot and describe the initial visual impression before analysis
Explore how scatter plots are used by data scientists to gain insights into data and as a first step in feature engineering for machine learning

modes.reason: Accurate plotting — correct axis labelling, appropriate scale, point placement — is foundational for all subsequent interpretation work. Errors here undermine N2 association description and N3 causation reasoning.

nodes.label: Describing association
nodes.checkpoint: Students can describe the association between two variables in terms of strength (strong, moderate, weak), direction (positive, negative, none) and linearity (linear, non-linear).
criteria: Student correctly describes a scatterplot's association using strength, direction and linearity with appropriate vocabulary
Student explains what the direction of association means in the specific context of the data

width.minimum: Describe the association shown in a given scatterplot using strength, direction and linearity vocabulary.
width.typical: Describe association across multiple scatterplots in varied contexts; use precise vocabulary (strong positive linear, weak negative, no association, non-linear); explain what positive and negative association means in context; use a line of good fit by eye to assess linearity informally.
wider: Investigate AI systems that analyse bivariate data to forecast or make predictions using correlation analysis — discussing limitations including inability to capture causality or account for contextual factors
Explore how the same data can appear to show different associations depending on scale choices, and discuss how this connects to the misleading representations work of AC9M10ST01

modes.reason: Association description vocabulary (strength, direction, linearity) needs to be applied across varied contexts for it to become reliable. Students who only describe association in one domain (e.g. physical science data) may lack the language flexibility for social, biological or economic scatterplots.

nodes.label: Association vs causation
nodes.checkpoint: Students can distinguish between association and causation and give examples of associated variables that are not causally related.
criteria: Student correctly explains the distinction between association and causation
Student gives a plausible alternative explanation (e.g. confounding variable or common cause) for a described association

width.minimum: State the distinction between association and causation; give one example of two variables that are associated but where causation is not established.
width.typical: Explain why association does not imply causation; identify confounding variables that might explain an association; discuss multiple plausible explanations for an observed association (direct causation, reverse causation, common cause, coincidence); apply this reasoning to contexts such as health, climate and social media.
wider: Investigate the relationship between two variables of spear throwers used by First Peoples of Australia — construct and describe the scatterplot, make comparisons and draw conclusions within the limits of the data

Analyse a specific claimed association in the media (e.g. social media use and wellbeing, climate variables) using statistical evidence — making, justifying and critiquing claims about association vs causation

modes.reason: Association vs causation is a genuine conceptual hinge — students who understand it in one context frequently revert to causal language in new contexts. Multiple examples from health, social science, climate and technology are needed to stabilise the distinction.

The causation discussion integrates scatterplot construction (node 1), association description (node 2), and statistical reasoning about evidence into the full critical analysis of bivariate relationships. It is the endpoint of this descriptor's learning progression.

descriptors.title: Two-way tables and categorical relationships
descriptors.description: construct two-way tables and discuss possible relationship between categorical variables
descriptors.knowledge: Students can construct scatterplots and describe association in terms of strength, direction and linearity (AC9M10ST03). They have not yet used two-way tables specifically to investigate relationships between categorical variables — this extends bivariate analysis from numerical to categorical data.
descriptors.endpoint: Students construct two-way tables from categorical data sets and discuss possible relationships between categorical variables using frequencies and proportions.

nodes.label: Constructing two-way tables
nodes.checkpoint: Students can organise categorical bivariate data into a two-way table with correct row and column structure.
criteria: Student correctly constructs a two-way table with accurate cell counts and marginal totals
Student labels rows and columns to correctly identify which variable is in which dimension

width.minimum: Given a data set with two categorical variables, construct a two-way frequency table with appropriate row and column labels and correct cell counts.
width.typical: Construct two-way tables from raw data for multiple context types (survey data, observational data, experimental data); calculate row totals, column totals and grand total; verify accuracy by checking that margins sum correctly.
wider: Investigate a litter survey context — collect data on two categorical variables (e.g. type of litter and day of week) and construct a two-way table, explaining what the row and column structure reveals
Explore how two-way frequency tables are used in medical research and public health to organise data from observational studies

modes.reason: Tally and tabulation errors (double-counting, miscounting) are common. Fluency with accurate data organisation needs practice before proportional analysis.

nodes.label: Using proportions to identify patterns
nodes.checkpoint: Students can calculate row or column proportions (or percentages) from a two-way table and use them to identify patterns across categories.
criteria: Student calculates row or column proportions correctly for a given two-way table
Student explains why proportions are more useful than raw counts for comparing categories of different sizes
nodes.hinge_reason: Using the wrong conditional direction (row vs column proportions) in N2 produces a fundamentally incorrect reading of the two-way table — N3 discussion of possible relationships is invalidated if the proportional comparison is pointed the wrong way.

width.minimum: Calculate row or column percentages for a given two-way table; identify one pattern suggested by comparing proportions across categories.
width.typical: Calculate and interpret row proportions and column proportions for a two-way table; explain why proportions are more informative than raw counts when row/column sizes differ; identify patterns and associations by comparing conditional distributions across categories.
wider: Investigate survey responses using five-point Likert scales across two categories of respondents (e.g. junior vs senior students); use proportions to compare response patterns and discuss what the comparison reveals
Explore how two-way tables connect to conditional probability — P(response | group) is the conditional distribution, linking statistics to the probability work in AC9M10P01

modes.reason: Deciding whether to use row or column proportions requires explicit reasoning about which variable is being conditioned on. Students frequently use the wrong conditional direction — a systematic process for deciding is needed.

nodes.label: Discussing possible relationships
nodes.checkpoint: Students can use proportional patterns in a two-way table to make a defensible claim about a possible relationship between two categorical variables, using appropriate hedging language.
criteria: Student makes a claim about a possible relationship supported by proportional evidence from the table
Student uses hedging language that correctly reflects the strength of the evidence

width.minimum: Identify a pattern in a two-way table's proportions and state whether it suggests a possible relationship between the two variables, using appropriate language ('suggests', 'appears to').
width.typical: Discuss possible relationships between categorical variables using proportional evidence from two-way tables; use hedging language ('possible relationship', 'the data suggests'); acknowledge alternative explanations; discuss what additional data would strengthen or weaken the inference.
wider: Conduct a school-based litter survey collecting two categorical variables; construct the two-way table, calculate proportions and write a report discussing whether the data suggests a relationship — acknowledging limitations
Analyse a published two-way table from a public health or social context; evaluate the strength of the claimed relationship and identify what the table cannot tell us

modes.reason: The rhetorical skill of making a defensible but appropriately hedged statistical claim varies across context — the language appropriate for a school litter survey is different from medical research. Multiple context types build appropriate calibration of claim strength.

Discussing relationships integrates table construction (node 1), proportion calculation (node 2), and statistical reasoning about evidence strength into the full analysis act. This is the endpoint of the descriptor.

descriptors.title: Statistical investigations with bivariate data
descriptors.description: plan and conduct statistical investigations of situations that involve bivariate data; evaluate and report findings with consideration of limitations of any inferences
descriptors.knowledge: Students can plan and conduct statistical investigations and discuss strength of evidence for conclusions (AC9M9ST05). They have not yet conducted investigations specifically involving bivariate data, or evaluated the limitations of inferences including interpolation/extrapolation limits and data validity considerations at this level.
descriptors.endpoint: Students plan and conduct statistical investigations involving bivariate data, evaluating and reporting findings with explicit consideration of the limitations of any inferences drawn.

nodes.label: Formulating bivariate investigation questions
nodes.checkpoint: Students can formulate a statistical investigation question that specifies two variables whose relationship will be investigated.
criteria: Student writes an investigation question that clearly specifies two variables and their possible relationship
Student identifies the explanatory and response variable for the question
nodes.hinge_reason: A vague or poorly specified investigation question cascades through N2 and N3 — data collection (N2) lacks direction, and findings evaluation (N3) cannot be meaningfully scoped to limitations if the original question was ill-defined.

width.minimum: Write a statistical question that specifies two variables and a claim about their possible relationship that can be investigated with data.
width.typical: Formulate statistical investigation questions for bivariate data in multiple contexts (observational, experimental, secondary data); identify the explanatory and response variable; specify how the data will be collected (observation, experiment, measurement, secondary source); identify what constitutes an adequate sample.
wider: Investigate anecdotal claims about bivariate relationships (e.g. 'social media use is linked to wellbeing', 'housing affordability is related to income') and evaluate whether the claim is appropriately formulated as an investigation question
Design a bivariate investigation to address the question 'Is there a relationship between vaccines and immunity?' — specifying variables, data collection method and sample

modes.reason: Formulating a well-defined bivariate investigation question requires deliberate reasoning about variable specification, directionality and testability. Students frequently produce questions that are too vague or confound multiple variables. Explicit scaffolding of question formation is needed.

nodes.label: Collecting, displaying and describing bivariate data
nodes.checkpoint: Students can collect or access bivariate data, display it using an appropriate graph, and describe the initial visual pattern.
criteria: Student produces an appropriate display for the bivariate data collected
Student describes the initial pattern using association vocabulary appropriate to the data type

width.minimum: Collect or access a bivariate data set; display it in a scatterplot or two-way table as appropriate; describe the initial visual pattern using association vocabulary.
width.typical: Collect bivariate data through observation, experiment or secondary sources; display using appropriate graphs (scatterplot for numerical, two-way table for categorical); describe association in terms of strength, direction and linearity; identify potential outliers or unusual features in the display.
wider: Investigate biodiversity changes in Australia before and after colonisation by comparing relevant bivariate data sets; discuss data provenance and how the historical context affects interpretation
Access and use secondary data sets for a real bivariate investigation (e.g. climate data, health data, ecological data) and evaluate the quality and representativeness of the data

modes.reason: Data collection for bivariate investigations varies substantially across methods — observational, experimental, and secondary source data each involve different quality considerations and display choices. Multiple collection types build flexible data handling.

nodes.label: Evaluating and reporting findings
nodes.checkpoint: Students can evaluate the strength of their statistical findings and report conclusions with explicit acknowledgement of limitations, including interpolation/extrapolation limits and data validity.
criteria: Student states a conclusion that is supported by the data and uses appropriate hedging language
Student identifies at least two limitations of the inference and explains why each is relevant
Student communicates findings clearly for a specified audience

width.minimum: State a conclusion supported by the data; identify at least one limitation of the inference (e.g. sample size, data validity, interpolation/extrapolation).
width.typical: Report statistical findings using appropriate inferential language (hedged claims, strength-of-evidence statements); evaluate data validity; identify interpolation and extrapolation limits; acknowledge alternative explanations; discuss what further investigation would be needed to strengthen the conclusion; communicate findings for a specified audience.
wider: Investigate biodiversity changes in Australia before and after colonisation by comparing related bivariate data; discuss and report on associations with consideration of data provenance, historical framing and the limitations of available data

Conduct a full bivariate statistical investigation of a real anecdotal claim (e.g. about climate, housing, or natural resources), reporting findings to a specified audience with explicit discussion of what the data can and cannot establish

modes.reason: The limitations of bivariate inferences vary substantially across investigation types — interpolation limits matter more for regression contexts, data validity matters more for observational studies, sample representativeness matters more for surveys. Multiple context types build comprehensive evaluation.

Evaluating and reporting findings integrates question formulation (node 1), data display and description (node 2), and critical evaluation of evidence into the full statistical investigation cycle. It is the capability endpoint of the descriptor.
